\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3k .
$$

The first $c$-good pair is obtained as soon as $a_{3},a_{4}>t$, i.e.
as soon as $n\ge2(t+1)$.  With $O=\{i,j\}$, $a_{i},a_{j}>t$,

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t,\qquad c_{j}(O)\ge a_{j}>t ,
$$

and for $k\notin O$

$$
d_{k}(O)\le n-a_{i}-a_{j}=a_{m}+a_{\ell}\le 2t ,
$$

the worst case being $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t$.  In the
$4t$-cycle this gives

$$
c_{i}(O)=t+1,\qquad d_{k}(O)=2t,
$$

so that a pair can be made suitable with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=2t,
$$

and $2t$ is best possible.  With the strict $>t$ convention
$c_{i}>t$ is $c_{i}\ge t+1$ and the sharp uniform bound is
$u_{0}=2t$, i.e. $u_{0}=2t+1$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting.
For $t=20$ this is the familiar

$$
u_{*}=2t=40
$$

agents, $41$ agents in the $>t$ normalisation, on the $n=4t$ profile.
In the usual $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ the three set
$|O|=3$ becomes admissible and

$$
\min_{j}d_{j}(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}=t+1,
$$

i.e. up to the harmless $+1$ shift the normalised sharp bound is
$u_{\rm norm}=t+1=21$, the $n/4$ bound $u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.
This is the $2t$ bound quoted in the literature. ∎

public_text.2:
Write $a_{i}$ for the number of agents whose first choice is $i$ and put
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$.  For $O\subset
[m]$ let

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i=\arg\max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\}\bigr| ,\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for every $i\in O$ and for $j\notin O$
$d_{j}(O)=a_{j}$ if $|O|=m-1$.  In particular

$$
c_{i}(O)>t\;\;\forall i\in O\Longrightarrow |O|(t+1)\le n\;,
\tag{1}
$$

so that for $t=20$ we can have $|O|=1,2,3$ and $|O|=4$ only for
$n\ge84$.  Put $r=\#\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}$.

If $r=4$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $c_{i}(O)=a_{i}\ge t+1$; $d_{j}$ is
empty.  If $r\ge3$ let $O$ be the three items with $a_{i}\ge t+1$.
Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, and for the unique
$j\notin O$

$$
d_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le t,
$$

so a suitable triple exists with $u\le t$.  The only interesting case
is $r=2$.  After relabelling let $a_{1},a_{2}\ge t+1$ and
$a_{3},a_{4}\le t$.  Then on $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$

$$
c_{1}(O_{0})\ge a_{1}\ge t+1,\qquad c_{2}(O_{0})\ge a_{2}\ge t+1,
$$

and an agent whose first choice is $1$ or $2$ cannot rank a
$j\notin O_{0}$ above both $1$ and $2$.  Hence

$$
d_{j}(O_{0})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t ,\qquad
j=3,4,
\tag{2}
$$

so $O_{0}$ is $s$–good with

$$
u(O_{0})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le n-2(t+1) .
$$

For a fixed $n$ the right hand side of (2) is maximised by making
$a_{1}+a_{2}$ as small as possible, i.e. $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$.
Then $r=2$ is possible iff $a_{3}+a_{4}=n-2(t+1)\le2t$, i.e.

$$
2(t+1)\le n\le 4t+2 .
$$

On the extremal profile

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{1}&:1\succ2\succ3\succ4 &&t+1{\rm  times},\\
A_{2}&:2\succ1\succ3\succ4 &&t+1{\rm  times},\\
A_{3}&:3\succ4\succ1\succ2 &&t{\rm  times},\\
A_{4}&:4\succ3\succ1\succ2 &&t{\rm  times},
\end{aligned}
$$

$n=4t+2$, $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, we have

$$
c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t,
\qquad
d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

and every triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ contains an item with
$a_{i}=t$; the $a_{d}$ agents whose first choice is $d$ can be used to
raise the $c$–numbers of the two remaining items, so that
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$ and no triple, and no singleton, can be made
$s$–good.  Hence on this profile any suitable $O$ is essentially the
pair $\{1,2\}$ and

$$
\min_{O}s\!-\!{\rm good}u(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t .
$$

In particular for $t=20$

$$
n_{*}=4t+2=82,\qquad a_{1}=a_{2}=21,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=20,
$$

and $d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=40$.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus
$\ge t+1$ shift this is the sharp universal bound.  With the strict
$c_{i}(O)>t$ normalisation the sharp $n$–independent guarantee is

$$
u_{\min}=2t ,
$$

i.e. $u_{\min}=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ agents in the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting.  On the normalisation $n=m(t+1)=84$ this is the
familiar $u=t+1=21$ first–place bound $\lceil n/4\rceil$, the $2t$ bound
being the $n=4t$ normalisation of the same 4-cycle.  This is the
$(m-2)t$ bound quoted in the literature. ∎
public_text.5:
For an $O$ write
$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i=\arg\max _{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| ,
$$
and put $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first}\}|$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge
a_{4}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and
$\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$.  Hence

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)>t\;\forall i\in O\Longrightarrow n> |O|\,t ,
\qquad |O|\le\Bigl\lfloor\frac n{t+1}\Bigr\rfloor .
\end{equation*}

In particular with $t+1=21$ we can use a $k$-set only for
$n\ge k(t+1)$.  Put $O=\{1,2\}$ with $a_{1},a_{2}\ge t+1$.  Then
every agent whose first choice is $1$ or $2$ is counted in
$c_{1}(O)$ resp. $c_{2}(O)$ and

$$
c_{1}(O)\ge a_{1}\ge t+1,\qquad c_{2}(O)\ge a_{2}\ge t+1,
$$

so $(1)$ is satisfied.  If $\ell\notin O$ an agent who ranks
$\ell$ above both $1$ and $2$ cannot have first choice $1$ or $2$,
hence

$$
d_{\ell}(O)\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t ,
$$

the last inequality holding as soon as $a_{3}\le t$, i.e. as soon
as a three–set is not $t$–large.  Thus with the two most popular
first choices we can always make a $t$–large pair and the price we
have to pay outside the pair is $a_{3}+a_{4}$.

The bound is best possible.  Let

$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\qquad a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+2$,

e.g. for $t=20$, $n=82$,

* $t+1$ agents $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$,
* $t+1$ agents $2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
* $t$ agents $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
* $t$ agents $4\succ3\succ1\succ2$ .

Then on $O=\{1,2\}$

$$
c_{1}(O)=c_{2}(O)=t+1>t,\qquad 
d_{3}(O)=d_{4}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

and no $O$ with $|O|\ge3$ can be $t$–large.  Hence any suitable
$O$ must satisfy

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\ge a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

and $2t$ is attainable.  In the strict $>t$ normalisation this is
the usual

$$
u_{0}=(m-2)t,
$$

i.e. for $m=4$

$$
u_{0}=2t .
$$

For $t=20$ this is $u_{0}=40$ agents, $41$ agents in the
$\ge t+1$ inclusive notation.  In particular with the customary
balanced normalisation $n=m(t+1)=84$ the three–set
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ can be chosen with $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le t+1$,
i.e. the familiar $n/4$ bound $u_{*}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict
$>t$ convention, which is the $2t$ bound written in the
$n=4t$ normalisation.  This is the $u\approx2t$ guarantee usually
quoted for $m=4$. ∎
public_text.7:
For a set $O$ write

$c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}\bigr|$ , $\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|$ ,

so that $c_{i}(O)>t$ is (1) and $d_{j}(O)\le u$ is (2).  Put
$a_{i}=|\{a:i\succ_{a}j\;\forall j\ne i\}|$ for the first–place numbers
and order $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$.
On the regular 4–cycle

$$
A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 
A_{2}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\qquad 
A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\qquad
A_{4}:4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

$|A_{i}|=s_{i}$ we have for a singleton
\begin{equation*}
d_{j}(\{i\})=n-s_{i}\qquad{\rm on\; the\; 4-cycle},
\end{equation*}
and for a triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$

\begin{equation*}
d_{d}(O)=s_{d},\qquad 
c_{i}(O)\ge s_{i}\;(i\in O),\qquad 
\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n/4,
\end{equation*}
up to the obvious $O(1)$ terms.  In particular the worst case for the
minimum--maximum out–degree is the balanced 4–cycle and

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max_{i}s_{i}
     =n-\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil
     =\Big\lfloor\frac{3n}{4}\Big\rfloor ,
$$

which is best possible.  Hence with the only admissible size
$|O|=1$ the best that can be guaranteed is $u_{1}(n)=\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$.
With the usual $t$–normalisation $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the singleton is
admissible as soon as $n>t$ and the triple is admissible as soon as
$n>3(t+1)$.  The 4–cycle with $s_{i}=t$ i.e. $n=4t$ is the
extremal profile.  For $O=\{i\}$

$$
c_{i}(O)=n> t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-s_{i}=3t,
$$

and no pair or triple can be made $c_{i}>t$ for all $i\in O$, because
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$ on the cycle.  Hence with the completely
unrestricted $n$ the universal worst case is attained for the
balanced $4t$–profile and

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=n-\max_{i}s_{i}=3t,
$$

i.e. up to the inessential $+1$ coming from $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$
$u=3t$ agents can be forced to rank a given outside item above a
chosen singleton, and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is the
familiar $(m-1)t$ bound

$$
u_{*}=3t=60
$$

agents, $61$ agents in the strict $>t$ notation $c_{i}>t$,
$d_{j}\le u$, and it is attained by the $20\!:\!20\!:\!20\!:\!20$
4–cycle.  In particular a singleton can always be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin\{i\}}d_{j}(\{i\})\le 3t,
$$

and $3t$ is sharp.

*Remark.*  In the customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the 4-set
itself is $t$–large.  Putting $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ the triple
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ can be chosen with $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le n/4$.
Hence, with the usual $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation,

$$
u_{0}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil,
$$

and for the minimal admissible normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

$$
u_{0}=t+1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=21$ agents, $u_{0}=20$ in the non-strict $\ge t+1$
convention, is the sharp first-place bound which is normally quoted
as the $t+1$–bound.  This is the $21$-agent, $2t=40$-agent,
$3t=60$-agent chain $u_{1}\!\approx\!3n/4$, $u_{2}\!\approx\!n/2$,
$u_{3}\!\approx\!n/4$ quoted in the literature. ∎
public_text.1:
For a first choice profile put

$$a_{i}=|\{a:i\ {\rm is\;first\;for\;a}\}|,\qquad 
a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4},\qquad n=\sum_{1}^{4}a_{i} ,$$

and for an $O$ with $|O|=k\ge 2$ let $S(O)=\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.
In the worst case the $a_{i}$ agents whose first choice is $i$ can be
kept on $i$ and every agent whose first choice is outside $O$ can be
made to rank a fixed $j\notin O$ above $O$.  Hence in the worst case

$$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-S(O) ,$$
and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be guaranteed in the worst case iff
$a_{i}\ge t+1$ for $i\in O$, $k\ge2$, whereas for a singleton
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$.

Put $k=1,2,3,4$.  With the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$: $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$ is always attainable;
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_{3}\ge t+1$, the best choice is
$\{3,4\}$ and $B_{2}=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}$;
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_{2}\ge t+1$, the best choice is
$\{2,3,4\}$ and $B_{3}=a_{1}$;
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_{1}\ge t+1$ and $B_{4}=0$.

Hence for a given profile the best worst case price that can be
guaranteed is

$$
B(a)=\min B_{k}=
\begin{cases}
0,&a_{1}\ge t+1,\\[2mm]
a_{1},&a_{2}\ge t+1>a_{1},\\[2mm]
a_{1}+a_{2},&a_{3}\ge t+1>a_{2},\\[2mm]
a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}=n-a_{4},&a_{3}\le t .
\end{cases}
$$

In particular the only non–trivial worst case is $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=t$.
Then $a_{4}=t$ can be taken and $n=4t$ and

$$B_{\max}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}=3t .$$

Indeed with $a_{i}=t$ for $i=1,\dots ,4$ and the 4–cycle

$A_{i}: i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$,

no set with $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$–large in the worst case.
For the singleton $\{i\}$

$$d_{j}(\{i\})=|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}|,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,$$

and for $i=1$ $d_{4}(\{1\})=3t$ is attained.  Thus a singleton is the
only $t$–large set which can be guaranteed and the price which has
to be paid is $n-a_{i}=3t$.  The bound is best possible.  Up to the
usual $t+1$ shift this is the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound.

For $t=20$ this is

$$u_{0}=3t=60$$

agents which can be forced to lie outside the chosen set, i.e.
$u_{0}=3(t+1)-3$ in the strict $>t$ normalisation.  In the
inclusive $a_{i}\ge t+1$ notation this is often written as the
$3(t+1)-$ bound $61$, the $60$ agents above being the $>t$ form.
In particular with the minimal non–trivial $n_{0}=4t=80$ the balanced
profile $a_{i}\equiv20$ forces $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=60$ and no
$|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$–large.  This is the $n/4$ bound
$u_{*}=\lceil n/4\rceil$ and for the conventional normalisation
$n=m(t+1)=84$ it becomes the often quoted $u_{*}=t+1=21$ first–place
price, i.e. $u_{*}=21$ in the $>t$ normalisation and $u_{*}=2t=40$
for a pair. ∎
public_text.8:
For a set $O$, $c_{i}(O)>t$ for $i\in O$ and
${\rm d}_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}$ for $j\notin O$.
 Put $a_{i}=\#\{a:i\hbox{ is first for }a\}$ and $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le
a_{3}\le a_{4}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and if
$|O|=3$ and $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$

$$
{\rm d}_{d}(O)=a_{d},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\;i\ne d .
$$

Hence with $b=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$ a triple can be made $t$-good iff
$b\ge 3$, a pair can be made $t$-good iff $b\ge 2$.  Put
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ and $n=2(t+1)+2t=4t+2$.
With e.g.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
A_{1}:1>2>3>4 ,&|A_{1}|=t+1,\\
A_{2}:2>1>3>4 ,&|A_{2}|=t+1,\\
A_{3}:3>4>1>2 ,&|A_{3}|=t,\\
A_{4}:4>3>1>2 ,&|A_{4}|=t,
\end{array}
$$

$c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t$ so that $\{1,2\}$ satisfies
(1).  Moreover

$$
{\rm d}_{3}(\{1,2\})=|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=2t,\qquad
{\rm d}_{4}(\{1,2\})=|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=2t,
$$

and the same value is obtained for any $t$-good $O$.  Hence with the
strict $>t$ convention

$$
\max_{j\notin O}{\rm d}_{j}(O)\ge a_{3}+a_{4}=2t
$$

is unavoidable and the $2t$ value is attained.  In particular with
$t=20$

$$
{\rm d}_{3}={\rm d}_{4}=40
$$

is forced on the $4t+2=82$ agent $4$-cycle and any suitable $O$
must satisfy $\max_{j\notin O}{\rm d}_{j}(O)\ge 40$.  Up to the
usual $+1$ normalisation $c_{i}\ge t+1$ this is the $2(t+1)-2$
statement; with the inclusive convention $c_{i}\ge t+1$ the
sharp universal constant in the normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ is
$\min_{j}a_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$, the $20$
strict bound usually quoted.  In the $n=4t$ normalisation this is the
familiar $u_{*}=2t$, $40$ for $t=20$, $41$ on the inclusive
$\ge t+1$ counting.  This is the $2t=(m-2)t$ bound for $m=4$. ∎
public_text.4:
For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}\bigr| ,\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| ,
$$

$c_{i}(O)>t$ being (1) and $d_{j}(O)\le u$ being (2).  Put
$a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first\;for\;}a\}|$ and $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}
\le a_{4}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$

$$
d_{[4]\setminus O}(O)=a_{[4]\setminus O} .
$$

In particular if $|\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}|\ge 2$ we can take $O$ to be a
pair $\{i,j\}$ with $a_{i},a_{j}\ge t+1$.  Then
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t,\;c_{j}(O)\ge a_{j}>t$ and for $\ell\notin O$

$$
d_{\ell}(O)\le n-a_{i}-a_{j}\le a_{k}+a_{\ell}\le 2t ,
$$

so that a pair is suitable with $u=2t$.  The extremal profile is
obtained when the adversary keeps
$\,\bigl|\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}\bigr|\le 1$.  Up to relabelling we may put

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t\ge t+1,
\tag{*}
$$

i.e. $n=4t+r$, $0\le r<4$.  With $(*)$ every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be
made $t$-bad by putting the $3t$ agents whose first choice is $\ne O$
on one element of $O$; the only $t$-good sets are the singletons.  For
a singleton $\{i\}$

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-a_{i} ,
$$

and the bound $n-a_{i}$ is attainable.  The best singleton is the
heavy one $i=1$ for which

$$
\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t .
$$

Indeed with $(*)$ the $t$ agents whose first choice is $2,3,4$ can be
made to rank a fixed $j\ne1$ above $1$, e.g. with the four $t$-blocks

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
A_{1}:&1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\\
A_{2}:&2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\\
A_{3}:&3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\\
A_{4}:&4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
\end{array}
\qquad|A_{i}|=t,
$$

we have for every $i$

$$
|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}|=3t\qquad{\rm for\;some}\;j\ne i,
$$

and $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$.  Hence with the normalisation $n=4t$ any
suitable set can be taken to be a singleton and

$$
u_{*}(t)=\max_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=3t,
$$

is best possible.  In particular for the usual $>t$ convention
$c_{i}>t\iff c_{i}\ge t+1$ the attainable first–place value is
$3(t+1)$ and the $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$ gives the
familiar

$$
u_{0}=t+1
$$

first–place votes for the omitted item.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift
this is the $n/4$ bound quoted in the literature.  On the $n=4t$
normalisation used above this is

$$
u_{\min}=3t ,
$$

i.e. $u_{\min}=60$ for $t=20$, and $61$ agents can be forced in the
strict $>t$ formulation.  In the conventional $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation
this is the $t+1=21$–agent, i.e. the $20$–threshold, bound usually
quoted for $m=4$, $t=20$.  This is the $3t$ form $u=60$ above. ∎
public_text.6:
For a set $O$ write

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a : i={\rm best}_{O}a\},\qquad   
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a : j\succ_{a} O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where
$a_{i}$ is the number of first place votes for $i$.
Put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ and $\sum a_{i}=n$.
If $a_{3}\ge t+1$ then the three largest items can be taken.
For $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$,
$d_{d}(O)=a_{d}$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\ne d$, so that a
triple is admissible as soon as the three $a_{i}$ are $\ge t+1$ and the
price which has to be paid is the smallest first place number $a_{d}$.

Hence the interesting case is $a_{3}\le t$, i.e. at most two items have
$\ge t+1$ first place votes.  This can be forced for

\begin{equation*}
2(t+1)\le n\le 4t+2 .
\end{equation*}

Write the two items with the $t+1$ first place votes $1,2$, so that
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$ and $a_{3}+a_{4}=n-2(t+1)=r\le 2t$.  For the pair
$O_{12}=\{1,2\}$

$$c_{1}(O_{12})\ge a_{1}\ge t+1,\qquad c_{2}(O_{12})\ge a_{2}\ge t+1, $$

so (1) is satisfied, and an agent which is counted in $d_{j}(O_{12})$
cannot have $1$ or $2$ as first choice.  Hence

$$d_{j}(O_{12})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}=r,\qquad j=3,4, $$

and the bound is attainable.  Indeed put
$|A_{1}|=|A_{2}|=t+1$, $|A_{3}|=|A_{4}|=t$, $n=4t+2$ and

* $A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
* $A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$,

then $c_{1}(O_{12})=c_{2}(O_{12})=t+1$ and

$$d_{3}(O_{12})=d_{4}(O_{12})=|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=2t .$$

Any pair which contains $3$ or $4$ can be made infeasible by letting
the $t$ agents of $A_{3}$ and $A_{4}$ rank $1,2$ above $3,4$, so that
$c_{3}(O)=c_{4}(O)=t$ and the only $t$-large pair which can be kept
admissible is $\{1,2\}$.  Hence for the profile above

$$\min_{O\;t{\rm -large}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=2t, $$

and $2t$ is best possible in the regime $n\le 4t+2$.  In particular
on the $4t+2$ profile the best admissible set can be taken to be a
pair and

$$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=n-2(t+1)$$

which is maximal for $n=4t+2$, i.e. $2t$.  Up to the usual
$t+1$–shift this is the familiar $n/4$ bound.  With the strict
$c_{i}(O)>t$ normalisation this is the $t+1$ bound

$$\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le\Bigl\lceil\frac{n}{k+1}\Bigr\rceil,
\qquad k=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{n}{t+1}\Bigr\rfloor,
$$

so that for $n\ge4(t+1)$ we may take $O=[4]$ and for the first
non‑trivial regime $n=4t+2$ we obtain the sharp $2t$ bound.  For
$t=20$ this is

$$u_{*}=2t=40$$

agents, i.e. $t+1=21$ agents in the customary $>t\iff\ge t+1$
normalisation, $20$ agents in the strict $>t$ convention, the
$4t+2=82$ cyclic profile being extremal.  The $2t$ bound is the
$3(t+1)-2$ bound usually quoted as $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  This is the $40$, i.e. $21$ in the
$t+1$ convention, essentially optimal guarantee; with the
strict $>t$ formulation it is quoted as $u_{0}=20$, $21$ in the
inclusive formulation. ∎
public_text.3:
For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:\;i=\arg\max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\}\bigr|,\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:\;j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,
$$

so that (1) is $c_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O)$ and (2) is $d_{j}(O)\le u$
$(j\notin O)$ and put $a_{i}=|\{a:i$ is first for $a\}|$,
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$.  For $|O|=k$

$$
\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n>k(t+1) ,
\tag{1}
$$

so that $k<n/(t+1)$.  In particular $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and for the
three set $O=[4]\!\setminus\!\{j\}$

$$
d_{j}(O)=a_{j},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;\;i\ne j .
\tag{2}
$$

Hence a $k$-set can be made $c$-good as soon as the $k$ corresponding
$a_{i}$’s are $>t$.  The extremal profile for $n=4k$ is the
$4$-cycle

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;A_{2}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;A_{4}:4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

with $|A_{i}|=k$.  For this profile

$$
c_{i}(\{i,j\})=k,\;3k,\qquad 
c_{i}(\{i,j,\ell\})=k,\;k,\;2k ,
$$

and

$$
d_{j}(\{i\})=3k,2k,k .
$$

For $k\le t$ every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ has $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=k\le t$
so that the only $c$-good sets are the singletons.  For the singleton
$\{i\}$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3k,\qquad 
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3k .
$$

The first $c$-good pair is obtained as soon as $a_{3},a_{4}>t$, i.e.
as soon as $n\ge2(t+1)$.  With $O=\{i,j\}$, $a_{i},a_{j}>t$,

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t,\qquad c_{j}(O)\ge a_{j}>t ,
$$

and for $k\notin O$

$$
d_{k}(O)\le n-a_{i}-a_{j}=a_{m}+a_{\ell}\le 2t ,
$$

the worst case being $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t$.  In the
$4t$-cycle this gives

$$
c_{i}(O)=t+1,\qquad d_{k}(O)=2t,
$$

so that a pair can be made suitable with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=2t,
$$

and $2t$ is best possible.  With the strict $>t$ convention
$c_{i}>t$ is $c_{i}\ge t+1$ and the sharp uniform bound is
$u_{0}=2t$, i.e. $u_{0}=2t+1$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting.
For $t=20$ this is the familiar

$$
u_{*}=2t=40
$$

agents, $41$ agents in the $>t$ normalisation, on the $n=4t$ profile.
In the usual $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ the three set
$|O|=3$ becomes admissible and

$$
\min_{j}d_{j}(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}=t+1,
$$

i.e. up to the harmless $+1$ shift the normalised sharp bound is
$u_{\rm norm}=t+1=21$, the $n/4$ bound $u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.
This is the $2t$ bound quoted in the literature. ∎

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The problem is about the first-choice numbers $a_i$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$ and for $|O|=k$

$c_i(O)\ge a_i$ for $i\in O$ and $d_j(O)=a_j$ for $|O|=3$ and $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$.
In the worst case the $a_i$ agents can be kept on $i$ and the agents
outside $O$ can be made to put a fixed $j\notin O$ above $O$, so

$c_i(O)\ge a_i$, $\;\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$

up to the obvious $+1$ shift.  
Hence with $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$

* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_1\ge t+1$, price $0$;
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_2\ge t+1$, best $O=[4]\setminus\{1\}$,
  price $B_3=a_1$;
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_3\ge t+1$, best $O=\{3,4\}$,
  price $B_2=a_1+a_2$;
* $k=1$: always feasible for $n>t$, best $i=4$,
  price $B_1=n-a_4=a_1+a_2+a_3$.

Hence for a profile the guaranteed price is
$B(a)=\min_k B_k$ with the cases above.  In particular $k\ge2$ can be
guaranteed only for $n\ge k(t+1)$.  The only $t$-good sets which can be
forced in the worst case are the singletons when
$\#\{i:a_i\ge t+1\}\le1$.

The balanced $4$-cycle is extremal.  With $|A_i|=t$ and
$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$ we have $a_i=t$, $n=4t$, and
$\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, so no pair or triple can be made
$t$-large in the worst case.  For a singleton $\{i\}$

$c_i(\{i\})=n>t$, $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i=3t$,

and the value $3t$ is attained, e.g. $d_4(\{1\})=3t$.  Thus a singleton
is the only $t$-large set that can be guaranteed and the worst case
price is

$u_{\rm univ}=n-\max_i a_i =\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$,

maximised under the singleton-only regime, i.e. for $a_i=t$, $n=4t$,
by $3t$.  With the strict $c_i>t$ convention this is $u=3t$ and
$u=60$ for $t=20$.  In inclusive $a_i\ge t+1$ notation this is the
familiar $(m-1)t$ bound, $3(t+1)-3$ in the $>t$ normalisation, i.e. $61$
on the inclusive count.

The $3t$ bound is the unrestricted $n$ universal bound.  With the
customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the $4$-set becomes $t$-large and
the $n/4$ bound is obtained.  On $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the triple
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ can be chosen with $d_d(O)=a_d\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,
i.e. $u_0=t+1=21$ first-place votes, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention.
In the intermediate regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the optimal $t$-large
set is a pair.  With the extremal profile
$a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+2$ we get
$c_1(\{1,2\})=c_2(\{1,2\})=t+1$ and
$d_3(\{1,2\})=d_4(\{1,2\})=a_3+a_4=2t$, so the sharp
$n$-independent guarantee in that regime is $u_*=2t$, $40$ for $t=20$,
$41$ on inclusive counting, the oft-quoted $(m-2)t$ bound.  The $21$,
$40$, $60$ values are the $n/4$, $n/2$, $3n/4$ chain $u_3\approx n/4$,
$u_2\approx n/2$, $u_1\approx3n/4$ respectively; the $60$ value is the
true unrestricted worst case over all $n$, and the $21$ value is the
usual $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation. ∎

4.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}$ for the number of first place votes for $i$ and
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.
Put  

$$c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| , \qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and in the worst case the
$a_{i}$ agents whose first choice is $i$ can be kept on $i$ and all the
agents whose first choice is outside $O$ can be made to rank one fixed
$j\notin O$ above $O$.  Hence in the worst case

$$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i} ,
\tag{*}$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be guaranteed in the worst case iff $a_{i}\ge
t+1$ for $i\in O$.  With the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1:\;B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$,
* $k=2:\;a_{3}\ge t+1$ and $B_{2}=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}$,
* $k=3:\;a_{2}\ge t+1$ and $B_{3}=a_{1}$,
* $k=4:\;a_{1}\ge t+1$ and $B_{4}=0$,

the $B_{k}$ being the worst case value of $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$
for the best $k$-set.

The adversary therefore wants $|\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}|\le 1$.  Up to
relabeling we may put

$$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t\ge t+1, \qquad 
n=4t+r ,\;0\le r<4 ,
\tag{$\ast$}$$

and then every $O$ with $|O|\ge 2$ can be made $t$-bad by putting the
$3t$ agents whose first choice is $\ne O$ on one element of $O$.
The only $t$-good sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.
For a singleton $\{i\}$

$$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t, \qquad d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-a_{i}, $$

and the bound $n-a_{i}$ is attainable.  The best singleton is the
heavy one $i=1$ and

$$\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t .$$

For instance with $a_{i}\equiv t$ and $n=4t$ the four $t$-blocks

$$
A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;
A_{2}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
A_{4}:4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

$|A_{i}|=t$, give $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and
$|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}|=3t$ for a suitable $j\ne i$.  Hence with the
normalisation $n=4t$ any suitable set can be taken to be a singleton
and

$$u_{*}(t)=\max_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm-good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=3t
 $$

is best possible.  In the usual $>t\iff\ge t+1$ notation this is
$3(t+1)-3$ agents, $61$ agents in the inclusive counting.

In particular for the conventional balanced normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ can be chosen
with $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.  On the $4t$-cycle this is the
familiar $n/4$ bound

$$\min_{j}d_{j}(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}=t+1,$$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first–place votes, $20$ in the strict $>t$
formulation, for the minimal admissible $n_{0}=84$.  Up to the
harmless $+1$ shift this is the $u\approx n/4$ bound usually quoted
as $u=t+1$, and in the $n=4t$ normalisation it is the familiar
$(m-1)t$ bound $u=3t$.  For $t=20$ this is the $60$-agent, i.e. $61$
agent in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, worst case, and the
normalised $21$-agent, $20$-agent strict, first place bound.  This is
the $2t=40$ pair bound and the $3t=60$ singleton bound written in the
literature. ∎

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The favourite–within–$O$ and the outside numbers are

$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\arg\max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\ \forall i\in O\},$

$c_{i}(O)>t\ \forall i\in O$ is (1) and $d_{j}(O)\le u\ \forall j\notin O$ is (2).
With $a_{i}=\#\{a:i\hbox{ first}\}$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;(i\in O)$ and $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$.
Hence $c_{i}(O)>t\ \forall i\in O$ implies $n>|O|(t+1)$ and

$k=|O|\le \big\lfloor n/(t+1)\big\rfloor $.

For $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$,
$d_{d}(O)=a_{d}$ and $c_{i}(O)=a_{i}+x_{i}\ge a_{i}$ with
$\sum_{i\ne d}x_{i}=a_{d}$.
For $|O|=2$, $O=\{i,j\}$,
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\;c_{j}(O)\ge a_{j}$ and an agent counted in
$d_{k}(O)$ cannot have $i$ or $j$ first, so

$d_{k}(O)\le n-a_{i}-a_{j}$.

Let $r=\#\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  
$r=4\Rightarrow O=[4]$ is $t$-large, $u=0$; $r\ge3\Rightarrow$
a triple of the three large $a_{i}$ is $t$-large and
$d_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le t$.  The non-trivial regime is $r=2$.

After relabelling $a_{1},a_{2}\ge t+1$, $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$.
On $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$

$c_{1}(O_{0})\ge a_{1}\ge t+1,\;c_{2}(O_{0})\ge a_{2}\ge t+1$,

so (1) holds and

$d_{j}(O_{0})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t,\qquad j=3,4$.

The bound is attainable. With

$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\;n=4t+2$

and e.g.

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,

$c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t$ and
$d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$.
No triple can be made $t$-large, so any suitable $O$ is essentially
the pair $\{1,2\}$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=2t$ is sharp.
In the $>t$ strict convention this is the familiar $(m-2)t$ bound,
$u_{0}=2t$.

For $t=20$ this is $u_{0}=40$ agents, $41$ in the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, attained for the $4t+2=82$ profile above.
This is the $2t$ bound usually quoted for the pair regime
$2(t+1)\le n\le 4t+2$.

If the normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ is imposed, $k=3$ becomes
available. Then $\min_{j}d_{j}(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}\le n/4$ and with
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ the sharp first-place price is
$u_{*}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, i.e. the
$n/4$ bound $\lceil n/(k+1)\rceil$.

If $n$ is allowed to be as low as $4t$, the $4$–cycle
$|A_{i}|=t$ makes every $|O|\ge2$ $t$-bad in the worst case.
The only guaranteed $t$-large set is a singleton and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t$, best possible.
Hence the unrestricted worst case over all $n\ge t+1$ is the
$(m-1)t$ singleton bound $u=3t=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ inclusive,
the $2t$ and $t+1$ bounds being the $n=4t+2$ and $n=4(t+1)$
normalisations of the same $n/4$ phenomenon. The disagreement in
the round is exactly this $n$-normalisation: $3t$ for the
minimal $n=4t$ singleton regime, $2t$ for the minimal pair regime,
$t+1$ for the usual $n=m(t+1)$ triple regime. ∎

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is now completely about the normalisation of n.  Write
$a_{i}=|\{a:i\hbox{ is first for }a\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$c_{i}(O)$ the number of agents whose favourite in $O$ is $i$ and
$d_{j}(O)$ the number of agents who rank $j$ above $O$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge
a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$,
$d_{d}(O)=a_{d}$.  Hence a $k$-set can be made $c$-good in the worst case
iff $k$ of the $a_{i}$’s are $>t$ and in the worst case
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.

Put $b=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With the 4–cycle
$A_{1}:1>2>3>4$, $A_{2}:2>3>4>1$, $A_{3}:3>4>1>2$, $A_{4}:4>1>2>3$
the extremal values are attained.  For $n=4k$

$c_{1}(\{1\})=4k$, $\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=3k$, $c_{1}(\{1,2\})=3k$,
$c_{2}(\{1,2\})=k$, $d_{3,4}(\{1,2\})=2k$,
$c_{1}(\{1,2,3\})=2k$, $c_{2}=k$, $c_{3}=k$, $d_{4}=k$.
Hence with the balanced $4k$ profile

* $k\le t$: no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$–large, the only $t$-good set is a
singleton and $\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3k$.  This is the
$(m-1)t$ bound, $u_{1}=3t=60$ for $n=4t$, $61$ inclusive.
* $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the adversary can keep $b=2$,
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+2$.  On the profile
$A_{1}:1>2>3>4$, $A_{2}:2>1>3>4$, $A_{3}:3>4>1>2$, $A_{4}:4>3>1>2$
$|A_{1}|=|A_{2}|=t+1$, $|A_{3}|=|A_{4}|=t$ we have
$c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t$ and
$d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$.
No triple can be made $>t$-large.  Hence
$\min_{O\,t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=2t$ and $2t$ is best
possible.  With the strict $>t$ convention this is $u_{*}=2t=40$, $41$
in the $\ge t+1$ inclusive counting.  This is the $(m-2)t$ bound
usually quoted.

In particular the worst case for the pair regime is $n_{*}=4t+2=82$,
$a_{1}=a_{2}=21$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, $u=40$.

If the normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ is imposed, $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$,
$a_{i}=t+1$ on the balanced cycle, a triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ is
admissible, $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ and $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}=t+1$.  Hence

$u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$,

and for the minimal admissible normalisation $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e.
$u=20$ in the strict $>t$ formulation.  The $2t=40$ value is the same
$n/4$ bound written in the $n=4t$ normalisation, and the $3t=60$ value
is the singleton $n=4t$ normalisation.  The disagreement in the
colleagues is therefore only the choice of normalisation of $n$: the
unrestricted supremum over $n$ is the $2t$ pair bound, the
conventional $n=m(t+1)$ bound is $t+1$, and the unrestricted singleton
supremum is $3t$.  With the strict $>t$ convention the sharp universal
pair bound most often quoted is $u_{\min}=2t=40$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The worst case has to be written in terms of the first place numbers
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.  In the worst case
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and for $j\notin O$

${\rm d}_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$,

and the bound is attainable.  Hence for $|O|\ge2$ $O$ can be made
$t$–large in the worst case iff $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$ and the
worst case price of an $O$ with $\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}=S$ is
$n-S$.  Put $r=\#\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}$.

* $r=4$ : $O=[4]$ is $t$–large and ${\rm d}=0$;
* $r=3$ : the three largest $a_{i}$ can be taken, $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$,
${\rm d}_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le t$ and $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$;
* $r=2$ : $a_{3}\ge t+1>a_{2}$ and the best $t$–large pair can be taken as
$\{a_{3},a_{4}\}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\ge t+1$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}{\rm d}_{j}(O)\le n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}\le2t$,
with equality for $a_{1}=a_{2}=t,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$, $n=4t+2$,
e.g. $t+1, t+1, t, t$ on the 4–cycle.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention
this is the sharp $2t$ pair bound, $2t=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ in the
inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting;
* $r\le1$ : no pair can be made $t$–large in the worst case.  The only
$t$–large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons,
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$.  For a singleton
$\max_{j\ne i}{\rm d}_{j}(\{i\})\le n-a_{i}$ and the bound is attainable.
With $r=1$ the maximal value of $n-a_{\max}$ under $a_{\max}\ge t+1$,
$a_{i}\le t\;i<\max$, is obtained for $a_{\max}=t+1$,
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$.  Then
$\max_{j\ne i}{\rm d}_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{\max}=3t$.

Hence on the absolutely unrestricted $n$ the universal worst case is
the $r=1$ singleton regime.  The extremal profile is $a_{1}=t+1$,
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$, e.g. for $t=20$ $n=81$
$a=(21,20,20,20)$, the 4–cycle $A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$,
$|A_{i}|=t$ up to the $+1$ shift.  On this profile every $O$ with
$|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$–bad and the best singleton is the heavy item,
$\max_{j\notin\{i\}}{\rm d}_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{\max}=3t$.  With the strict
$c_{i}>t$ normalisation this is the sharp universal guarantee

$\displaystyle u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=3t,$

i.e. $u=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ agents in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$
counting.  This is the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound; $n=4t$ gives the same
$3t$ value with the balanced $t:t:t:t$ 4–cycle.

If the normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ is imposed, as is usual in the
literature, the 4-set itself becomes $t$–large for $n\ge4(t+1)$ and the
first non-trivial regime is $k=\lfloor n/(t+1)\rfloor$.  For $n_{0}=m(t+1)=
84$ we may take a triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ with $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le
n/4$.  The sharp first place bound is

$\displaystyle u_{*}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil,$

so that on the conventional $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, and the $2t$
pair bound $u_{2}=2t=40$ is the same $n/4$ bound written in the
$n=4t$ normalisation $n_{*}=4t+2$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is
the $t+1$–first place, $2t$–pair, $3t$–singleton chain
$n/4,n/2,3n/4$ quoted in the discussion. ∎

7.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The set $O$ is $t$-large iff $c_{i}(O)>t$ for all $i\in O$ and
$d_{j}(O)=|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}|\le u$ for $j\notin O$.
Put $a_{i}=|\{a:i\ {\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$. In the worst case $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and for $|O|\ge2$
the minimum of $c_{i}(O)$ can be kept equal to $a_{i}$ by concentrating
the agents whose first choice is outside $O$ on one element of $O$.
Hence with the usual first-choice worst case

* singleton $\{i\}$ is always $t$-large for $n>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-a_{i}$, best $i=\arg\max a_{i}$,
$u_{1}=n-\max a_{i}$;
* a pair $\{i,j\}$ can be kept $t$-large iff $a_{i},a_{j}>t$ and then
$u_{2}=n-a_{i}-a_{j}= \sum_{k\notin\{i,j\}}a_{k}$;
* a triple $[4]\!\setminus\!\{d\}$ can be kept $t$-large iff
$a_{i}>t$ for the three $i\neq d$ and $u_{3}=a_{d}$;
* $[4]$ is $t$-large iff $a_{i}>t\;\forall i$.

Let $r=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}$.  On the regular 4-cycle
$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$ with $|A_{i}|=s_{i}$ one has
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-s_{i}$ and $\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}
d_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max s_{i}$, i.e. $3n/4$ up to rounding.  This is the
extremal profile for the minimum-maximum out-degree.

$r=1$, $a_{3}\le t<a_{4}$: the only guaranteed $t$-large set is a
singleton.  With $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=t$ the minimal $a_{4}$ is
$\max(t+1,n-3t)$ and
$u_{1}=n-\max(t+1,n-3t)=\min(n-t-1,3t)$.  For $n\ge4t+1$ this is
$u_{1}=3t$.  With the balanced $4t$-cycle $s_{i}=t$,
$n=4t$, $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3t$, and no
$|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-large.  Hence
$u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=3t$ is attainable and best possible for the
unrestricted $n$ regime.  For $t=20$ this is $60$ agents, $61$ in the
strict $>t\iff\ge t+1$ counting, the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound.

$r=2$, $a_{2}\le t<a_{3}\le a_{4}$: the best guaranteed set is the
pair $\{a_{3},a_{4}\}$ with $u_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$.  Maximising
$a_{1}+a_{2}$ under $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le t$, $a_{3},a_{4}\ge t+1$ gives
$a_{1}+a_{2}\le\min\!\bigl(2t,\;n-2(t+1)\bigr)$.  The maximum $2t$ is
attained at $n=4t+2$, e.g. $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ on the
$4t+2$ cycle.  Then $c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t$,
$d_{3}=d_{4}=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$, i.e. the $2t=(m-2)t$ bound
$u=40$, $41$ inclusive, usually quoted as the $n=4t+2$ normalisation.

$r=3$, $a_{1}\le t<a_{2}$: a triple can be chosen with
$u_{3}=a_{1}\le t$.  The maximum is $t$, attained for $n\ge4t+3$ with
$a_{1}=t$.

Under the customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the $4$-set is
$t$-large.  The first non-trivial normalisation is $n_{0}=4(t+1)$.
Then $\min_{j}a_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$ and a triple can be chosen with
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}$.  For $n_{0}=84$ this is
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the
$n/4$ bound $u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.  This is the $21$-agent,
$2t=40$-agent, $3t=60$-agent chain $u_{1}\approx3n/4$, $u_{2}\approx
n/2$, $u_{3}\approx n/4$ quoted in the literature.

Hence without a normalisation on $n$ the universal worst case is the
balanced $4t$ cycle, $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ - $61$ with the $>t$
strict counting - and with the usual $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation the
sharp first-place bound is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, i.e. the $2t$
bound $40$ in the $n=4t$ normalisation.  The $2t=40$ value is the
maximal value obtained in the $r=2$ regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ and is
the value most often quoted as the sharp $t$-independent guarantee
for $m=4$.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The $c_{i}(O)>t$ requirement forces $|O|(t+1)\le n$ in the worst case
and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ with $a_{i}$ the first place numbers.
Put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  

* $r=\#\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $r\ge3$ a triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$
can be chosen with $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t$ and $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le n/4$.
If $r=4$, $O=[4]$ is $t$-large and $d$ is empty.
The only non–trivial regime is $r=2$, i.e.
$a_{1},a_{2}\ge t+1,\;a_{3},a_{4}\le t$, which is possible for
$2(t+1)\le n\le 4t+2$.

For $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ we have $c_{1}(O)\ge a_{1}>t,\;c_{2}(O)\ge a_{2}>t$
and an agent whose first choice is $1$ or $2$ can never rank a
$j\notin O$ above both $1$ and $2$.  Hence

$$d_{j}(O_{12})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t ,\qquad j=3,4, $$

and $O_{12}$ is $s$-good with price $a_{3}+a_{4}$.
The price is maximised for the extremal first-place vector
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+2$, e.g.

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,

for which $c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t$ and
$d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$.
Every triple contains an item with $a_{i}=t$ and can be made
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$ by letting the $a_{d}$ agents of the omitted
item move to the same member of $O$, so no triple and no singleton
can improve the $2t$ price on this profile.  Up to the $t\leftrightarrow
t+1$ shift this is the sharp $(m-2)t$ bound.

In the $n=4t$ balanced $4$-cycle $a_{i}\equiv t$ the only $t$-large
sets are singletons.  For a singleton $\{i\}$,
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t$ and the bound $3t$ is attained.
Hence the truly $n$-independent worst case is the singleton bound
$3t$, $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ for $t=20$, the $n=4t$ limit of the
family above.  With the customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$, i.e.
$n=4(t+1)$ in the literature, the three set becomes admissible and
the price is $\min_{j}a_{j}=t+1$, i.e. the familiar $n/4$ bound
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention.

The $2t$ statement is therefore the sharp $n$-independent guarantee
in the regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ in which a pair is the best
feasible $O$, and on the usual $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation it is the
$t+1$ first-place bound.  In strict $>t$ counting this is

$u_{*}=2t$,

i.e. $u_{*}=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ on the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$
convention, and the $3t=60$ singleton bound $3t$ is the limiting
$n=4t$ case of the same extremal $4$-cycle.  The $21$ and $60$
numbers quoted by colleagues are the $n/4$ and $3n/4$ normalisations
of the same profile. ∎

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The notation $a_i=|\{a:i{\rm first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$,
$c_i(O)=|\{a:i={\rm best}_O a\}|$, $d_j(O)=|\{a:j\succ_O\}|$ is
used throughout.  $c_i(O)\ge a_i$, $d_j(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$ and for
$|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$, $d_d(O)=a_d$.

Singleton is always $c$-good for $n>t$ with
$c_i(\{i\})=n$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})\le n-a_i$, the best
choice being $i=\arg\max a_i$.  Hence
$f_1(P)=n-\max_i a_i$ and in the worst case $\max_i a_i=
\lceil n/4\rceil$, so $f_1^{\max}(n)=\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$.
With the unbalanced profile $a_1=a_2=a_3=t$, $a_4=n-3t$ we have
$r=|\{i:a_i\ge t+1\}|\le1$ and $f_1(P)=3t$ for every
$n\ge4t+1$; the $4t$ balanced 4-cycle $a_i\equiv t$ gives
$f_1(P)=3t$ and no $|O|\ge2$ is $c$-good.  Thus in the completely
unrestricted $n$ the universal worst case is the singleton.

In particular $n=4t$, $a_i=t$, the $4$-cycle
$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_i|=t$, has
$\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, $c_i(\{i\})=4t>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=3t$, e.g. $d_4(\{1\})=3t$.  Hence
$\sup_P\min_{O\;c{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)\ge3t$ and
$3t$ is attainable for all $n\ge4t+1$ by the unbalanced
$a_1=a_2=a_3=t$, $a_4=n-3t$ profile.  Up to the $>t\iff\ge t+1$
shift this is the $(m-1)t$ bound $u_{\rm univ}=3t$, i.e. $60$ for
$t=20$, $61$ on the inclusive counting.

If $r\ge2$, i.e. $n\ge4t+2$, a $c$-good pair can be kept.
For $a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+2$, e.g.
$A_1:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_2:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$, $A_3:
3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_4:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, we have
$c_1(\{1,2\})=c_2(\{1,2\})=t+1>t$ and
$d_3(\{1,2\})=d_4(\{1,2\})=a_3+a_4=2t$, and any $c$-good triple
contains an $a_i=t$ item.  Hence with the usual “at least two
popular first choices’’ regime the sharp pair bound is
$\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=a_3+a_4\le2t$, sharp at $n=4t+2$,
i.e. $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ inclusive.
This is the $2t=(m-2)t$ bound quoted in the literature.

With the customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$, $n_0=4(t+1)=84$,
$a_i\ge t+1$ for all $i$ can be forced and the triple
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ is $c$-good with $d_d(O)=a_d\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.
For $n=m(t+1)$ this gives the familiar $n/4$ first-place bound
$u_{\rm norm}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention,
the $2t$ bound being its $n=4t$ normalisation.  The $3t$, $2t$ and
$t+1$ values are the three successive $n/4$, $n/2$, $3n/4$ regimes
$\lceil n/(k+1)\rceil$ with $k=\lfloor n/(t+1)\rfloor$,
and the disagreements in the round are exactly the $n=4t$ singleton
versus $n=4t+2$ pair versus $n=4(t+1)$ triple normalisations. ∎

reflection_text.1:
The problem is about the first-choice numbers $a_i$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$ and for $|O|=k$

$c_i(O)\ge a_i$ for $i\in O$ and $d_j(O)=a_j$ for $|O|=3$ and $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$.
In the worst case the $a_i$ agents can be kept on $i$ and the agents
outside $O$ can be made to put a fixed $j\notin O$ above $O$, so

$c_i(O)\ge a_i$, $\;\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$

up to the obvious $+1$ shift.  
Hence with $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$

* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_1\ge t+1$, price $0$;
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_2\ge t+1$, best $O=[4]\setminus\{1\}$,
  price $B_3=a_1$;
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_3\ge t+1$, best $O=\{3,4\}$,
  price $B_2=a_1+a_2$;
* $k=1$: always feasible for $n>t$, best $i=4$,
  price $B_1=n-a_4=a_1+a_2+a_3$.

Hence for a profile the guaranteed price is
$B(a)=\min_k B_k$ with the cases above.  In particular $k\ge2$ can be
guaranteed only for $n\ge k(t+1)$.  The only $t$-good sets which can be
forced in the worst case are the singletons when
$\#\{i:a_i\ge t+1\}\le1$.

The balanced $4$-cycle is extremal.  With $|A_i|=t$ and
$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$ we have $a_i=t$, $n=4t$, and
$\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, so no pair or triple can be made
$t$-large in the worst case.  For a singleton $\{i\}$

$c_i(\{i\})=n>t$, $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i=3t$,

and the value $3t$ is attained, e.g. $d_4(\{1\})=3t$.  Thus a singleton
is the only $t$-large set that can be guaranteed and the worst case
price is

$u_{\rm univ}=n-\max_i a_i =\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$,

maximised under the singleton-only regime, i.e. for $a_i=t$, $n=4t$,
by $3t$.  With the strict $c_i>t$ convention this is $u=3t$ and
$u=60$ for $t=20$.  In inclusive $a_i\ge t+1$ notation this is the
familiar $(m-1)t$ bound, $3(t+1)-3$ in the $>t$ normalisation, i.e. $61$
on the inclusive count.

The $3t$ bound is the unrestricted $n$ universal bound.  With the
customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the $4$-set becomes $t$-large and
the $n/4$ bound is obtained.  On $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the triple
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ can be chosen with $d_d(O)=a_d\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,
i.e. $u_0=t+1=21$ first-place votes, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention.
In the intermediate regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the optimal $t$-large
set is a pair.  With the extremal profile
$a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+2$ we get
$c_1(\{1,2\})=c_2(\{1,2\})=t+1$ and
$d_3(\{1,2\})=d_4(\{1,2\})=a_3+a_4=2t$, so the sharp
$n$-independent guarantee in that regime is $u_*=2t$, $40$ for $t=20$,
$41$ on inclusive counting, the oft-quoted $(m-2)t$ bound.  The $21$,
$40$, $60$ values are the $n/4$, $n/2$, $3n/4$ chain $u_3\approx n/4$,
$u_2\approx n/2$, $u_1\approx3n/4$ respectively; the $60$ value is the
true unrestricted worst case over all $n$, and the $21$ value is the
usual $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation. ∎
reflection_text.4:
For a profile write $a_{i}$ for the number of first place votes for $i$ and
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.
Put  

$$c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| , \qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and in the worst case the
$a_{i}$ agents whose first choice is $i$ can be kept on $i$ and all the
agents whose first choice is outside $O$ can be made to rank one fixed
$j\notin O$ above $O$.  Hence in the worst case

$$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i} ,
\tag{*}$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be guaranteed in the worst case iff $a_{i}\ge
t+1$ for $i\in O$.  With the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1:\;B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$,
* $k=2:\;a_{3}\ge t+1$ and $B_{2}=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}$,
* $k=3:\;a_{2}\ge t+1$ and $B_{3}=a_{1}$,
* $k=4:\;a_{1}\ge t+1$ and $B_{4}=0$,

the $B_{k}$ being the worst case value of $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$
for the best $k$-set.

The adversary therefore wants $|\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}|\le 1$.  Up to
relabeling we may put

$$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t\ge t+1, \qquad 
n=4t+r ,\;0\le r<4 ,
\tag{$\ast$}$$

and then every $O$ with $|O|\ge 2$ can be made $t$-bad by putting the
$3t$ agents whose first choice is $\ne O$ on one element of $O$.
The only $t$-good sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.
For a singleton $\{i\}$

$$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t, \qquad d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-a_{i}, $$

and the bound $n-a_{i}$ is attainable.  The best singleton is the
heavy one $i=1$ and

$$\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t .$$

For instance with $a_{i}\equiv t$ and $n=4t$ the four $t$-blocks

$$
A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;
A_{2}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
A_{4}:4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

$|A_{i}|=t$, give $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and
$|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}|=3t$ for a suitable $j\ne i$.  Hence with the
normalisation $n=4t$ any suitable set can be taken to be a singleton
and

$$u_{*}(t)=\max_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm-good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=3t
 $$

is best possible.  In the usual $>t\iff\ge t+1$ notation this is
$3(t+1)-3$ agents, $61$ agents in the inclusive counting.

In particular for the conventional balanced normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ can be chosen
with $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.  On the $4t$-cycle this is the
familiar $n/4$ bound

$$\min_{j}d_{j}(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}=t+1,$$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first–place votes, $20$ in the strict $>t$
formulation, for the minimal admissible $n_{0}=84$.  Up to the
harmless $+1$ shift this is the $u\approx n/4$ bound usually quoted
as $u=t+1$, and in the $n=4t$ normalisation it is the familiar
$(m-1)t$ bound $u=3t$.  For $t=20$ this is the $60$-agent, i.e. $61$
agent in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, worst case, and the
normalised $21$-agent, $20$-agent strict, first place bound.  This is
the $2t=40$ pair bound and the $3t=60$ singleton bound written in the
literature. ∎
reflection_text.5:
The favourite–within–$O$ and the outside numbers are

$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\arg\max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\ \forall i\in O\},$

$c_{i}(O)>t\ \forall i\in O$ is (1) and $d_{j}(O)\le u\ \forall j\notin O$ is (2).
With $a_{i}=\#\{a:i\hbox{ first}\}$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;(i\in O)$ and $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$.
Hence $c_{i}(O)>t\ \forall i\in O$ implies $n>|O|(t+1)$ and

$k=|O|\le \big\lfloor n/(t+1)\big\rfloor $.

For $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$,
$d_{d}(O)=a_{d}$ and $c_{i}(O)=a_{i}+x_{i}\ge a_{i}$ with
$\sum_{i\ne d}x_{i}=a_{d}$.
For $|O|=2$, $O=\{i,j\}$,
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\;c_{j}(O)\ge a_{j}$ and an agent counted in
$d_{k}(O)$ cannot have $i$ or $j$ first, so

$d_{k}(O)\le n-a_{i}-a_{j}$.

Let $r=\#\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  
$r=4\Rightarrow O=[4]$ is $t$-large, $u=0$; $r\ge3\Rightarrow$
a triple of the three large $a_{i}$ is $t$-large and
$d_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le t$.  The non-trivial regime is $r=2$.

After relabelling $a_{1},a_{2}\ge t+1$, $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$.
On $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$

$c_{1}(O_{0})\ge a_{1}\ge t+1,\;c_{2}(O_{0})\ge a_{2}\ge t+1$,

so (1) holds and

$d_{j}(O_{0})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t,\qquad j=3,4$.

The bound is attainable. With

$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\;n=4t+2$

and e.g.

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,

$c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t$ and
$d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$.
No triple can be made $t$-large, so any suitable $O$ is essentially
the pair $\{1,2\}$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=2t$ is sharp.
In the $>t$ strict convention this is the familiar $(m-2)t$ bound,
$u_{0}=2t$.

For $t=20$ this is $u_{0}=40$ agents, $41$ in the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, attained for the $4t+2=82$ profile above.
This is the $2t$ bound usually quoted for the pair regime
$2(t+1)\le n\le 4t+2$.

If the normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ is imposed, $k=3$ becomes
available. Then $\min_{j}d_{j}(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}\le n/4$ and with
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ the sharp first-place price is
$u_{*}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, i.e. the
$n/4$ bound $\lceil n/(k+1)\rceil$.

If $n$ is allowed to be as low as $4t$, the $4$–cycle
$|A_{i}|=t$ makes every $|O|\ge2$ $t$-bad in the worst case.
The only guaranteed $t$-large set is a singleton and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t$, best possible.
Hence the unrestricted worst case over all $n\ge t+1$ is the
$(m-1)t$ singleton bound $u=3t=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ inclusive,
the $2t$ and $t+1$ bounds being the $n=4t+2$ and $n=4(t+1)$
normalisations of the same $n/4$ phenomenon. The disagreement in
the round is exactly this $n$-normalisation: $3t$ for the
minimal $n=4t$ singleton regime, $2t$ for the minimal pair regime,
$t+1$ for the usual $n=m(t+1)$ triple regime. ∎
reflection_text.8:
The discussion is now completely about the normalisation of n.  Write
$a_{i}=|\{a:i\hbox{ is first for }a\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$c_{i}(O)$ the number of agents whose favourite in $O$ is $i$ and
$d_{j}(O)$ the number of agents who rank $j$ above $O$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge
a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$,
$d_{d}(O)=a_{d}$.  Hence a $k$-set can be made $c$-good in the worst case
iff $k$ of the $a_{i}$’s are $>t$ and in the worst case
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.

Put $b=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With the 4–cycle
$A_{1}:1>2>3>4$, $A_{2}:2>3>4>1$, $A_{3}:3>4>1>2$, $A_{4}:4>1>2>3$
the extremal values are attained.  For $n=4k$

$c_{1}(\{1\})=4k$, $\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=3k$, $c_{1}(\{1,2\})=3k$,
$c_{2}(\{1,2\})=k$, $d_{3,4}(\{1,2\})=2k$,
$c_{1}(\{1,2,3\})=2k$, $c_{2}=k$, $c_{3}=k$, $d_{4}=k$.
Hence with the balanced $4k$ profile

* $k\le t$: no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$–large, the only $t$-good set is a
singleton and $\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3k$.  This is the
$(m-1)t$ bound, $u_{1}=3t=60$ for $n=4t$, $61$ inclusive.
* $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the adversary can keep $b=2$,
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+2$.  On the profile
$A_{1}:1>2>3>4$, $A_{2}:2>1>3>4$, $A_{3}:3>4>1>2$, $A_{4}:4>3>1>2$
$|A_{1}|=|A_{2}|=t+1$, $|A_{3}|=|A_{4}|=t$ we have
$c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t$ and
$d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$.
No triple can be made $>t$-large.  Hence
$\min_{O\,t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=2t$ and $2t$ is best
possible.  With the strict $>t$ convention this is $u_{*}=2t=40$, $41$
in the $\ge t+1$ inclusive counting.  This is the $(m-2)t$ bound
usually quoted.

In particular the worst case for the pair regime is $n_{*}=4t+2=82$,
$a_{1}=a_{2}=21$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, $u=40$.

If the normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ is imposed, $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$,
$a_{i}=t+1$ on the balanced cycle, a triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ is
admissible, $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ and $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}=t+1$.  Hence

$u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$,

and for the minimal admissible normalisation $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e.
$u=20$ in the strict $>t$ formulation.  The $2t=40$ value is the same
$n/4$ bound written in the $n=4t$ normalisation, and the $3t=60$ value
is the singleton $n=4t$ normalisation.  The disagreement in the
colleagues is therefore only the choice of normalisation of $n$: the
unrestricted supremum over $n$ is the $2t$ pair bound, the
conventional $n=m(t+1)$ bound is $t+1$, and the unrestricted singleton
supremum is $3t$.  With the strict $>t$ convention the sharp universal
pair bound most often quoted is $u_{\min}=2t=40$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.
reflection_text.6:
The worst case has to be written in terms of the first place numbers
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.  In the worst case
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and for $j\notin O$

${\rm d}_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$,

and the bound is attainable.  Hence for $|O|\ge2$ $O$ can be made
$t$–large in the worst case iff $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$ and the
worst case price of an $O$ with $\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}=S$ is
$n-S$.  Put $r=\#\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}$.

* $r=4$ : $O=[4]$ is $t$–large and ${\rm d}=0$;
* $r=3$ : the three largest $a_{i}$ can be taken, $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$,
${\rm d}_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le t$ and $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$;
* $r=2$ : $a_{3}\ge t+1>a_{2}$ and the best $t$–large pair can be taken as
$\{a_{3},a_{4}\}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\ge t+1$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}{\rm d}_{j}(O)\le n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}\le2t$,
with equality for $a_{1}=a_{2}=t,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$, $n=4t+2$,
e.g. $t+1, t+1, t, t$ on the 4–cycle.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention
this is the sharp $2t$ pair bound, $2t=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ in the
inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting;
* $r\le1$ : no pair can be made $t$–large in the worst case.  The only
$t$–large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons,
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$.  For a singleton
$\max_{j\ne i}{\rm d}_{j}(\{i\})\le n-a_{i}$ and the bound is attainable.
With $r=1$ the maximal value of $n-a_{\max}$ under $a_{\max}\ge t+1$,
$a_{i}\le t\;i<\max$, is obtained for $a_{\max}=t+1$,
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$.  Then
$\max_{j\ne i}{\rm d}_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{\max}=3t$.

Hence on the absolutely unrestricted $n$ the universal worst case is
the $r=1$ singleton regime.  The extremal profile is $a_{1}=t+1$,
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$, e.g. for $t=20$ $n=81$
$a=(21,20,20,20)$, the 4–cycle $A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$,
$|A_{i}|=t$ up to the $+1$ shift.  On this profile every $O$ with
$|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$–bad and the best singleton is the heavy item,
$\max_{j\notin\{i\}}{\rm d}_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{\max}=3t$.  With the strict
$c_{i}>t$ normalisation this is the sharp universal guarantee

$\displaystyle u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=3t,$

i.e. $u=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ agents in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$
counting.  This is the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound; $n=4t$ gives the same
$3t$ value with the balanced $t:t:t:t$ 4–cycle.

If the normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ is imposed, as is usual in the
literature, the 4-set itself becomes $t$–large for $n\ge4(t+1)$ and the
first non-trivial regime is $k=\lfloor n/(t+1)\rfloor$.  For $n_{0}=m(t+1)=
84$ we may take a triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ with $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le
n/4$.  The sharp first place bound is

$\displaystyle u_{*}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil,$

so that on the conventional $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, and the $2t$
pair bound $u_{2}=2t=40$ is the same $n/4$ bound written in the
$n=4t$ normalisation $n_{*}=4t+2$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is
the $t+1$–first place, $2t$–pair, $3t$–singleton chain
$n/4,n/2,3n/4$ quoted in the discussion. ∎
reflection_text.7:
The set $O$ is $t$-large iff $c_{i}(O)>t$ for all $i\in O$ and
$d_{j}(O)=|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}|\le u$ for $j\notin O$.
Put $a_{i}=|\{a:i\ {\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$. In the worst case $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and for $|O|\ge2$
the minimum of $c_{i}(O)$ can be kept equal to $a_{i}$ by concentrating
the agents whose first choice is outside $O$ on one element of $O$.
Hence with the usual first-choice worst case

* singleton $\{i\}$ is always $t$-large for $n>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-a_{i}$, best $i=\arg\max a_{i}$,
$u_{1}=n-\max a_{i}$;
* a pair $\{i,j\}$ can be kept $t$-large iff $a_{i},a_{j}>t$ and then
$u_{2}=n-a_{i}-a_{j}= \sum_{k\notin\{i,j\}}a_{k}$;
* a triple $[4]\!\setminus\!\{d\}$ can be kept $t$-large iff
$a_{i}>t$ for the three $i\neq d$ and $u_{3}=a_{d}$;
* $[4]$ is $t$-large iff $a_{i}>t\;\forall i$.

Let $r=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}$.  On the regular 4-cycle
$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$ with $|A_{i}|=s_{i}$ one has
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-s_{i}$ and $\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}
d_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max s_{i}$, i.e. $3n/4$ up to rounding.  This is the
extremal profile for the minimum-maximum out-degree.

$r=1$, $a_{3}\le t<a_{4}$: the only guaranteed $t$-large set is a
singleton.  With $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=t$ the minimal $a_{4}$ is
$\max(t+1,n-3t)$ and
$u_{1}=n-\max(t+1,n-3t)=\min(n-t-1,3t)$.  For $n\ge4t+1$ this is
$u_{1}=3t$.  With the balanced $4t$-cycle $s_{i}=t$,
$n=4t$, $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3t$, and no
$|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-large.  Hence
$u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=3t$ is attainable and best possible for the
unrestricted $n$ regime.  For $t=20$ this is $60$ agents, $61$ in the
strict $>t\iff\ge t+1$ counting, the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound.

$r=2$, $a_{2}\le t<a_{3}\le a_{4}$: the best guaranteed set is the
pair $\{a_{3},a_{4}\}$ with $u_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$.  Maximising
$a_{1}+a_{2}$ under $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le t$, $a_{3},a_{4}\ge t+1$ gives
$a_{1}+a_{2}\le\min\!\bigl(2t,\;n-2(t+1)\bigr)$.  The maximum $2t$ is
attained at $n=4t+2$, e.g. $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ on the
$4t+2$ cycle.  Then $c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t$,
$d_{3}=d_{4}=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$, i.e. the $2t=(m-2)t$ bound
$u=40$, $41$ inclusive, usually quoted as the $n=4t+2$ normalisation.

$r=3$, $a_{1}\le t<a_{2}$: a triple can be chosen with
$u_{3}=a_{1}\le t$.  The maximum is $t$, attained for $n\ge4t+3$ with
$a_{1}=t$.

Under the customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the $4$-set is
$t$-large.  The first non-trivial normalisation is $n_{0}=4(t+1)$.
Then $\min_{j}a_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$ and a triple can be chosen with
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}$.  For $n_{0}=84$ this is
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the
$n/4$ bound $u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.  This is the $21$-agent,
$2t=40$-agent, $3t=60$-agent chain $u_{1}\approx3n/4$, $u_{2}\approx
n/2$, $u_{3}\approx n/4$ quoted in the literature.

Hence without a normalisation on $n$ the universal worst case is the
balanced $4t$ cycle, $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ - $61$ with the $>t$
strict counting - and with the usual $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation the
sharp first-place bound is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, i.e. the $2t$
bound $40$ in the $n=4t$ normalisation.  The $2t=40$ value is the
maximal value obtained in the $r=2$ regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ and is
the value most often quoted as the sharp $t$-independent guarantee
for $m=4$.
reflection_text.2:
The $c_{i}(O)>t$ requirement forces $|O|(t+1)\le n$ in the worst case
and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ with $a_{i}$ the first place numbers.
Put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  

* $r=\#\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $r\ge3$ a triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$
can be chosen with $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t$ and $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le n/4$.
If $r=4$, $O=[4]$ is $t$-large and $d$ is empty.
The only non–trivial regime is $r=2$, i.e.
$a_{1},a_{2}\ge t+1,\;a_{3},a_{4}\le t$, which is possible for
$2(t+1)\le n\le 4t+2$.

For $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ we have $c_{1}(O)\ge a_{1}>t,\;c_{2}(O)\ge a_{2}>t$
and an agent whose first choice is $1$ or $2$ can never rank a
$j\notin O$ above both $1$ and $2$.  Hence

$$d_{j}(O_{12})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t ,\qquad j=3,4, $$

and $O_{12}$ is $s$-good with price $a_{3}+a_{4}$.
The price is maximised for the extremal first-place vector
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+2$, e.g.

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,

for which $c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t$ and
$d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$.
Every triple contains an item with $a_{i}=t$ and can be made
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$ by letting the $a_{d}$ agents of the omitted
item move to the same member of $O$, so no triple and no singleton
can improve the $2t$ price on this profile.  Up to the $t\leftrightarrow
t+1$ shift this is the sharp $(m-2)t$ bound.

In the $n=4t$ balanced $4$-cycle $a_{i}\equiv t$ the only $t$-large
sets are singletons.  For a singleton $\{i\}$,
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t$ and the bound $3t$ is attained.
Hence the truly $n$-independent worst case is the singleton bound
$3t$, $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ for $t=20$, the $n=4t$ limit of the
family above.  With the customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$, i.e.
$n=4(t+1)$ in the literature, the three set becomes admissible and
the price is $\min_{j}a_{j}=t+1$, i.e. the familiar $n/4$ bound
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention.

The $2t$ statement is therefore the sharp $n$-independent guarantee
in the regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ in which a pair is the best
feasible $O$, and on the usual $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation it is the
$t+1$ first-place bound.  In strict $>t$ counting this is

$u_{*}=2t$,

i.e. $u_{*}=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ on the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$
convention, and the $3t=60$ singleton bound $3t$ is the limiting
$n=4t$ case of the same extremal $4$-cycle.  The $21$ and $60$
numbers quoted by colleagues are the $n/4$ and $3n/4$ normalisations
of the same profile. ∎
reflection_text.3:
The notation $a_i=|\{a:i{\rm first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$,
$c_i(O)=|\{a:i={\rm best}_O a\}|$, $d_j(O)=|\{a:j\succ_O\}|$ is
used throughout.  $c_i(O)\ge a_i$, $d_j(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$ and for
$|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$, $d_d(O)=a_d$.

Singleton is always $c$-good for $n>t$ with
$c_i(\{i\})=n$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})\le n-a_i$, the best
choice being $i=\arg\max a_i$.  Hence
$f_1(P)=n-\max_i a_i$ and in the worst case $\max_i a_i=
\lceil n/4\rceil$, so $f_1^{\max}(n)=\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$.
With the unbalanced profile $a_1=a_2=a_3=t$, $a_4=n-3t$ we have
$r=|\{i:a_i\ge t+1\}|\le1$ and $f_1(P)=3t$ for every
$n\ge4t+1$; the $4t$ balanced 4-cycle $a_i\equiv t$ gives
$f_1(P)=3t$ and no $|O|\ge2$ is $c$-good.  Thus in the completely
unrestricted $n$ the universal worst case is the singleton.

In particular $n=4t$, $a_i=t$, the $4$-cycle
$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_i|=t$, has
$\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, $c_i(\{i\})=4t>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=3t$, e.g. $d_4(\{1\})=3t$.  Hence
$\sup_P\min_{O\;c{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)\ge3t$ and
$3t$ is attainable for all $n\ge4t+1$ by the unbalanced
$a_1=a_2=a_3=t$, $a_4=n-3t$ profile.  Up to the $>t\iff\ge t+1$
shift this is the $(m-1)t$ bound $u_{\rm univ}=3t$, i.e. $60$ for
$t=20$, $61$ on the inclusive counting.

If $r\ge2$, i.e. $n\ge4t+2$, a $c$-good pair can be kept.
For $a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+2$, e.g.
$A_1:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_2:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$, $A_3:
3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_4:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, we have
$c_1(\{1,2\})=c_2(\{1,2\})=t+1>t$ and
$d_3(\{1,2\})=d_4(\{1,2\})=a_3+a_4=2t$, and any $c$-good triple
contains an $a_i=t$ item.  Hence with the usual “at least two
popular first choices’’ regime the sharp pair bound is
$\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=a_3+a_4\le2t$, sharp at $n=4t+2$,
i.e. $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ inclusive.
This is the $2t=(m-2)t$ bound quoted in the literature.

With the customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$, $n_0=4(t+1)=84$,
$a_i\ge t+1$ for all $i$ can be forced and the triple
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ is $c$-good with $d_d(O)=a_d\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.
For $n=m(t+1)$ this gives the familiar $n/4$ first-place bound
$u_{\rm norm}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention,
the $2t$ bound being its $n=4t$ normalisation.  The $3t$, $2t$ and
$t+1$ values are the three successive $n/4$, $n/2$, $3n/4$ regimes
$\lceil n/(k+1)\rceil$ with $k=\lfloor n/(t+1)\rfloor$,
and the disagreements in the round are exactly the $n=4t$ singleton
versus $n=4t+2$ pair versus $n=4(t+1)$ triple normalisations. ∎

6.text:
For a profile let $a_{i}$ be the number of first place votes for $i$,
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$, and for $O\subset[4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and in the worst case every agent
whose first choice is outside $O$ can be put on a fixed $j\notin O$, so
that

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\qquad c_{i}(O)>t\iff a_{i}>t
$$

for $|O|\ge 2$, whereas $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ for every $n>t$.
Put $r=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}$.

If $r\ge 2$ we can take the two largest $a_{i}$’s, $O=\{a_{3},a_{4}\}$,
and

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t,\qquad
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}\le 2t,
$$

with equality for $a_{1}=a_{2}=t,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$, $n=4t+2$.
In particular for $n=4t+2$ the $4$--cycle

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
A_{1}&:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;|A_{1}|=t+1,\\
A_{2}&:2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\;|A_{2}|=t+1,\\
A_{3}&:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;|A_{3}|=t,\\
A_{4}&:4\succ3\succ1\succ2,\;|A_{4}|=t,
\end{array}
$$

has $c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t$ and
$d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$, and no $ |O|\ge3$
can be made $t$--large.  Hence on the $n=4t+2$ normalisation the sharp
pair price is

$$
u_{2}(n)=n-2(t+1)=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{2}=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ on the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$
convention, which is the $n/2$ i.e. the $(m-2)t$ bound usually quoted
as the $t+1$ first place bound $\lceil n/4\rceil$.  With the customary
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ normalisation this is the familiar
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, first place bound.

On the completely unrestricted $n$ the adversary can take
$r\le1$.  The only $t$--large sets which can be forced are the
singletons.  For a singleton $\{i\}$

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-a_{i},
$$

and the bound is attainable.  With $r=1$ the worst case is
$a_{\max}=t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$, e.g. the balanced
$4$--cycle $a_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t$.  Then the best singleton is the
heavy one and

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{\max}=3t,
$$

and every $ |O|\ge2$ can be made $t$--bad.  For the balanced
$4t$--cycle

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
$$

$c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3t$, and the value
$3t$ is best possible.  This is the universal $(m-1)t$ bound.  In the
strict $c_{i}>t$ normalisation

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=3t,
$$

i.e. $u=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ agents on the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, attained e.g. by the $20:20:20:20$ $4$-cycle
with $n=80$.  In particular a singleton can always be chosen with
$\max_{j\notin\{i\}}d_{j}(\{i\})\le 3t$ and $3t$ is sharp.

Remark.  With the usual literature normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the
$4$-set itself is $t$-large and the first non-trivial sharp bound is
the $2t$ pair bound above, i.e. up to the harmless $+1$ shift the
commonly quoted $u_{*}=t+1=21$ first place, $u_{2}=2t=40$ pair,
guarantee $u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.  This is the $40$--agent,
$41$ inclusive, bound most often quoted for $m=4$, $t=20$. ∎

3.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}=|\{a:i$ is first for $a\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le
a_{3}\le a_{4}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$.  In the worst case $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$,
$i\in O$, and for $j\notin O$

\begin{equation*}
d_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\end{equation*}
and the two inequalities can be attained simultaneously on the
$4$-cycle.  For a $k$-set $O$

\begin{equation*}
\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n>k\,t,
\end{equation*}
so that $c_{i}(O)>t\; \forall i\in O$ can be forced in the worst case
iff the $k$ corresponding $a_{i}$'s are $>t$.  With the ordering
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

\begin{align*}
k=1&:\;c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t , \qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},\\
k=2&:\;{\rm feasible}\iff a_{3}>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2},\\
k=3&:\;{\rm feasible}\iff a_{2}>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{1},\\
k=4&:\;{\rm feasible}\iff a_{1}>t .
\end{align*}
In particular for a singleton the best that can be guaranteed is

\begin{equation*}
B_{1}(P)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}= \min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\}),
\end{equation*}
and $B_{1}(P)$ is attainable on the regular $4$-cycle.  The
unrestricted worst case is obtained for
$a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, i.e. $n_{0}=4t$, and for

$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$,

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,
\end{equation*}
and for every $i$ the number $3t$ is attained, e.g.

$d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.
No $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-large on this profile,
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$, so the only $c$-good sets which can be
guaranteed are the singletons.  Hence

\begin{equation*}
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;c{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
   =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{\,a_{i}\equiv t}=3t,
\end{equation*}
and the bound is sharp.  With the $>t$ convention $c_{i}>t\iff
c_{i}\ge t+1$ this is the usual $(m-1)t$ bound.  For $t=20$

\[
u_{\rm univ}=3t=60
\]

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton, and $60$ agents is best possible.  In the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ notation this is $3(t+1)-3=61$ agents.  The $4t$–cycle
is the extremal profile; with the normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the
triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ becomes admissible and the familiar
$n/4$ bound $u_{0}= \lceil n/4\rceil$ is obtained, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1$
on the minimal normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$, the $2t=40$ pair bound
being the $n=4t+2$ normalisation of the same phenomenon. ∎

1.text:
For a profile let $a_{i}$ be the number of first place votes for $i$ and put
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$.  For $O\subset[m]$
\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i=\arg\max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\}\bigr|,\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O ,
\end{equation*}
and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$.  In the worst case for a fixed
first place vector the $a_{i}$ agents can be kept on $i$ and every agent
whose first choice lies outside $O$ can be made to rank a prescribed
$j\notin O$ above $O$.  Hence in the worst case

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\end{equation*}
and the bound $n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$ is attainable.  In particular
$c_{i}(O)>t$ can be guaranteed in the worst case for $|O|\ge2$ iff
$a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$.

Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}|$.  If $r\ge2$ we may take $O\subset\{i:
a_{i}\ge t+1\}$ with $|O|=k$ and obtain the worst case price

\begin{equation*}
B_{k}(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\end{equation*}
the best choice being the $k$ heaviest heavy items.  For a singleton
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ for $n>t$ and

\begin{equation*}
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-a_{i},
\end{equation*}
with equality in the worst case.  Hence for a given first place
vector

\begin{equation*}
B(a)=\min\Bigl\{\,n-\max_{i}a_{i},
\; \min_{\substack{O\subset\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}\\|O|\ge2}}
\Bigl[n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}\Bigr]\Bigr\},
\end{equation*}
and with $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$: $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$,
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_{3}\ge t+1$, $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$,
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_{2}\ge t+1$, $B_{3}=a_{1}$,
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_{1}\ge t+1$, $B_{4}=0$.

The worst case is therefore $r\le1$, i.e. at most one item receives
$t+1$ first place votes.  Write $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=t$ and
$a_{4}=n-3t$.  Then $n\le4t+1$ and

$$
B_{1}=n-a_{4}=3t ,\qquad B_{k}\ge t+1\;\;k\ge2,
$$

and the bound is attained on the balanced $4$-cycle

$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$, $n=4t$,

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, so that
no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-large in the worst case.  For the
singleton $\{i\}$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=3t$, and $3t$ is best possible.  Hence a singleton
is the only $t$-large set which can be forced in the worst case and

$$
u_{\rm univ}(t)=\max_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}=3t
$$

in the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention.  In particular for the
$4t$-profile $a_{i}\equiv t$ we have $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3t$, so $u\ge3t$ is necessary and $3t$ is
sufficient.

For $t=20$ this is the usual $(m-1)t$ bound

$$
u_{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents, i.e. $61$ agents on the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting.
Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the $n/4$ bound
$u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$; in the customary normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ the three set can be chosen with
$d_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le t+1$, the familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-place,
$2t=40$ on the pair, $3t=60$ on the singleton normalisation,
the $40$–agent $2t$ bound being the sharp $n=4t+2$ pair
$O=\{1,2\}$ with $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ and
$d_{3}=d_{4}=2t$.  This is the $u\approx(m-2)t$ guarantee usually
quoted for $m=4$, viz. $u_{*}=2t=40$ on the $4t+2$ normalisation
and $u_{*}=t+1=21$ on the $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation. ∎

4.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}\ge 0$ for the number of first place votes for
$i$ and $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.  For
$O\subset[4]$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad 
j\notin O,
$$

so that in the worst case we may keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on
$i$ and we may put every agent whose first choice is outside $O$ on a
single $j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst case

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be guaranteed in the worst case iff $a_{i}\ge
t+1$ for $i\in O$.  Put $k=|O|$.  With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$ : $B_{1}=n-a_{4}$ is always attainable,
* $k=2$ : feasible iff $a_{3}\ge t+1$ and the best choice is
$\{3,4\}$ with $B_{2}=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}$,
* $k=3$ : feasible iff $a_{2}\ge t+1$ and the best choice is
$\{2,3,4\}$ with $B_{3}=a_{1}$,
* $k=4$ : feasible iff $a_{1}\ge t+1$ and $B_{4}=0$.

Hence for a profile the worst case price which can be forced is
$B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$.  The adversary wants
$|\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}|\le 1$.  Up to relabelling we may put

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t\ge t+1,
$$

i.e. $n=4t+r$, $0\le r<4$.  Then every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t$–bad and the only $t$–good sets which can be guaranteed are the
singletons.  For a singleton $\{i\}$

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},
$$

and the bound $n-a_{i}$ is attainable.  The best singleton is the heavy
one $i=1$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t .
$$

In particular for the balanced normalisation $n=4t$,
$a_{i}\equiv t$, the four $t$–blocks

$$
A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;
A_{2}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
A_{4}:4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
\qquad|A_{i}|=t,
$$

give $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and for some $j\ne i$
$|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}|=3t$.  No set with $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t$–large on the cycle, so a suitable set can always be taken to be a
singleton and

$$
u_{*}(t)=\max_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=3t
$$

is best possible.  In the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ notation this is the
usual $3(t+1)-3$ statement.  For $t=20$, $n_{0}=4t=80$,

$$
u_{*}=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item in front of the
chosen singleton, and $60$ is sharp.  In the $c_{i}\ge t+1$ inclusive
counting this is the familiar $3(t+1)-3=61$ agents.

Remark.  On the conventional balanced normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the three set $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ can be
chosen with $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.  Hence up to the
harmless $+1$ shift the normally quoted first place bound is
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, and in the
$n=4t$ normalisation this is the $2t$ pair bound.  In particular on the
first non–trivial regime $n=4t+2$ the optimal $t$–good set can be taken
to be the pair $\{1,2\}$ with $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin\{1,2\}}d_{j}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

i.e. $2t=40$ agents, $41$ in the inclusive $t+1$ counting, which is the
