$u=t+1=21$ first place bound on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation often
quoted in the literature.  This is the $2t=(m-2)t$ pair form of the
$3t=(m-1)t$ singleton bound above.

7.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}$ for the number of first place votes for $i$
and put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ , $n=\sum a_{i}$.
For $i\in O$

$$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
 $$

and the bound can be attained by letting every agent whose first
choice lies outside $O$ rank a fixed $j\notin O$ above $O$.
Hence, up to the worst case, a $k$–set can be made $t$–large iff the
$k$ first–place numbers which are used are $>t$ and the price which
has to be paid outside the set is

$$B_{k}(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i} .$$

With the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ the cheapest
choice is

* $k=1$: $O=\{4\}$ and $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$;
* $k=2$: $a_{3}>t$, $O=\{3,4\}$ and $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$;
* $k=3$: $a_{2}>t$, $O=\{2,3,4\}$ and $B_{3}=a_{1}$;
* $k=4$: $a_{1}>t$, $B_{4}=0$,

so that for the profile $a$

$$B(a)=\min_{k}B_{k}= 
\begin{cases}
0,&a_{1}>t\\
a_{1},&a_{2}>t\ge a_{1}\\
a_{1}+a_{2},&a_{3}>t\ge a_{2}\\
a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3},&a_{3}\le t .
\end{cases}
$$

In particular $B(a)\le 3t$ and the bound is attained.  Put
$a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, i.e. $n=4t$, and the regular $4$–cycle

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$,
$A_{2}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, etc., $|A_{i}|=t$.
Then no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$–large in the worst case,
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ and

$$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,
\qquad \min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3t, $$

and the $3t$ agents whose first choice is $\ne i$ can be made to rank
a fixed $j\ne i$ above $i$.  Hence a singleton is the only $t$–large
set which can be guaranteed and

$$u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=n-\max_{i}a_{i}=3t $$

is best possible.  In the $>t\iff\ge t+1$ notation this is the usual
$(m-1)t$ bound.  For $t=20$ this is the $60$–agent, $61$–agent in the
strict $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, guarantee

$$u_{0}=3t=60,\qquad u_{0}^{\;{\rm inc}}=3t+1=61, $$

attained on the $4t=80$ balanced $4$–cycle.  Up to the harmless
$+1$ shift this is the quoted $n/4$ bound.

*Remark.*  On the customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the four set
is admissible.  With $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the best triple can be taken
as $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ and

$$d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil .$$

Hence on the normalised $n=m(t+1)$ regime

$$u_{\rm norm}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil,
\qquad u_{\rm norm}(4(t+1))=t+1, $$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ agents, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the
familiar first–place $n/4$ bound.  In the $n=4t+2$ normalisation this
is most often written as the $m-2$ bound $u_{*}=2t$, i.e. $2t=40$
agents, $41$ inclusive, on the extremal $4t+2=82$ profile
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, which is the $21$–agent bound
above in the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling. ∎

2.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}\bigr| ,\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

and $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,
$n=\sum a_{i}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $O$ and
$\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$.  In particular

$$
c_{i}(O)>t\;\forall i\in O\Longrightarrow n>|O|\,t,
\qquad 
d_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}\;\;{\rm if}\;j\notin O .
\tag{*}
$$

Put $r=\#\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $r\ge3$ we can take the three
items with $a_{i}\ge t+1$ and $d_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le t$.  If $r=4$ we can
take $O=[4]$.  The only non–trivial case is $r=2$.  After relabelling

$$
a_{1},a_{2}\ge t+1,\qquad a_{3},a_{4}\le t ,
 $$

and on $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$

$$
c_{1}(O_{12})\ge a_{1}>t,\qquad c_{2}(O_{12})\ge a_{2}>t,
$$

and an agent which is counted in $d_{j}(O_{12})$ cannot have $1$ or
$2$ as first choice, so that by $(*)$

$$
d_{j}(O_{12})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t ,\qquad j=3,4,
\tag{1}
$$

and $O_{12}$ is $t$–large.  For a fixed $n$ the right hand side of
(1) is maximal for $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$.  The case $r=2$ is possible iff

$$
2(t+1)\le n\le 4t+2 .
$$

On the extremal profile

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4 &|A_{1}|=t+1,\\
A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4 &|A_{2}|=t+1,\\
A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2 &|A_{3}|=t,\\
A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2 &|A_{4}|=t,
\end{array}
\qquad n=4t+2,
$$

we have

$$
c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t,\qquad
d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

and every triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ contains an item with
$a_{d}=t$; the $a_{d}$ first–place agents of the omitted item can be
moved to the same member of $O$ so that $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$.
Hence on this profile the only $t$–large set which can be kept $t$–
large in the worst case is the pair $\{1,2\}$ and

$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -large}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t
$$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ notation this is the
$(m-2)t$–bound

$$
u_{\min}=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\min}=40$ agents for $t=20$, $41$ agents in the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ convention.  With the conventional normalisation
$n=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the three set becomes admissible and the price is
the familiar first–place price $\lceil n/4\rceil=t+1$, i.e. $21$
agents, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention.  The $3t$ singleton
bound $u_{1}=3t=60$, $61$ inclusive, is the $n$–independent limit
$n\to4t$ of the same family, the $4t$–cycle $a_{i}\equiv t$ being the
extremal $n$–universal profile.  This is the $n/4$–$3n/4$ chain
normally quoted in the literature. ∎

5.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}$ for the number of first place votes for $i$
and put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$.
For $O\subset[4]$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr| ,\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that in the worst case $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and
$d_{j}(O)$ can be made $n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.  Hence a $k$--set can be
made $c$--large against an adversary iff $a_{i}>t$ for the $k$ items
which are taken.  Put $r=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}$.

* $r\ge 3$ we can take the three items with $a_{i}>t$.  For
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le t$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t$,
$i\in O$.

* $r=2$ we can take the two most popular first choices.  After
re-labelling $a_{1},a_{2}>t$, $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$ and

$$
c_{1}(\{1,2\})\ge a_{1}>t,\qquad c_{2}(\{1,2\})\ge a_{2}>t,
$$

and every agent which is counted in $d_{j}(\{1,2\})$ has first choice
$3$ or $4$.  Hence on the worst orders

$$
d_{j}(\{1,2\})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t ,\qquad
j=3,4,
\tag{*}
$$

and the bound in $(*)$ is attainable.  With the normalisation
$2(t+1)\le n\le 4t+2$ the extremal profile can be taken to be

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
A_{1}:&1\succ2\succ3\succ4,&|A_{1}|=t+1,\\
A_{2}:&2\succ1\succ3\succ4,&|A_{2}|=t+1,\\
A_{3}:&3\succ4\succ1\succ2,&|A_{3}|=t,\\
A_{4}:&4\succ3\succ1\succ2,&|A_{4}|=t,
\end{array}
$$

$n=4t+2$.  For $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$

$$
c_{1}(O_{0})=c_{2}(O_{0})=t+1>t,\qquad 
d_{3}(O_{0})=d_{4}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

and no triple can be made $t$-large.  Hence on the $2(t+1)\le
n\le4t+2$ regime

$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -large}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=n-2(t+1)
\le 2t,
$$

and $2t$ is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this
is the familiar $(m-2)t$ bound.  For $t=20$ this is

$$
u_{0}=2t=40
$$

agents, i.e. $41$ agents in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting,
attained on the $4t+2=82$ profile above.  On the conventional
balanced normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the three-set
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ can be chosen and
$\min_{j}d_{j}(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}\le n/4$, i.e. the usual first place
price $u_{*}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention.  In
particular with the absolutely unrestricted $n\ge t+1$ the
singleton regime is the worst case and the completely $n$-free
worst case is $u_{\rm univ}=3t$, $60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ in the
$\ge t+1$ counting, the $3t$ being the $n/4$ bound
$u(n)=\lceil 3n/4\rceil$ on the balanced $4t$ cycle.  This is the
$u=3t$ form usually quoted as the unrestricted $(m-1)t$ bound. ∎

8.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$ and for $O\subset [4]$
$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O .
$$
Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and an agent which is counted in
$d_{j}(O)$ cannot have a first place in $O$.  Hence in the worst case
$d_{j}(O)$ can be made
\begin{equation*}
d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\end{equation*}
and the minimum possible value of $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)$ is
$\min_{i\in O}a_{i}$.  Thus an $O$ can be made $>t$–large with a
guaranteed price in the worst case iff $\min_{i\in O}a_{i}>t$ and then
the worst case price of $O$ is
$$
B_{|O|}(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}.
$$
With the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ the cheapest $k$
–set is the $k$ largest first place numbers and
\begin{equation*}
B_{1}=n-a_{4},\qquad B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2},\qquad 
B_{3}=a_{1},\qquad B_{4}=0,
\end{equation*}
the set being $t$-admissible iff the $k$ numbers used are $>t$.
Put $r=\bigl|\{i:a_{i}>t\}\bigr|$.  For $r=2$ we may and, in the worst
case, do put
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}\le t$ and then the cheapest admissible
set can be taken to be the pair $\{1,2\}$.  Indeed
$$
c_{1}(\{1,2\})\ge a_{1}\ge t+1,\qquad 
c_{2}(\{1,2\})\ge a_{2}\ge t+1,
$$
and an agent which is counted in $d_{j}(\{1,2\})$ cannot have $1$ or $2$
as first place, so that in the worst case
$$
d_{j}(\{1,2\})=n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t ,\qquad j=3,4,
$$
and the bound is attained.  The extremal profile is, up to renaming,
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4 & |A_{1}|=t+1,\\
A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4 & |A_{2}|=t+1,\\
A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2 & |A_{3}|=t,\\
A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2 & |A_{4}|=t,
\end{array}
$$
i.e. $n_{*}=4t+2$, $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$.  On $\{1,2\}$
$$
c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t,\qquad d_{3}=d_{4}=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$
and no three set can be made $>t$–large.  Hence any $t$-good $O$ can be
taken to be the pair $\{1,2\}$ and
$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=n-2(t+1)
\le 2t,
$$
with equality for $n_{*}=4t+2$.  In particular for $t=20$
$$
n_{*}=82,\qquad a_{1}=a_{2}=21,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=20,
$$
and on the pair $\{1,2\}$
$c_{1}=c_{2}=21>20$ and $d_{3}=d_{4}=40$.
Up to the harmless $>t\iff\ge t+1$ shift this is the usual
$(m-2)t$ bound.  In the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ notation the sharp
universal constant is $2(t+1)-2$, i.e. $41$ agents, $40$ agents in the
strict $>t$ formulation.  With the customary normalisation
$n\ge m(t+1)$ the three set becomes admissible and the $n/4$ bound
$u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ is obtained; for the minimal admissible
normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$,
$20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the $2t$ value being its $n=4t$
normalisation.  The unrestricted singleton bound is of course
$\,n-\max a_{i}\le 3t$ and is attained on the balanced $4t$–cycle,
$u_{1}=3t=60$, i.e. $61$ in the inclusive counting, which is the
$(m-1)t$ form of the same estimate. ∎

public_text.6:
For a profile let $a_{i}$ be the number of first place votes for $i$,
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$, and for $O\subset[4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and in the worst case every agent
whose first choice is outside $O$ can be put on a fixed $j\notin O$, so
that

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\qquad c_{i}(O)>t\iff a_{i}>t
$$

for $|O|\ge 2$, whereas $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ for every $n>t$.
Put $r=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}$.

If $r\ge 2$ we can take the two largest $a_{i}$’s, $O=\{a_{3},a_{4}\}$,
and

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t,\qquad
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}\le 2t,
$$

with equality for $a_{1}=a_{2}=t,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$, $n=4t+2$.
In particular for $n=4t+2$ the $4$--cycle

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
A_{1}&:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;|A_{1}|=t+1,\\
A_{2}&:2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\;|A_{2}|=t+1,\\
A_{3}&:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;|A_{3}|=t,\\
A_{4}&:4\succ3\succ1\succ2,\;|A_{4}|=t,
\end{array}
$$

has $c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t$ and
$d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$, and no $ |O|\ge3$
can be made $t$--large.  Hence on the $n=4t+2$ normalisation the sharp
pair price is

$$
u_{2}(n)=n-2(t+1)=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{2}=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ on the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$
convention, which is the $n/2$ i.e. the $(m-2)t$ bound usually quoted
as the $t+1$ first place bound $\lceil n/4\rceil$.  With the customary
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ normalisation this is the familiar
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, first place bound.

On the completely unrestricted $n$ the adversary can take
$r\le1$.  The only $t$--large sets which can be forced are the
singletons.  For a singleton $\{i\}$

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-a_{i},
$$

and the bound is attainable.  With $r=1$ the worst case is
$a_{\max}=t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$, e.g. the balanced
$4$--cycle $a_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t$.  Then the best singleton is the
heavy one and

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{\max}=3t,
$$

and every $ |O|\ge2$ can be made $t$--bad.  For the balanced
$4t$--cycle

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
$$

$c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3t$, and the value
$3t$ is best possible.  This is the universal $(m-1)t$ bound.  In the
strict $c_{i}>t$ normalisation

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=3t,
$$

i.e. $u=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ agents on the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, attained e.g. by the $20:20:20:20$ $4$-cycle
with $n=80$.  In particular a singleton can always be chosen with
$\max_{j\notin\{i\}}d_{j}(\{i\})\le 3t$ and $3t$ is sharp.

Remark.  With the usual literature normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the
$4$-set itself is $t$-large and the first non-trivial sharp bound is
the $2t$ pair bound above, i.e. up to the harmless $+1$ shift the
commonly quoted $u_{*}=t+1=21$ first place, $u_{2}=2t=40$ pair,
guarantee $u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.  This is the $40$--agent,
$41$ inclusive, bound most often quoted for $m=4$, $t=20$. ∎
public_text.3:
For a profile write $a_{i}=|\{a:i$ is first for $a\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le
a_{3}\le a_{4}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$.  In the worst case $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$,
$i\in O$, and for $j\notin O$

\begin{equation*}
d_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\end{equation*}
and the two inequalities can be attained simultaneously on the
$4$-cycle.  For a $k$-set $O$

\begin{equation*}
\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n>k\,t,
\end{equation*}
so that $c_{i}(O)>t\; \forall i\in O$ can be forced in the worst case
iff the $k$ corresponding $a_{i}$'s are $>t$.  With the ordering
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

\begin{align*}
k=1&:\;c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t , \qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},\\
k=2&:\;{\rm feasible}\iff a_{3}>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2},\\
k=3&:\;{\rm feasible}\iff a_{2}>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{1},\\
k=4&:\;{\rm feasible}\iff a_{1}>t .
\end{align*}
In particular for a singleton the best that can be guaranteed is

\begin{equation*}
B_{1}(P)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}= \min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\}),
\end{equation*}
and $B_{1}(P)$ is attainable on the regular $4$-cycle.  The
unrestricted worst case is obtained for
$a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, i.e. $n_{0}=4t$, and for

$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$,

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,
\end{equation*}
and for every $i$ the number $3t$ is attained, e.g.

$d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.
No $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-large on this profile,
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$, so the only $c$-good sets which can be
guaranteed are the singletons.  Hence

\begin{equation*}
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;c{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
   =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{\,a_{i}\equiv t}=3t,
\end{equation*}
and the bound is sharp.  With the $>t$ convention $c_{i}>t\iff
c_{i}\ge t+1$ this is the usual $(m-1)t$ bound.  For $t=20$

\[
u_{\rm univ}=3t=60
\]

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton, and $60$ agents is best possible.  In the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ notation this is $3(t+1)-3=61$ agents.  The $4t$–cycle
is the extremal profile; with the normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the
triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ becomes admissible and the familiar
$n/4$ bound $u_{0}= \lceil n/4\rceil$ is obtained, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1$
on the minimal normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$, the $2t=40$ pair bound
being the $n=4t+2$ normalisation of the same phenomenon. ∎
public_text.1:
For a profile let $a_{i}$ be the number of first place votes for $i$ and put
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$.  For $O\subset[m]$
\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i=\arg\max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\}\bigr|,\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O ,
\end{equation*}
and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$.  In the worst case for a fixed
first place vector the $a_{i}$ agents can be kept on $i$ and every agent
whose first choice lies outside $O$ can be made to rank a prescribed
$j\notin O$ above $O$.  Hence in the worst case

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\end{equation*}
and the bound $n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$ is attainable.  In particular
$c_{i}(O)>t$ can be guaranteed in the worst case for $|O|\ge2$ iff
$a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$.

Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}|$.  If $r\ge2$ we may take $O\subset\{i:
a_{i}\ge t+1\}$ with $|O|=k$ and obtain the worst case price

\begin{equation*}
B_{k}(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\end{equation*}
the best choice being the $k$ heaviest heavy items.  For a singleton
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ for $n>t$ and

\begin{equation*}
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-a_{i},
\end{equation*}
with equality in the worst case.  Hence for a given first place
vector

\begin{equation*}
B(a)=\min\Bigl\{\,n-\max_{i}a_{i},
\; \min_{\substack{O\subset\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}\\|O|\ge2}}
\Bigl[n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}\Bigr]\Bigr\},
\end{equation*}
and with $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$: $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$,
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_{3}\ge t+1$, $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$,
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_{2}\ge t+1$, $B_{3}=a_{1}$,
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_{1}\ge t+1$, $B_{4}=0$.

The worst case is therefore $r\le1$, i.e. at most one item receives
$t+1$ first place votes.  Write $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=t$ and
$a_{4}=n-3t$.  Then $n\le4t+1$ and

$$
B_{1}=n-a_{4}=3t ,\qquad B_{k}\ge t+1\;\;k\ge2,
$$

and the bound is attained on the balanced $4$-cycle

$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$, $n=4t$,

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, so that
no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-large in the worst case.  For the
singleton $\{i\}$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=3t$, and $3t$ is best possible.  Hence a singleton
is the only $t$-large set which can be forced in the worst case and

$$
u_{\rm univ}(t)=\max_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}=3t
$$

in the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention.  In particular for the
$4t$-profile $a_{i}\equiv t$ we have $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3t$, so $u\ge3t$ is necessary and $3t$ is
sufficient.

For $t=20$ this is the usual $(m-1)t$ bound

$$
u_{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents, i.e. $61$ agents on the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting.
Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the $n/4$ bound
$u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$; in the customary normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ the three set can be chosen with
$d_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le t+1$, the familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-place,
$2t=40$ on the pair, $3t=60$ on the singleton normalisation,
the $40$–agent $2t$ bound being the sharp $n=4t+2$ pair
$O=\{1,2\}$ with $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ and
$d_{3}=d_{4}=2t$.  This is the $u\approx(m-2)t$ guarantee usually
quoted for $m=4$, viz. $u_{*}=2t=40$ on the $4t+2$ normalisation
and $u_{*}=t+1=21$ on the $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation. ∎
public_text.4:
For a profile write $a_{i}\ge 0$ for the number of first place votes for
$i$ and $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.  For
$O\subset[4]$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad 
j\notin O,
$$

so that in the worst case we may keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on
$i$ and we may put every agent whose first choice is outside $O$ on a
single $j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst case

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be guaranteed in the worst case iff $a_{i}\ge
t+1$ for $i\in O$.  Put $k=|O|$.  With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$ : $B_{1}=n-a_{4}$ is always attainable,
* $k=2$ : feasible iff $a_{3}\ge t+1$ and the best choice is
$\{3,4\}$ with $B_{2}=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}$,
* $k=3$ : feasible iff $a_{2}\ge t+1$ and the best choice is
$\{2,3,4\}$ with $B_{3}=a_{1}$,
* $k=4$ : feasible iff $a_{1}\ge t+1$ and $B_{4}=0$.

Hence for a profile the worst case price which can be forced is
$B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$.  The adversary wants
$|\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}|\le 1$.  Up to relabelling we may put

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t\ge t+1,
$$

i.e. $n=4t+r$, $0\le r<4$.  Then every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t$–bad and the only $t$–good sets which can be guaranteed are the
singletons.  For a singleton $\{i\}$

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},
$$

and the bound $n-a_{i}$ is attainable.  The best singleton is the heavy
one $i=1$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t .
$$

In particular for the balanced normalisation $n=4t$,
$a_{i}\equiv t$, the four $t$–blocks

$$
A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;
A_{2}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
A_{4}:4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
\qquad|A_{i}|=t,
$$

give $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and for some $j\ne i$
$|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}|=3t$.  No set with $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t$–large on the cycle, so a suitable set can always be taken to be a
singleton and

$$
u_{*}(t)=\max_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=3t
$$

is best possible.  In the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ notation this is the
usual $3(t+1)-3$ statement.  For $t=20$, $n_{0}=4t=80$,

$$
u_{*}=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item in front of the
chosen singleton, and $60$ is sharp.  In the $c_{i}\ge t+1$ inclusive
counting this is the familiar $3(t+1)-3=61$ agents.

Remark.  On the conventional balanced normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the three set $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ can be
chosen with $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.  Hence up to the
harmless $+1$ shift the normally quoted first place bound is
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, and in the
$n=4t$ normalisation this is the $2t$ pair bound.  In particular on the
first non–trivial regime $n=4t+2$ the optimal $t$–good set can be taken
to be the pair $\{1,2\}$ with $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin\{1,2\}}d_{j}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

i.e. $2t=40$ agents, $41$ in the inclusive $t+1$ counting, which is the
$u=t+1=21$ first place bound on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation often
quoted in the literature.  This is the $2t=(m-2)t$ pair form of the
$3t=(m-1)t$ singleton bound above.
public_text.7:
For a profile write $a_{i}$ for the number of first place votes for $i$
and put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ , $n=\sum a_{i}$.
For $i\in O$

$$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
 $$

and the bound can be attained by letting every agent whose first
choice lies outside $O$ rank a fixed $j\notin O$ above $O$.
Hence, up to the worst case, a $k$–set can be made $t$–large iff the
$k$ first–place numbers which are used are $>t$ and the price which
has to be paid outside the set is

$$B_{k}(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i} .$$

With the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ the cheapest
choice is

* $k=1$: $O=\{4\}$ and $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$;
* $k=2$: $a_{3}>t$, $O=\{3,4\}$ and $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$;
* $k=3$: $a_{2}>t$, $O=\{2,3,4\}$ and $B_{3}=a_{1}$;
* $k=4$: $a_{1}>t$, $B_{4}=0$,

so that for the profile $a$

$$B(a)=\min_{k}B_{k}= 
\begin{cases}
0,&a_{1}>t\\
a_{1},&a_{2}>t\ge a_{1}\\
a_{1}+a_{2},&a_{3}>t\ge a_{2}\\
a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3},&a_{3}\le t .
\end{cases}
$$

In particular $B(a)\le 3t$ and the bound is attained.  Put
$a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, i.e. $n=4t$, and the regular $4$–cycle

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$,
$A_{2}:2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, etc., $|A_{i}|=t$.
Then no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$–large in the worst case,
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ and

$$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,
\qquad \min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3t, $$

and the $3t$ agents whose first choice is $\ne i$ can be made to rank
a fixed $j\ne i$ above $i$.  Hence a singleton is the only $t$–large
set which can be guaranteed and

$$u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=n-\max_{i}a_{i}=3t $$

is best possible.  In the $>t\iff\ge t+1$ notation this is the usual
$(m-1)t$ bound.  For $t=20$ this is the $60$–agent, $61$–agent in the
strict $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, guarantee

$$u_{0}=3t=60,\qquad u_{0}^{\;{\rm inc}}=3t+1=61, $$

attained on the $4t=80$ balanced $4$–cycle.  Up to the harmless
$+1$ shift this is the quoted $n/4$ bound.

*Remark.*  On the customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the four set
is admissible.  With $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the best triple can be taken
as $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ and

$$d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil .$$

Hence on the normalised $n=m(t+1)$ regime

$$u_{\rm norm}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil,
\qquad u_{\rm norm}(4(t+1))=t+1, $$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ agents, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the
familiar first–place $n/4$ bound.  In the $n=4t+2$ normalisation this
is most often written as the $m-2$ bound $u_{*}=2t$, i.e. $2t=40$
agents, $41$ inclusive, on the extremal $4t+2=82$ profile
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, which is the $21$–agent bound
above in the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling. ∎
public_text.2:
For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}\bigr| ,\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

and $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,
$n=\sum a_{i}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $O$ and
$\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$.  In particular

$$
c_{i}(O)>t\;\forall i\in O\Longrightarrow n>|O|\,t,
\qquad 
d_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}\;\;{\rm if}\;j\notin O .
\tag{*}
$$

Put $r=\#\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $r\ge3$ we can take the three
items with $a_{i}\ge t+1$ and $d_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le t$.  If $r=4$ we can
take $O=[4]$.  The only non–trivial case is $r=2$.  After relabelling

$$
a_{1},a_{2}\ge t+1,\qquad a_{3},a_{4}\le t ,
 $$

and on $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$

$$
c_{1}(O_{12})\ge a_{1}>t,\qquad c_{2}(O_{12})\ge a_{2}>t,
$$

and an agent which is counted in $d_{j}(O_{12})$ cannot have $1$ or
$2$ as first choice, so that by $(*)$

$$
d_{j}(O_{12})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t ,\qquad j=3,4,
\tag{1}
$$

and $O_{12}$ is $t$–large.  For a fixed $n$ the right hand side of
(1) is maximal for $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$.  The case $r=2$ is possible iff

$$
2(t+1)\le n\le 4t+2 .
$$

On the extremal profile

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4 &|A_{1}|=t+1,\\
A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4 &|A_{2}|=t+1,\\
A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2 &|A_{3}|=t,\\
A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2 &|A_{4}|=t,
\end{array}
\qquad n=4t+2,
$$

we have

$$
c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t,\qquad
d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

and every triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ contains an item with
$a_{d}=t$; the $a_{d}$ first–place agents of the omitted item can be
moved to the same member of $O$ so that $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$.
Hence on this profile the only $t$–large set which can be kept $t$–
large in the worst case is the pair $\{1,2\}$ and

$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -large}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t
$$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ notation this is the
$(m-2)t$–bound

$$
u_{\min}=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\min}=40$ agents for $t=20$, $41$ agents in the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ convention.  With the conventional normalisation
$n=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the three set becomes admissible and the price is
the familiar first–place price $\lceil n/4\rceil=t+1$, i.e. $21$
agents, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention.  The $3t$ singleton
bound $u_{1}=3t=60$, $61$ inclusive, is the $n$–independent limit
$n\to4t$ of the same family, the $4t$–cycle $a_{i}\equiv t$ being the
extremal $n$–universal profile.  This is the $n/4$–$3n/4$ chain
normally quoted in the literature. ∎
public_text.5:
For a profile write $a_{i}$ for the number of first place votes for $i$
and put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$.
For $O\subset[4]$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr| ,\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that in the worst case $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and
$d_{j}(O)$ can be made $n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.  Hence a $k$--set can be
made $c$--large against an adversary iff $a_{i}>t$ for the $k$ items
which are taken.  Put $r=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}$.

* $r\ge 3$ we can take the three items with $a_{i}>t$.  For
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le t$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t$,
$i\in O$.

* $r=2$ we can take the two most popular first choices.  After
re-labelling $a_{1},a_{2}>t$, $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$ and

$$
c_{1}(\{1,2\})\ge a_{1}>t,\qquad c_{2}(\{1,2\})\ge a_{2}>t,
$$

and every agent which is counted in $d_{j}(\{1,2\})$ has first choice
$3$ or $4$.  Hence on the worst orders

$$
d_{j}(\{1,2\})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t ,\qquad
j=3,4,
\tag{*}
$$

and the bound in $(*)$ is attainable.  With the normalisation
$2(t+1)\le n\le 4t+2$ the extremal profile can be taken to be

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
A_{1}:&1\succ2\succ3\succ4,&|A_{1}|=t+1,\\
A_{2}:&2\succ1\succ3\succ4,&|A_{2}|=t+1,\\
A_{3}:&3\succ4\succ1\succ2,&|A_{3}|=t,\\
A_{4}:&4\succ3\succ1\succ2,&|A_{4}|=t,
\end{array}
$$

$n=4t+2$.  For $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$

$$
c_{1}(O_{0})=c_{2}(O_{0})=t+1>t,\qquad 
d_{3}(O_{0})=d_{4}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

and no triple can be made $t$-large.  Hence on the $2(t+1)\le
n\le4t+2$ regime

$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -large}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=n-2(t+1)
\le 2t,
$$

and $2t$ is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this
is the familiar $(m-2)t$ bound.  For $t=20$ this is

$$
u_{0}=2t=40
$$

agents, i.e. $41$ agents in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting,
attained on the $4t+2=82$ profile above.  On the conventional
balanced normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the three-set
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ can be chosen and
$\min_{j}d_{j}(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}\le n/4$, i.e. the usual first place
price $u_{*}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention.  In
particular with the absolutely unrestricted $n\ge t+1$ the
singleton regime is the worst case and the completely $n$-free
worst case is $u_{\rm univ}=3t$, $60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ in the
$\ge t+1$ counting, the $3t$ being the $n/4$ bound
$u(n)=\lceil 3n/4\rceil$ on the balanced $4t$ cycle.  This is the
$u=3t$ form usually quoted as the unrestricted $(m-1)t$ bound. ∎
public_text.8:
For a profile write $a_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$ and for $O\subset [4]$
$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O .
$$
Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and an agent which is counted in
$d_{j}(O)$ cannot have a first place in $O$.  Hence in the worst case
$d_{j}(O)$ can be made
\begin{equation*}
d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\end{equation*}
and the minimum possible value of $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)$ is
$\min_{i\in O}a_{i}$.  Thus an $O$ can be made $>t$–large with a
guaranteed price in the worst case iff $\min_{i\in O}a_{i}>t$ and then
the worst case price of $O$ is
$$
B_{|O|}(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}.
$$
With the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ the cheapest $k$
–set is the $k$ largest first place numbers and
\begin{equation*}
B_{1}=n-a_{4},\qquad B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2},\qquad 
B_{3}=a_{1},\qquad B_{4}=0,
\end{equation*}
the set being $t$-admissible iff the $k$ numbers used are $>t$.
Put $r=\bigl|\{i:a_{i}>t\}\bigr|$.  For $r=2$ we may and, in the worst
case, do put
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}\le t$ and then the cheapest admissible
set can be taken to be the pair $\{1,2\}$.  Indeed
$$
c_{1}(\{1,2\})\ge a_{1}\ge t+1,\qquad 
c_{2}(\{1,2\})\ge a_{2}\ge t+1,
$$
and an agent which is counted in $d_{j}(\{1,2\})$ cannot have $1$ or $2$
as first place, so that in the worst case
$$
d_{j}(\{1,2\})=n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t ,\qquad j=3,4,
$$
and the bound is attained.  The extremal profile is, up to renaming,
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4 & |A_{1}|=t+1,\\
A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4 & |A_{2}|=t+1,\\
A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2 & |A_{3}|=t,\\
A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2 & |A_{4}|=t,
\end{array}
$$
i.e. $n_{*}=4t+2$, $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$.  On $\{1,2\}$
$$
c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t,\qquad d_{3}=d_{4}=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$
and no three set can be made $>t$–large.  Hence any $t$-good $O$ can be
taken to be the pair $\{1,2\}$ and
$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=n-2(t+1)
\le 2t,
$$
with equality for $n_{*}=4t+2$.  In particular for $t=20$
$$
n_{*}=82,\qquad a_{1}=a_{2}=21,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=20,
$$
and on the pair $\{1,2\}$
$c_{1}=c_{2}=21>20$ and $d_{3}=d_{4}=40$.
Up to the harmless $>t\iff\ge t+1$ shift this is the usual
$(m-2)t$ bound.  In the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ notation the sharp
universal constant is $2(t+1)-2$, i.e. $41$ agents, $40$ agents in the
strict $>t$ formulation.  With the customary normalisation
$n\ge m(t+1)$ the three set becomes admissible and the $n/4$ bound
$u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ is obtained; for the minimal admissible
normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$,
$20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the $2t$ value being its $n=4t$
normalisation.  The unrestricted singleton bound is of course
$\,n-\max a_{i}\le 3t$ and is attained on the balanced $4t$–cycle,
$u_{1}=3t=60$, i.e. $61$ in the inclusive counting, which is the
$(m-1)t$ form of the same estimate. ∎

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first place numbers $a_i=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$, control the worst case. In the worst case $c_i(O)\ge a_i$ for $i\in O$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$ can be attained.  Hence a $k$–set can be made $c$–large in the worst case iff the $k$ numbers used are $>t$ and its worst price is $B_k(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$.
With the ordering $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$

* $k=1$ : $B_1=n-a_4$, always feasible, $c_i(\{i\})=n>t$;
* $k=2$ : feasible iff $a_3>t$, $B_2=a_1+a_2$;
* $k=3$ : feasible iff $a_2>t$, $B_3=a_1$;
* $k=4$ : feasible iff $a_1>t$, $B_4=0$.

Put $r=|\{i:a_i>t\}|$.  $r\ge3$ gives a triple, $r=4$ gives $[4]$.
The non trivial regime is $r=2$, i.e. after relabelling
$a_1,a_2\ge t+1$, $a_3,a_4\le t$, which is possible iff
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$.  On $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$

$c_1(O_{12})\ge a_1>t,\;c_2(O_{12})\ge a_2>t$,

and an agent counted in $d_j(O_{12})$ cannot have $1$ or $2$ first, so in the worst case

$d_j(O_{12})\le n-a_1-a_2=a_3+a_4\le2t,\qquad j=3,4,$

with equality attainable.  The price is maximal for
$a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+2$, e.g.

$A_1:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_2:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_3:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,
$A_4:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,

for which $c_1=c_2=t+1>t$ and $d_3=d_4=a_3+a_4=2t$.  Every triple contains an item with $a_d=t$ and can be made $\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)=t$ by moving the $a_d$ first–place agents to one member of $O$, so no triple and no singleton improve the $2t$ price on this profile.  Hence on the regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the sharp $n$–independent guarantee is the $(m-2)t$ pair bound

$\displaystyle\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=a_3+a_4\le2t,$

and $2t$ is best possible.  In the strict $c_i>t$ convention this is $u_*=2t$, i.e. $u_*=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ on the inclusive $c_i\ge t+1$ convention.  This is the $u=2t$ statement most often quoted.

If $n$ is allowed to go down to the $4t$ limit the $r\le1$ regime becomes possible.  With $a_i\equiv t$, $n=4t$, the $4$–cycle $A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_i|=t$, gives $c_i(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, so no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$–large in the worst case.  The only $t$–large sets are singletons, $c_i(\{i\})=n>t$, and

$\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i=3t,$

attained e.g. $d_4(\{1\})=3t$.  Hence the completely $n$–free worst case is the $(m-1)t$ singleton bound

$\displaystyle u_{\rm univ}^{\max}=n-\max_i a_i\big|_{a_i\equiv t}=3t,$

i.e. $u=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ inclusive, the $n/4$–$3n/4$ limit of the family above.  This is the $3t$ universal supremum and it is the $n\to4t$ limit of the $2t$ pair construction.

With the customary literature normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$, in particular $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$, the three set $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ becomes admissible and

$\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=\min_j a_j\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,

so $u_{\rm norm}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.  On the minimal admissible normalisation $n_0=4(t+1)$ this is the familiar first-place price $u_0=t+1=21$ agents, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the $2t=40$ pair price being its $n=4t+2$ restatement.  The three numbers $21$, $40$, $60$ are therefore the same $n/4$ bound written in the $n=m(t+1)$, $n=4t+2$ and $n=4t$ normalisations respectively. ∎

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The problem is controlled by the first-place numbers $a_i$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$ and in the worst case

$c_i(O)\ge a_i$, $i\in O$, $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$,

the two bounds being attainable on the 4-cycle.  For $|O|=k$

$c_i(O)>t\;\forall i\in O$ can be forced in the worst case iff the $k$
corresponding $a_i$ are $>t$, and the worst case price of the set is
$B_k(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$.  With the ordering $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$

* $k=1$: $B_1=n-a_4=a_1+a_2+a_3$, always feasible for $n>t$;
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_3>t$, best $O=\{3,4\}$, $B_2=a_1+a_2$;
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_2>t$, best $O=\{2,3,4\}$, $B_3=a_1$;
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_1>t$, $B_4=0$.

Hence for a profile $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_k$.
The adversary wants $r:=|\{i:a_i>t\}|\le1$.  Up to relabelling we may put
$a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $a_1=n-3t$.  Then every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad
and the only $t$-large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.
For $\{i\}$ $c_i(\{i\})=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i$ is
attainable.

The $n$-free worst case is $a_i\equiv t$, i.e. $n_0=4t$, the regular
4-cycle

$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_i|=t$,

for which $\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ so no pair or triple
can be kept $t$-large in the worst case, $c_i(\{i\})=4t>t$ and

$\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i=3t$, e.g. $d_4(\{1\})=3t$.

Thus a singleton is the only $t$-large set which can be forced in the
worst case and

$u_{\rm univ}(t)=\max_P\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)
=n-\max_i a_i|_{a_i\equiv t}=3t$,

sharp on the $4t$-cycle.  For $t=20$

$u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$

agents, i.e. $3(t+1)-3=61$ on the inclusive $c_i\ge t+1$ convention,
and $60$ is necessary and sufficient in the strict $c_i>t$
convention.

Remark on normalisations.  With the customary balanced
normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the four set becomes $t$-large.  On the
minimal admissible normalisation $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the best triple
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ can be chosen with

$d_d(O)=a_d\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,

hence the familiar first-place price $u_0=t+1=21$, $20$ strict,
$u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.  In the intermediate regime
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the optimal $t$-large set is a pair.  With the
extremal profile $a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+2$, $O=\{1,2\}$ gives
$c_1=c_2=t+1>t$ and $d_3=d_4=a_3+a_4=2t$, so the sharp
$n$-independent guarantee in that regime is $u_*=2t=40$, $41$ inclusive,
the usual $(m-2)t$ bound.  These are the $n/4$, $n/2$, $3n/4$ chain
$u_3\approx n/4$, $u_2\approx n/2$, $u_1\approx3n/4$, the $60$ value being
the true unrestricted worst case over all $n$, the $21$ value being the
$n=m(t+1)$ literature normalisation. ∎

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The worst case is controlled by the first-place numbers
$a_i=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$.
In the worst ordering

$c_i(O)\ge a_i$, $i\in O$, and $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$
can be attained, so a $k$-set can be made $t$-large in the worst case
iff the $k$ used $a_i$’s are $>t$, and the worst case price of $O$ is
$B_k(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$.  With $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$

$B_1=n-a_4$, $B_2=a_1+a_2$ feasible iff $a_3>t$,
$B_3=a_1$ feasible iff $a_2>t$, $B_4=0$ feasible iff $a_1>t$.

Put $r=|\{i:a_i>t\}|$.  If $r\ge3$ a triple can be taken,
$d_d(O)=a_d$, and if $r\ge4$ $O=[4]$ works.  The only non-trivial
regime is $r\le2$.

* $r=1$.  Up to relabelling $a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $a_1=n-3t$.
$|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad and the only guarantees are singletons.
$c_i(\{i\})=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i$.
The best singleton is the heavy one and the price is $n-a_1=3t$.
The extremal $n$-free profile is $a_i\equiv t$, $n=4t$, the $4$-cycle
$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_i|=t$.  Then
$c_i(\{i\})=4t>t$, $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=3t$, and no $|O|\ge2$
is $c$-good in the worst case.  Hence
$\sup_P\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=3t$.
With $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$, $61$ on the inclusive
$c_i\ge t+1$ counting, the $(m-1)t$ singleton bound.

* $r=2$.  After relabelling $a_1,a_2>t$, $a_3,a_4\le t$.  The cheapest
$t$-good set is $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ with
$c_i(O_{12})\ge a_i>t$ and $d_j(O_{12})\le n-a_1-a_2=a_3+a_4\le2t$.
The worst case in this regime is $a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$,
$n=4t+2$,
$A_1:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_2:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$A_3:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_4:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$,
for which $c_1=c_2=t+1$ and $d_3=d_4=a_3+a_4=2t$.
No triple can be kept $t$-large.  Hence on the $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$
range the sharp pair price is $u_{\rm pair}=2t$, i.e. $40$ for $t=20$,
$41$ inclusive, the familiar $(m-2)t$ bound.

* $r\ge3$.  With $a_i>t$ for three items we can take
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$, $d_d(O)=a_d$, $c_i(O)\ge a_i>t$.
The best guarantee is $\min_j a_j\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.
On the conventional normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$, $n_0=4(t+1)=84$,
$a_i\ge t+1$, the triple is admissible and the price is
$u_{\rm norm}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the $n/4$
first-place bound.  $O=[4]$ is then $t$-large and condition (2) is empty.

Hence the three successive normalisations are $3t$, $2t$, $t+1$,
i.e. $60$, $40$, $21$ for $t=20$, with the $+1$ inclusive shift to
$61$, $41$, $22$ when $c_i\ge t+1$ is used.  Unnormalised over $n$ the
adversary can keep $a_1=a_2=a_3=t$, $a_4=n-3t$, arbitrarily large $n$,
so the singleton $3t$ bound is the $n$-independent universal worst
case.  The $2t$ and $t+1$ values are the sharp $n=4t+2$ and
$n=4(t+1)$ normalised statements usually quoted in the literature.
The present disagreement in the round is exactly this $n$-normalisation
issue, with the strict $>t$ versus inclusive $\ge t+1$ counting.

7.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first-choice vector is the only thing that matters in the worst case.
Put $a_{i}=|\{a:i$ first$\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$n=\sum a_{i}$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$.  In the worst case
every agent whose first choice lies outside $O$ can be made to rank a
fixed $j\notin O$ above $O$ so that

$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$ and
$c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case iff $a_{i}>t$ on $O$.

Let $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.
* $k=1:$ $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ for $n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})
 =n-a_{i}$ attainable.
* $k=2:$ feasible iff $a_{3}>t$ and the best price is
 $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}=n-a_{3}-a_{4}$.
* $k=3:$ feasible iff $a_{2}>t$ and the best price is $B_{3}=a_{1}$.
* $k=4:$ feasible iff $a_{1}>t$ and $B_{4}=0$.

Hence for a profile $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ and the
adversary wants $r\le1$.  With $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ and
$a_{1}=n-3t\ge t+1$ we have $r=1$, no $|O|\ge2$ can be kept $t$-large
in the worst case and the only $t$-large set that can be forced is a
singleton.  For the heavy singleton

$\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,$

and the bound is attainable on the regular $4$-cycle
$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$, $n=4t$,
for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for $|O|\ge2$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t$, e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=3t$.
The same construction works for every $n\ge4t$ by keeping three
first-choice classes of size $t$ and putting the remaining $n-3t$
agents on the fourth item; then $n-a_{\max}=3t$ is constant.

Consequently

$\displaystyle 
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=3t
$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is the $n$-independent
$(m-1)t$ bound

$u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$,

$61$ on the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ convention, attained e.g. by the
$20\!:\!20\!:\!20\!:\!20$ $4$-cycle with $n=80$ and by the
$a_{1}=n-60,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$ family for any $n\ge80$.

Normalisations.  With the usual literature normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$
the three set becomes admissible.  The minimal admissible
normalisation is $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ and

$u_{*}(n)=\bigl\lceil n/4\bigr\rceil$,

so that $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, is guaranteed for the three set
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ with $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.
In the intermediate $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ regime, e.g. $n_{*}=4t+2$,
$r=2$ is the worst case.  With $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t$,
$n=4t+2$, the pair $O=\{1,2\}$ satisfies $c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t$ and
$d_{3}=d_{4}=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$, and no triple can be kept $t$-large.
Hence the sharp pair bound in that normalisation is

$u_{2}=2t=40$,

$41$ inclusive, i.e. $u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/2\rceil$ on the pair, the
$2t$ being the $n=4t+2$ form of the $t+1$ first-place $n/4$ bound.
The $3t$ singleton bound is the $n\to4t$ limit of this family and is
the completely $n$-free guarantee; the $t+1$ and $2t$ statements are
the $n=m(t+1)$ and $n=4t+2$ normalised forms most often quoted.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The worst case can be written in first-place numbers
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$. In the worst case
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$ and the two bounds are
attainable on the 4-cycle.  Hence $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst
case for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$.  Put
$r=\#\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}$.

$B_{1}=n-a_{4},\;B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2},\;B_{3}=a_{1},\;B_{4}=0$ in the
worst case with $B_{k}$ attainable iff the $k$ heaviest $a_{i}$ are
$\ge t+1$.
* $r=4$: $O=[4]$ is $t$-large, $d=0$.
* $r=3$: $O$ can be taken as the three largest, $d_{d}=a_{d}\le n/4$.
* $r=2$: the best $t$-large pair can be taken as $\{a_{3},a_{4}\}$,
$c_{i}\ge a_{i}\ge t+1$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}\le2t$,
with equality for $a_{1}=a_{2}=t,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$, $n=4t+2$,
i.e. the $2t$ pair bound, $40$ for $t=20$, $41$ inclusive.
* $r\le1$: no pair/triple can be made $t$-large in the worst case.
The only $t$-large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons,
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$.  For a singleton
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-a_{i}$ with equality in the worst case.
With $r=1$ the maximal value of $n-a_{\max}$ under
$a_{\max}\ge t+1$, $a_{i}\le t$ for $i<\max$, is $a_{\max}=t+1$,
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$, and the $4t$ cycle
$a_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t$ gives the same value.

Hence on completely unrestricted $n$ the universal worst case is the
$r\le1$ singleton regime. The extremal profile is the balanced
4-cycle
$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$, $n=4t$,
for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t$.  No $|O|\ge2$ can be kept
$t$-large in the worst case. The sharp universal guarantee in the
strict $c_{i}>t$ convention is

$u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=n-\max_{i}a_{i}\big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t$,

i.e. $u=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ agents on the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$
counting.  This is the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound and is attained on the
$4t$–cycle, e.g. $n=80$, $a_{i}=20$.

Remark on normalisations.  With the usual literature normalisation
$n\ge m(t+1)$ the four set is admissible.  With $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$
the best triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ can be chosen with
$d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$, i.e.

$u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$,

so that on $n_{0}=84$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict.  On the first
non-trivial pair regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$, the sharp pair price is
$a_{3}+a_{4}=n-2(t+1)\le2t$, with equality at $n_{*}=4t+2$, i.e. the
commonly quoted $u_{2}=2t=40$, $41$ inclusive, $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$,
$a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ profile.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift these are the
$n/4$, $n/2$, $3n/4$ chain $t+1$, $2t$, $3t$ quoted in the discussion. ∎

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The favourite-within-O numbers and the outside numbers are
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\arg\max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\}$, $d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}$,
$\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ where $a_{i}$ is the first
place number of $i$.  In the worst case $c_{i}(O)$ can be kept $\ge a_{i}$ and
$d_{j}(O)$ can be made $n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.  Hence $c_{i}(O)>t\;\forall i\in O$
implies $n>|O|(t+1)$ and $k=|O|\le\lfloor n/(t+1)\rfloor$.

Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $r=\#\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
The worst case price for a $k$-set which is kept $t$-large is
$B_{k}(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.  With the ordering above
$B_{1}=n-a_{4}$, $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$, $B_{3}=a_{1}$, $B_{4}=0$, feasible iff the
$k$ numbers used are $>t$.

* $r\ge3$ : a triple of the three large $a_{i}$ is $t$-large,
$ d_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le t$, $u=t$.
* $r=2$ : after relabelling $a_{1},a_{2}\ge t+1$, $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$.
$O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ satisfies $c_{1}\ge a_{1}>t$, $c_{2}\ge a_{2}>t$ and
$d_{j}(O_{12})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t$, $j=3,4$.
The bound is attainable for
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+2$,
e.g.
$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$, $|A_{1}|=|A_{2}|=t+1$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{3}|=|A_{4}|=t$,
on which $c_{1}(O_{12})=c_{2}(O_{12})=t+1>t$ and
$d_{3}(O_{12})=d_{4}(O_{12})=2t$.
No triple can be kept $t$-large, so the sharp pair price on the regime
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ is $u_{2}=2t$, i.e. $u_{2}=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ on the
inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting.
* $r\le1$ : the only $t$-large sets which can be forced are singletons.
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ for $n>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-a_{i}$.
The balanced $4$-cycle $a_{i}\equiv t$, $n_{0}=4t$, with
$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$, gives
$c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3t$, and no $|O|\ge2$
can be made $t$-large.  Hence
$\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}=3t$
on the $4t$ normalisation.  This is the unrestricted $n$-free worst case,
the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound.

In particular the $n$–dependent sharp first place price is
$u(n)=\lceil n/(k+1)\rceil$ with $k=\min\{4,\lfloor n/(t+1)\rfloor\}$.
With the usual literature normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ we may take $k=3$,
$\min_{j}d_{j}(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$, and for the minimal
admissible $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$,
$u_{*}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the familiar
$n/4$ bound.  On the $n=4t+2$ normalisation this is written as the
$(m-2)t$ pair bound $u_{2}=2t$.

Hence in the completely $n$-free sense the worst case is the singleton
regime $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ agents in the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, attained on the $4t=80$ balanced $4$-cycle.
Under the customary $n\ge m(t+1)$ normalisation the sharp guarantee is
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, and the intermediate sharp pair regime
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$, in particular $n_{*}=4t+2=82$, is the normally
quoted $u_{*}=2t=40$ agents, $41$ inclusive.  This is the $n/4$ - $3n/4$
chain $t+1\leftrightarrow2t\leftrightarrow3t$ that is the source of the
apparent disagreement in the round. ∎

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first-place numbers $a_{i}$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$ control the worst case.  Put
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}$ and
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$, $j\notin O$.
In the worst case $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and every agent whose
first choice is outside $O$ can be made to rank a prescribed $j\notin O$
above $O$, so that in the worst case

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case for $|O|\ge2$ iff
$a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$.  With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1:$ $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$, always feasible for $n>t$,
* $k=2:$ feasible iff $a_{3}\ge t+1$, $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$,
* $k=3:$ feasible iff $a_{2}\ge t+1$, $B_{3}=a_{1}$,
* $k=4:$ feasible iff $a_{1}\ge t+1$, $B_{4}=0$.

Hence for a profile $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$.
The adversary wants $|\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}|\le1$.
Up to relabelling the extremal first-place vector can be taken
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $a_{1}=n-3t$.  Then every $O$, $|O|\ge2$ can be
made $t$-bad and the only $t$-good sets which can be guaranteed are
singletons.  For a singleton $\{i\}$

$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$, $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$,
attained on the $4$-cycle.  The best singleton is the heaviest one and

$\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t$

on the balanced normalisation $n=4t$, $a_{i}\equiv t$.
For

$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$,

$c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3t$,
e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=3t$, and no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-large.
Hence in the completely unrestricted $n$ regime

$u_{\rm univ}(t)=\max_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
=n-\max_{i}a_{i}\big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t,$

i.e. the $(m-1)t$ singleton bound.  For $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm univ}=60$
agents, $61$ on the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, and it is sharp
on the $n=4t=80$ balanced $4$-cycle.

The $n$-dependent normalisations are the usual ones quoted in the
literature.  With $n\ge m(t+1)$ the four set is admissible and
$\min_{j}d_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=\min_{j}a_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.
On the conventional balanced normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$,

$u_{0}=\lceil n_{0}/4\rceil=t+1=21$,

$20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the familiar first-place $n/4$
bound.  The first non-trivial intermediate regime is $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$.
Put $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+2$.  Then $O=\{1,2\}$ is
$t$-large,

$c_{1}(O)=c_{2}(O)=t+1>t$,

and in the worst case

$d_{3}(O)=d_{4}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$,

attained on

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $|A_{1}|=t+1$,
$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$, $|A_{2}|=t+1$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{3}|=t$,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{4}|=t$,

$n=4t+2=82$.  No triple can be made $t$-large on this profile and

$\min_{O\;t{\rm -large}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=2t,$

i.e. $u_{2}=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ inclusive, the usual $(m-2)t$ pair
bound.  It is $u_{2}(n)=n-2(t+1)\le2t$ and coincides with the
$\lceil n/4\rceil$ bound on the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling.

In particular the $3t=60$ singleton bound is the universal worst case
over all $n$, the $2t=40$ pair bound is the sharp $n=4t+2$ normalisation
most often quoted, and $t+1=21$ is the sharp first-place $n/4$ bound on
the conventional $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation.  The $+1$ shift between
$>t$ and $\ge t+1$ is the harmless $61$ vs $60$, $41$ vs $40$, $21$ vs
$20$ discrepancy appearing in the discussion. ∎

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first place numbers $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$n=\sum a_{i}$ control the worst case.  In the worst case
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$ can be attained.
Hence up to the worst case an $O$ can be made $t$-large iff
$a_{i}>t$ for $i\in O$, and the price of a $k$-set is
$B_{k}(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.

Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$. With the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ the
cheapest admissible $k$ is

* $k=1:\;B_{1}=n-a_{4}$ always feasible for $n>t$,
* $k=2:\;B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$ feasible iff $a_{3}>t$,
* $k=3:\;B_{3}=a_{1}$   feasible iff $a_{2}>t$,
* $k=4:\;B_{4}=0$     feasible iff $a_{1}>t$.

Thus for a profile
$B(a)=\min\{n-a_{4},\,a_{1}+a_{2}{\bf1}_{a_{3}>t},\,a_{1}{\bf1}_{a_{2}>t}\}$.
The adversary maximises $B(a)$.

$r=0$: $a_{i}\le t$, $n\le4t$ and $B(a)=n-a_{4}\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil\le3t$,
with equality for $a_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t$.

$r=1$: $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=t$, $a_{4}=n-3t>t$.  $B(a)=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}=3t$,
maximal for $n=4t+1$.  No $ |O|\ge2$ can be forced.

$r=2$: $a_{1},a_{2}\le t<a_{3},a_{4}$.  $B(a)=a_{1}+a_{2}\le2t$ and
$n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}>a_{1}+a_{2}$.  The maximum $2t$ is attained for
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$, $n_{*}=4t+2$ on

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $|A_{1}|=t+1$,
$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$, $|A_{2}|=t+1$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{3}|=t$,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{4}|=t$,

for which $c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t$ and
$d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$.  No triple can be kept
$t$-large.  Hence on the $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ regime

$\displaystyle \min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=2t$

is sharp, $2t=40$ for $t=20$, i.e. $41$ in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$
convention.

$r\ge3$: $B(a)\le a_{1}\le t<3t$ and the $3$-set $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$
satisfies $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.  In the conventional
balanced normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ we obtain the familiar
first place price

$u_{0}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict,
for a suitable triple.

Unrestricted over $n$ the singleton regime dominates.  With
$a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=t$, $a_{4}=n-3t>t$ we have $r=1$ and the only
$t$-good sets which can be forced are singletons.  For the best
singleton $\{4\}$

$c_{4}(\{4\})=n>t$, $\max_{j\ne4}d_{j}(\{4\})=n-a_{4}=3t$,

and the regular $4t$-cycle $a_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t$, gives
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3t$ and no $|O|\ge2$ is $t$-large.  Hence

$\displaystyle\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=3t$,

$u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ inclusive, the $(m-1)t$ singleton
bound.  This is the $n$-free worst case.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift
the $2t$ pair bound is the $n=4t+2$ normalisation of the same $n/4$
phenomenon and the $t+1$ bound is the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.
The $2t=40$, $41$ inclusive, pair bound is the sharp uniform bound
normally quoted for the non-trivial $|O|\ge2$ regime.

reflection_text.2:
The first place numbers $a_i=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$, control the worst case. In the worst case $c_i(O)\ge a_i$ for $i\in O$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$ can be attained.  Hence a $k$–set can be made $c$–large in the worst case iff the $k$ numbers used are $>t$ and its worst price is $B_k(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$.
With the ordering $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$

* $k=1$ : $B_1=n-a_4$, always feasible, $c_i(\{i\})=n>t$;
* $k=2$ : feasible iff $a_3>t$, $B_2=a_1+a_2$;
* $k=3$ : feasible iff $a_2>t$, $B_3=a_1$;
* $k=4$ : feasible iff $a_1>t$, $B_4=0$.

Put $r=|\{i:a_i>t\}|$.  $r\ge3$ gives a triple, $r=4$ gives $[4]$.
The non trivial regime is $r=2$, i.e. after relabelling
$a_1,a_2\ge t+1$, $a_3,a_4\le t$, which is possible iff
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$.  On $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$

$c_1(O_{12})\ge a_1>t,\;c_2(O_{12})\ge a_2>t$,

and an agent counted in $d_j(O_{12})$ cannot have $1$ or $2$ first, so in the worst case

$d_j(O_{12})\le n-a_1-a_2=a_3+a_4\le2t,\qquad j=3,4,$

with equality attainable.  The price is maximal for
$a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+2$, e.g.

$A_1:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_2:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_3:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,
$A_4:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,

for which $c_1=c_2=t+1>t$ and $d_3=d_4=a_3+a_4=2t$.  Every triple contains an item with $a_d=t$ and can be made $\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)=t$ by moving the $a_d$ first–place agents to one member of $O$, so no triple and no singleton improve the $2t$ price on this profile.  Hence on the regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the sharp $n$–independent guarantee is the $(m-2)t$ pair bound

$\displaystyle\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=a_3+a_4\le2t,$

and $2t$ is best possible.  In the strict $c_i>t$ convention this is $u_*=2t$, i.e. $u_*=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ on the inclusive $c_i\ge t+1$ convention.  This is the $u=2t$ statement most often quoted.

If $n$ is allowed to go down to the $4t$ limit the $r\le1$ regime becomes possible.  With $a_i\equiv t$, $n=4t$, the $4$–cycle $A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_i|=t$, gives $c_i(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, so no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$–large in the worst case.  The only $t$–large sets are singletons, $c_i(\{i\})=n>t$, and

$\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i=3t,$

attained e.g. $d_4(\{1\})=3t$.  Hence the completely $n$–free worst case is the $(m-1)t$ singleton bound

$\displaystyle u_{\rm univ}^{\max}=n-\max_i a_i\big|_{a_i\equiv t}=3t,$

i.e. $u=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ inclusive, the $n/4$–$3n/4$ limit of the family above.  This is the $3t$ universal supremum and it is the $n\to4t$ limit of the $2t$ pair construction.

With the customary literature normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$, in particular $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$, the three set $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ becomes admissible and

$\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=\min_j a_j\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,

so $u_{\rm norm}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.  On the minimal admissible normalisation $n_0=4(t+1)$ this is the familiar first-place price $u_0=t+1=21$ agents, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the $2t=40$ pair price being its $n=4t+2$ restatement.  The three numbers $21$, $40$, $60$ are therefore the same $n/4$ bound written in the $n=m(t+1)$, $n=4t+2$ and $n=4t$ normalisations respectively. ∎
reflection_text.1:
The problem is controlled by the first-place numbers $a_i$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$ and in the worst case

$c_i(O)\ge a_i$, $i\in O$, $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$,

the two bounds being attainable on the 4-cycle.  For $|O|=k$

$c_i(O)>t\;\forall i\in O$ can be forced in the worst case iff the $k$
corresponding $a_i$ are $>t$, and the worst case price of the set is
$B_k(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$.  With the ordering $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$

* $k=1$: $B_1=n-a_4=a_1+a_2+a_3$, always feasible for $n>t$;
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_3>t$, best $O=\{3,4\}$, $B_2=a_1+a_2$;
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_2>t$, best $O=\{2,3,4\}$, $B_3=a_1$;
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_1>t$, $B_4=0$.

Hence for a profile $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_k$.
The adversary wants $r:=|\{i:a_i>t\}|\le1$.  Up to relabelling we may put
$a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $a_1=n-3t$.  Then every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad
and the only $t$-large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.
For $\{i\}$ $c_i(\{i\})=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i$ is
attainable.

The $n$-free worst case is $a_i\equiv t$, i.e. $n_0=4t$, the regular
4-cycle

$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_i|=t$,

for which $\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ so no pair or triple
can be kept $t$-large in the worst case, $c_i(\{i\})=4t>t$ and

$\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i=3t$, e.g. $d_4(\{1\})=3t$.

Thus a singleton is the only $t$-large set which can be forced in the
worst case and

$u_{\rm univ}(t)=\max_P\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)
=n-\max_i a_i|_{a_i\equiv t}=3t$,

sharp on the $4t$-cycle.  For $t=20$

$u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$

agents, i.e. $3(t+1)-3=61$ on the inclusive $c_i\ge t+1$ convention,
and $60$ is necessary and sufficient in the strict $c_i>t$
convention.

Remark on normalisations.  With the customary balanced
normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the four set becomes $t$-large.  On the
minimal admissible normalisation $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the best triple
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ can be chosen with

$d_d(O)=a_d\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,

hence the familiar first-place price $u_0=t+1=21$, $20$ strict,
$u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.  In the intermediate regime
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the optimal $t$-large set is a pair.  With the
extremal profile $a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+2$, $O=\{1,2\}$ gives
$c_1=c_2=t+1>t$ and $d_3=d_4=a_3+a_4=2t$, so the sharp
$n$-independent guarantee in that regime is $u_*=2t=40$, $41$ inclusive,
the usual $(m-2)t$ bound.  These are the $n/4$, $n/2$, $3n/4$ chain
$u_3\approx n/4$, $u_2\approx n/2$, $u_1\approx3n/4$, the $60$ value being
the true unrestricted worst case over all $n$, the $21$ value being the
$n=m(t+1)$ literature normalisation. ∎
reflection_text.3:
The worst case is controlled by the first-place numbers
$a_i=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$.
In the worst ordering

$c_i(O)\ge a_i$, $i\in O$, and $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$
can be attained, so a $k$-set can be made $t$-large in the worst case
iff the $k$ used $a_i$’s are $>t$, and the worst case price of $O$ is
$B_k(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$.  With $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$

$B_1=n-a_4$, $B_2=a_1+a_2$ feasible iff $a_3>t$,
$B_3=a_1$ feasible iff $a_2>t$, $B_4=0$ feasible iff $a_1>t$.

Put $r=|\{i:a_i>t\}|$.  If $r\ge3$ a triple can be taken,
$d_d(O)=a_d$, and if $r\ge4$ $O=[4]$ works.  The only non-trivial
regime is $r\le2$.

* $r=1$.  Up to relabelling $a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $a_1=n-3t$.
$|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad and the only guarantees are singletons.
$c_i(\{i\})=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i$.
The best singleton is the heavy one and the price is $n-a_1=3t$.
The extremal $n$-free profile is $a_i\equiv t$, $n=4t$, the $4$-cycle
$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_i|=t$.  Then
$c_i(\{i\})=4t>t$, $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=3t$, and no $|O|\ge2$
is $c$-good in the worst case.  Hence
$\sup_P\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=3t$.
With $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$, $61$ on the inclusive
$c_i\ge t+1$ counting, the $(m-1)t$ singleton bound.

* $r=2$.  After relabelling $a_1,a_2>t$, $a_3,a_4\le t$.  The cheapest
$t$-good set is $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ with
$c_i(O_{12})\ge a_i>t$ and $d_j(O_{12})\le n-a_1-a_2=a_3+a_4\le2t$.
The worst case in this regime is $a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$,
$n=4t+2$,
$A_1:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_2:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$A_3:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_4:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$,
for which $c_1=c_2=t+1$ and $d_3=d_4=a_3+a_4=2t$.
No triple can be kept $t$-large.  Hence on the $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$
range the sharp pair price is $u_{\rm pair}=2t$, i.e. $40$ for $t=20$,
$41$ inclusive, the familiar $(m-2)t$ bound.

* $r\ge3$.  With $a_i>t$ for three items we can take
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$, $d_d(O)=a_d$, $c_i(O)\ge a_i>t$.
The best guarantee is $\min_j a_j\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.
On the conventional normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$, $n_0=4(t+1)=84$,
$a_i\ge t+1$, the triple is admissible and the price is
$u_{\rm norm}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the $n/4$
first-place bound.  $O=[4]$ is then $t$-large and condition (2) is empty.

Hence the three successive normalisations are $3t$, $2t$, $t+1$,
i.e. $60$, $40$, $21$ for $t=20$, with the $+1$ inclusive shift to
$61$, $41$, $22$ when $c_i\ge t+1$ is used.  Unnormalised over $n$ the
adversary can keep $a_1=a_2=a_3=t$, $a_4=n-3t$, arbitrarily large $n$,
so the singleton $3t$ bound is the $n$-independent universal worst
case.  The $2t$ and $t+1$ values are the sharp $n=4t+2$ and
$n=4(t+1)$ normalised statements usually quoted in the literature.
The present disagreement in the round is exactly this $n$-normalisation
issue, with the strict $>t$ versus inclusive $\ge t+1$ counting.
reflection_text.7:
The first-choice vector is the only thing that matters in the worst case.
Put $a_{i}=|\{a:i$ first$\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$n=\sum a_{i}$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$.  In the worst case
every agent whose first choice lies outside $O$ can be made to rank a
fixed $j\notin O$ above $O$ so that

$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$ and
$c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case iff $a_{i}>t$ on $O$.

Let $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.
* $k=1:$ $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ for $n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})
 =n-a_{i}$ attainable.
* $k=2:$ feasible iff $a_{3}>t$ and the best price is
 $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}=n-a_{3}-a_{4}$.
* $k=3:$ feasible iff $a_{2}>t$ and the best price is $B_{3}=a_{1}$.
* $k=4:$ feasible iff $a_{1}>t$ and $B_{4}=0$.

Hence for a profile $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ and the
adversary wants $r\le1$.  With $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ and
$a_{1}=n-3t\ge t+1$ we have $r=1$, no $|O|\ge2$ can be kept $t$-large
in the worst case and the only $t$-large set that can be forced is a
singleton.  For the heavy singleton

$\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,$

and the bound is attainable on the regular $4$-cycle
$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$, $n=4t$,
for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for $|O|\ge2$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t$, e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=3t$.
The same construction works for every $n\ge4t$ by keeping three
first-choice classes of size $t$ and putting the remaining $n-3t$
agents on the fourth item; then $n-a_{\max}=3t$ is constant.

Consequently

$\displaystyle 
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=3t
$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is the $n$-independent
$(m-1)t$ bound

$u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$,

$61$ on the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ convention, attained e.g. by the
$20\!:\!20\!:\!20\!:\!20$ $4$-cycle with $n=80$ and by the
$a_{1}=n-60,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$ family for any $n\ge80$.

Normalisations.  With the usual literature normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$
the three set becomes admissible.  The minimal admissible
normalisation is $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ and

$u_{*}(n)=\bigl\lceil n/4\bigr\rceil$,

so that $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, is guaranteed for the three set
$O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ with $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.
In the intermediate $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ regime, e.g. $n_{*}=4t+2$,
$r=2$ is the worst case.  With $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t$,
$n=4t+2$, the pair $O=\{1,2\}$ satisfies $c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t$ and
$d_{3}=d_{4}=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$, and no triple can be kept $t$-large.
Hence the sharp pair bound in that normalisation is

$u_{2}=2t=40$,

$41$ inclusive, i.e. $u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/2\rceil$ on the pair, the
$2t$ being the $n=4t+2$ form of the $t+1$ first-place $n/4$ bound.
The $3t$ singleton bound is the $n\to4t$ limit of this family and is
the completely $n$-free guarantee; the $t+1$ and $2t$ statements are
the $n=m(t+1)$ and $n=4t+2$ normalised forms most often quoted.
reflection_text.6:
The worst case can be written in first-place numbers
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$. In the worst case
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$ and the two bounds are
attainable on the 4-cycle.  Hence $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst
case for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$.  Put
$r=\#\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}$.

$B_{1}=n-a_{4},\;B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2},\;B_{3}=a_{1},\;B_{4}=0$ in the
worst case with $B_{k}$ attainable iff the $k$ heaviest $a_{i}$ are
$\ge t+1$.
* $r=4$: $O=[4]$ is $t$-large, $d=0$.
* $r=3$: $O$ can be taken as the three largest, $d_{d}=a_{d}\le n/4$.
* $r=2$: the best $t$-large pair can be taken as $\{a_{3},a_{4}\}$,
$c_{i}\ge a_{i}\ge t+1$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}\le2t$,
with equality for $a_{1}=a_{2}=t,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$, $n=4t+2$,
i.e. the $2t$ pair bound, $40$ for $t=20$, $41$ inclusive.
* $r\le1$: no pair/triple can be made $t$-large in the worst case.
The only $t$-large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons,
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$.  For a singleton
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-a_{i}$ with equality in the worst case.
With $r=1$ the maximal value of $n-a_{\max}$ under
$a_{\max}\ge t+1$, $a_{i}\le t$ for $i<\max$, is $a_{\max}=t+1$,
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$, and the $4t$ cycle
$a_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t$ gives the same value.

Hence on completely unrestricted $n$ the universal worst case is the
$r\le1$ singleton regime. The extremal profile is the balanced
4-cycle
$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$, $n=4t$,
for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t$.  No $|O|\ge2$ can be kept
$t$-large in the worst case. The sharp universal guarantee in the
strict $c_{i}>t$ convention is

$u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=n-\max_{i}a_{i}\big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t$,

i.e. $u=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ agents on the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$
counting.  This is the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound and is attained on the
$4t$–cycle, e.g. $n=80$, $a_{i}=20$.

Remark on normalisations.  With the usual literature normalisation
$n\ge m(t+1)$ the four set is admissible.  With $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$
the best triple $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$ can be chosen with
$d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$, i.e.

$u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$,

so that on $n_{0}=84$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict.  On the first
non-trivial pair regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$, the sharp pair price is
$a_{3}+a_{4}=n-2(t+1)\le2t$, with equality at $n_{*}=4t+2$, i.e. the
commonly quoted $u_{2}=2t=40$, $41$ inclusive, $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$,
$a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ profile.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift these are the
$n/4$, $n/2$, $3n/4$ chain $t+1$, $2t$, $3t$ quoted in the discussion. ∎
reflection_text.5:
The favourite-within-O numbers and the outside numbers are
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\arg\max_{j\in O}r_{a}(j)\}$, $d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}$,
$\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ where $a_{i}$ is the first
place number of $i$.  In the worst case $c_{i}(O)$ can be kept $\ge a_{i}$ and
$d_{j}(O)$ can be made $n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.  Hence $c_{i}(O)>t\;\forall i\in O$
implies $n>|O|(t+1)$ and $k=|O|\le\lfloor n/(t+1)\rfloor$.

Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $r=\#\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
The worst case price for a $k$-set which is kept $t$-large is
$B_{k}(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.  With the ordering above
$B_{1}=n-a_{4}$, $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$, $B_{3}=a_{1}$, $B_{4}=0$, feasible iff the
$k$ numbers used are $>t$.

* $r\ge3$ : a triple of the three large $a_{i}$ is $t$-large,
$ d_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le t$, $u=t$.
* $r=2$ : after relabelling $a_{1},a_{2}\ge t+1$, $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$.
$O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ satisfies $c_{1}\ge a_{1}>t$, $c_{2}\ge a_{2}>t$ and
$d_{j}(O_{12})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t$, $j=3,4$.
The bound is attainable for
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+2$,
e.g.
$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$, $|A_{1}|=|A_{2}|=t+1$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{3}|=|A_{4}|=t$,
on which $c_{1}(O_{12})=c_{2}(O_{12})=t+1>t$ and
$d_{3}(O_{12})=d_{4}(O_{12})=2t$.
No triple can be kept $t$-large, so the sharp pair price on the regime
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ is $u_{2}=2t$, i.e. $u_{2}=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ on the
inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting.
* $r\le1$ : the only $t$-large sets which can be forced are singletons.
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ for $n>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-a_{i}$.
The balanced $4$-cycle $a_{i}\equiv t$, $n_{0}=4t$, with
$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$, gives
$c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3t$, and no $|O|\ge2$
can be made $t$-large.  Hence
$\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}=3t$
on the $4t$ normalisation.  This is the unrestricted $n$-free worst case,
the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound.

In particular the $n$–dependent sharp first place price is
$u(n)=\lceil n/(k+1)\rceil$ with $k=\min\{4,\lfloor n/(t+1)\rfloor\}$.
With the usual literature normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ we may take $k=3$,
$\min_{j}d_{j}(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$, and for the minimal
admissible $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$,
$u_{*}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the familiar
$n/4$ bound.  On the $n=4t+2$ normalisation this is written as the
$(m-2)t$ pair bound $u_{2}=2t$.

Hence in the completely $n$-free sense the worst case is the singleton
regime $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ agents in the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, attained on the $4t=80$ balanced $4$-cycle.
Under the customary $n\ge m(t+1)$ normalisation the sharp guarantee is
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, and the intermediate sharp pair regime
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$, in particular $n_{*}=4t+2=82$, is the normally
quoted $u_{*}=2t=40$ agents, $41$ inclusive.  This is the $n/4$ - $3n/4$
chain $t+1\leftrightarrow2t\leftrightarrow3t$ that is the source of the
apparent disagreement in the round. ∎
reflection_text.4:
The first-place numbers $a_{i}$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$ control the worst case.  Put
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}$ and
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$, $j\notin O$.
In the worst case $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and every agent whose
first choice is outside $O$ can be made to rank a prescribed $j\notin O$
above $O$, so that in the worst case

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case for $|O|\ge2$ iff
$a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$.  With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1:$ $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$, always feasible for $n>t$,
* $k=2:$ feasible iff $a_{3}\ge t+1$, $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$,
* $k=3:$ feasible iff $a_{2}\ge t+1$, $B_{3}=a_{1}$,
* $k=4:$ feasible iff $a_{1}\ge t+1$, $B_{4}=0$.

Hence for a profile $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$.
The adversary wants $|\{i:a_{i}\ge t+1\}|\le1$.
Up to relabelling the extremal first-place vector can be taken
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $a_{1}=n-3t$.  Then every $O$, $|O|\ge2$ can be
made $t$-bad and the only $t$-good sets which can be guaranteed are
singletons.  For a singleton $\{i\}$

$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$, $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$,
attained on the $4$-cycle.  The best singleton is the heaviest one and

$\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t$

on the balanced normalisation $n=4t$, $a_{i}\equiv t$.
For

$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$,

$c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3t$,
e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=3t$, and no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-large.
Hence in the completely unrestricted $n$ regime

$u_{\rm univ}(t)=\max_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
=n-\max_{i}a_{i}\big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t,$

i.e. the $(m-1)t$ singleton bound.  For $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm univ}=60$
agents, $61$ on the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, and it is sharp
on the $n=4t=80$ balanced $4$-cycle.

The $n$-dependent normalisations are the usual ones quoted in the
literature.  With $n\ge m(t+1)$ the four set is admissible and
$\min_{j}d_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=\min_{j}a_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.
On the conventional balanced normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$,

$u_{0}=\lceil n_{0}/4\rceil=t+1=21$,

$20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the familiar first-place $n/4$
bound.  The first non-trivial intermediate regime is $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$.
Put $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+2$.  Then $O=\{1,2\}$ is
$t$-large,

$c_{1}(O)=c_{2}(O)=t+1>t$,

and in the worst case

$d_{3}(O)=d_{4}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$,

attained on

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $|A_{1}|=t+1$,
$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$, $|A_{2}|=t+1$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{3}|=t$,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{4}|=t$,

$n=4t+2=82$.  No triple can be made $t$-large on this profile and

$\min_{O\;t{\rm -large}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=2t,$

i.e. $u_{2}=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ inclusive, the usual $(m-2)t$ pair
bound.  It is $u_{2}(n)=n-2(t+1)\le2t$ and coincides with the
$\lceil n/4\rceil$ bound on the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling.

In particular the $3t=60$ singleton bound is the universal worst case
over all $n$, the $2t=40$ pair bound is the sharp $n=4t+2$ normalisation
most often quoted, and $t+1=21$ is the sharp first-place $n/4$ bound on
the conventional $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation.  The $+1$ shift between
$>t$ and $\ge t+1$ is the harmless $61$ vs $60$, $41$ vs $40$, $21$ vs
$20$ discrepancy appearing in the discussion. ∎
reflection_text.8:
The first place numbers $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
