$n=\sum a_{i}$ control the worst case.  In the worst case
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$ can be attained.
Hence up to the worst case an $O$ can be made $t$-large iff
$a_{i}>t$ for $i\in O$, and the price of a $k$-set is
$B_{k}(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.

Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$. With the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ the
cheapest admissible $k$ is

* $k=1:\;B_{1}=n-a_{4}$ always feasible for $n>t$,
* $k=2:\;B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$ feasible iff $a_{3}>t$,
* $k=3:\;B_{3}=a_{1}$   feasible iff $a_{2}>t$,
* $k=4:\;B_{4}=0$     feasible iff $a_{1}>t$.

Thus for a profile
$B(a)=\min\{n-a_{4},\,a_{1}+a_{2}{\bf1}_{a_{3}>t},\,a_{1}{\bf1}_{a_{2}>t}\}$.
The adversary maximises $B(a)$.

$r=0$: $a_{i}\le t$, $n\le4t$ and $B(a)=n-a_{4}\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil\le3t$,
with equality for $a_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t$.

$r=1$: $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=t$, $a_{4}=n-3t>t$.  $B(a)=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}=3t$,
maximal for $n=4t+1$.  No $ |O|\ge2$ can be forced.

$r=2$: $a_{1},a_{2}\le t<a_{3},a_{4}$.  $B(a)=a_{1}+a_{2}\le2t$ and
$n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}>a_{1}+a_{2}$.  The maximum $2t$ is attained for
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$, $n_{*}=4t+2$ on

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $|A_{1}|=t+1$,
$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$, $|A_{2}|=t+1$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{3}|=t$,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{4}|=t$,

for which $c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t$ and
$d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$.  No triple can be kept
$t$-large.  Hence on the $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ regime

$\displaystyle \min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=2t$

is sharp, $2t=40$ for $t=20$, i.e. $41$ in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$
convention.

$r\ge3$: $B(a)\le a_{1}\le t<3t$ and the $3$-set $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$
satisfies $d_{d}(O)=a_{d}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.  In the conventional
balanced normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ we obtain the familiar
first place price

$u_{0}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict,
for a suitable triple.

Unrestricted over $n$ the singleton regime dominates.  With
$a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=t$, $a_{4}=n-3t>t$ we have $r=1$ and the only
$t$-good sets which can be forced are singletons.  For the best
singleton $\{4\}$

$c_{4}(\{4\})=n>t$, $\max_{j\ne4}d_{j}(\{4\})=n-a_{4}=3t$,

and the regular $4t$-cycle $a_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t$, gives
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3t$ and no $|O|\ge2$ is $t$-large.  Hence

$\displaystyle\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=3t$,

$u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ inclusive, the $(m-1)t$ singleton
bound.  This is the $n$-free worst case.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift
the $2t$ pair bound is the $n=4t+2$ normalisation of the same $n/4$
phenomenon and the $t+1$ bound is the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.
The $2t=40$, $41$ inclusive, pair bound is the sharp uniform bound
normally quoted for the non-trivial $|O|\ge2$ regime.

7.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}=|\{a:i\ {\rm is\ first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le
a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$ and for $O\subset [4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}| ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\ \forall i\in O\}| ,\;j\notin O .
$$

In the worst case we may keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$ and
we may put every agent whose first choice is outside $O$ on a prescribed
$j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst case

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge 2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ on $O$.
Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.

* $k=1$: $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ for $n>t$ and 
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$ can be attained,
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_{3}>t$ and the worst price is
$B_{2}=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}$,
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_{2}>t$ and $B_{3}=a_{1}$,
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_{1}>t$ and $B_{4}=0$.

Hence for a first place vector

$$
B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}
      =\min\Bigl\{\,n-\max_{i}a_{i},
       \;n-\!\!\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}\Bigr\}
$$

is the best price which can be forced.  The adversary makes
$r\le1$.  Up to relabelling we may take

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t>t ,
\qquad n\ge4t+1,
$$

and then every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad in the worst case and the
only $t$-good sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.  For the
heavy singleton $\{1\}$

$$
c_{1}(\{1\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  The extremal profile is the balanced
$4$-cycle

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
$$

$n_{0}=4t$.  Then

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$, and no $O$ with
$|O|\ge2$ can be kept $t$-large in the worst case, $\min_{i\in O}
c_{i}(O)=t$.  Hence a singleton is the only universally forceable
$t$-good set and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
     =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t
$$

is best possible.  This is the $(m-1)t$ bound.  In particular for the
strict $c_{i}>t$ convention a singleton can always be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin\{i\}}d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-\max_{i}a_{i}\le 3t,
$$

and $3t$ is sharp.

For $t=20$ this is the $n$-free universal guarantee

$$
u_{\rm univ}= (m-1)t =3t =60
$$

agents, e.g. the $20:20:20:20$ $4$-cycle with $n=80$, 
$c_{i}(\{i\})=80>20$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=60$.
With the usual inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting this is $3t+1=61$
agents.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the quoted
$u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ first-place bound, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the
normalisation $n=m(t+1)=84$ and the familiar $2t=40$ pair bound
$u_{2}=n-2(t+1)$ on the $n=4t+2$ normalisation.  The $60$–agent,
$61$ inclusive, singleton bound is the completely $n$-independent
$(m-1)t$ form of the estimate. ∎

3.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le
a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$ and for $O\subset[4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;{\rm for\;all\;}i\in O\}\bigr| ,
\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and in the worst case the $n-
\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$ agents whose first choice is outside $O$ can be
made to rank a prescribed $j\notin O$ above $O$, so that in the worst
case

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)= n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},\qquad 
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},
$$

and the bound can be attained.  In particular $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be
forced in the worst case for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ for every $i\in O$,
whereas

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}
$$

is always attainable.

Put $r=\bigl|\{i:a_{i}>t\}\bigr|$.  If $r\ge2$ the cheapest $t$-large
set is a pair, e.g. $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ with

$$c_{1}(O_{12})\ge a_{1}>t,\qquad c_{2}(O_{12})\ge a_{2}>t,
\qquad  \max_{j\notin O_{12}}d_{j}(O_{12})=a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t ,$$

and if $r\ge3$ a triple can be taken with $\max d_{j}\le t$.  The
$n$–free worst case is $r\le1$.  Up to relabelling we may take

$$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t,$$

so that every $O$, $|O|\ge2$, can be made $t$–bad in the worst case and
the only sets which can be forced $t$-large are the singletons.  For a
singleton

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},
$$

and the best singleton is the heaviest one.  Hence for the profile

$$
B(P)=\min_{O\;t\!-\!{\rm good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
     =n-\max_{i}a_{i}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3},
$$

and with the above choice $B(P)=3t$, independent of $n$.

The bound is sharp.  On the balanced $4t$-cycle

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,\qquad n=4t,
$$

$a_{i}\equiv t$, $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$, and for $i=1$

$$
d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t,
$$

while for every $|O|\ge2$ we can let the $a_{i}$ first place agents of
$O$ stay on $i$ so that $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$.  Hence no
$|O|\ge2$ can be kept $>t$ in the worst case and

$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=3t
$$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is the
$(m-1)t$ universal bound.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton, and $60$ is best possible.  With the usual inclusive
notation $c_{i}\ge t+1$ this is the $3(t+1)-3=61$–agent statement.
On the conventional normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the pair price is the
familiar $2t$ bound, $2t=40$ agents, $41$ inclusive, and on
$n=m(t+1)$ the first-place price $t+1=21$ agents, $20$ strict, is
obtained. ∎

5.text:
For a profile let  

$$a_{i}=\bigl|\{a:i\ {\rm is\ first\ for\ }a\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4},\qquad n=\sum_{1}^{4}a_{i}$$

and for $O\subset[4]$

$$c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| ,\;j\notin O .
$$

In the worst case we may keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$
and we may put every agent whose first choice is outside $O$ on a
single $j\notin O$.  Hence on the worst ordering

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\end{equation*}
and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case for $|O|\ge2$ iff
$a_{i}>t$ for every $i\in O$.  Put $r=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}$.
With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$ : $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ for $n>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$;
* $k=2$ : feasible iff $a_{3}>t$ and
$B_{2}=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}$;
* $k=3$ : feasible iff $a_{2}>t$ and $B_{3}=a_{1}$;
* $k=4$ : feasible iff $a_{1}>t$ and $B_{4}=0$.

Hence for a profile

$$B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}
      =\min\Bigl\{n-\max_{i}a_{i},\,n-\!\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}\Bigr\}.$$

The adversary makes $r\le1$.  With $r=1$ the only $t$-large sets which
can be kept $t$-large in the worst case are the singletons.  The
cheapest singleton is the most popular one and

$$B_{1}(P)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}$$

is attainable.  The maximum of $n-\max_{i}a_{i}$ over all profiles is
obtained for the balanced first place vector $a_{i}\equiv t$, $n_{0}=4t$.
On the $4$-cycle

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
$$

we have $c_{i}(\{i\})=n_{0}=4t>t$ and

$$d_{j}(\{i\})=n_{0}-a_{i}=3t,\qquad j\ne i, $$

and no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-large, $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$.
Hence a singleton is the only $t$-good set which can be forced in the
worst case and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;c{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
      =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t
$$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is the
usual $(m-1)t$ bound.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton, $61$ agents in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, and
the $4t=80$ balanced $4$-cycle shows the bound is sharp.  This is the
$n/4$–$3n/4$ form $u(n)=\lceil3n/4\rceil$.

*Remark.*  On the customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the three set
becomes admissible.  With the minimal admissible normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the familiar first place price is

$$u_{\rm norm}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil,\qquad
u_{\rm norm}(4(t+1))=t+1,$$

i.e. $21$ agents, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention.  On the
intermediate normalisation $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$, and in particular on
$n_{*}=4t+2$, the sharp $t$-good set can be taken to be the pair
$\{1,2\}$ with $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$.  Then
$c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t$ and

$$\max_{j\notin\{1,2\}}d_{j}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t, $$

so that the normally quoted $(m-2)t$ pair bound is $u_{*}=2t=40$
agents, $41$ in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, attained e.g.
on the $4t+2=82$ profile $A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, which is the
$u=t+1$ first place bound in the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling. ∎

4.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le
a_{3}\le a_{4}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$ and for $O\subset [4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr|, \qquad j\notin O .
$$

In the worst case we may keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$
and we may put every agent whose first choice lies outside $O$ on a
single $j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst case

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i} ,
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ for every
$i\in O$.  Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With the ordering
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

\begin{align*}
k=1&:&B_{1}&=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3},\\
k=2&:&B_{2}&=a_{1}+a_{2}\quad{\rm iff}\;a_{3}>t,\\
k=3&:&B_{3}&=a_{1}\quad{\rm iff}\;a_{2}>t,\\
k=4&:&B_{4}&=0\quad{\rm iff}\;a_{1}>t,
\end{align*}
and $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ is the worst case price which
can be forced on the first place vector $a$.

The adversary can make $r\le 1$.  Up to relabelling we may take

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t\ge t+1,
$$

i.e. $n=4t+r$, $0\le r<4$.  Then every $O$, $|O|\ge2$, can be made
$t$–bad and the only $t$-large sets which can be guaranteed are the
singletons.  For a singleton

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},
$$

and the bound is attainable.  The best singleton is the heavy one and

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max_{i}a_{i}=3t
$$

on the balanced normalisation $n=4t$, $a_{i}\equiv t$.  E.g. with

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
 $$

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t ,
$$

and $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.  No $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t$-large on the cycle, so a suitable set can always be taken to be a
singleton and

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\min }(t)=\max_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3(m-1)t
$$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is the
$(m-1)t$ singleton bound.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=3t
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton and $3t$ is sharp.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=3\times20=60
$$

agents, i.e. $61$ agents in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ convention,
is the $n$-free worst case, attained e.g. on the $n=4t=80$ balanced
$4$-cycle $a_{i}\equiv20$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the
usual $n/4$ bound.

*Remark.*  On the conventional normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the four
set itself becomes $t$-large.  With the minimal admissible
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$

$$
u_{0}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,
\qquad u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the familiar
first-place $n/4$ bound.  In the first non-trivial intermediate regime
$n=4t+2$ the extremal profile is $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, 
$O_{0}=\{1,2\}$ is $t$-large and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{0}}d_{j}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

the often quoted $(m-2)t$ pair bound.  For $t=20$ this is
$u_{2}=2t=40$ agents, $41$ in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting,
on the $n_{*}=4t+2=82$ extremal profile
$|A_{1}|=|A_{2}|=21$, $|A_{3}|=|A_{4}|=20$, which is the $t+1=21$ first
place bound in the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling.  This is the $40$-agent form
commonly quoted in the literature. ∎

1.text:
For an $O\subset [m]$ write

$$c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:\,i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}\bigr|,\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr|, \qquad j\notin O, $$
and let $a_{i}=|\{a:i\ {\rm is\ first}\}|,\;a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le
a_{4},\;n=\sum a_{i}$.  In the worst realisation of the preferences
consistent with the first place vector

$$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}, $$

and the two bounds are attained on the four cycle.  In particular
$c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case for $|O|\ge 2$ iff
$a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$.  Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ the cheapest $t$-large set which can
be forced in the worst case is

\begin{equation*}
B_{1}=n-a_{4},\qquad 
B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}\;(a_{3}>t),\qquad 
B_{3}=a_{1}\;(a_{2}>t),\qquad B_{4}=0\;(a_{1}>t),
\end{equation*}
so that for a profile
$B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=B(a)$ in the worst case.

The adversary can keep $r\le1$.  Up to relabelling

$$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t, $$

so that every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$–bad in the worst case and the
only $t$–large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.
For a singleton $\{i\}$

$$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},  $$

and the bound is attainable.  The best singleton is the heaviest one
and

$$B_{1}(a)=n-\max_{i}a_{i} .$$

The $n$–free extremal profile is the regular $4$–cycle
$a_{i}\equiv t$, $n_{0}=4t$,

$$
A_{i}: i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
$$

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, so no
$|O|\ge2$ can be kept $t$–large in the worst case and

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,\qquad i=1,\dots ,4,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.
Hence

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;c{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
   =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t,
$$

is the universal $(m-1)t$ bound and it is sharp.  In the strict
$c_{i}(O)>t$ convention a singleton can always be chosen with

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})>t,\qquad \max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})\le 3t,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is the $3t=60$–agent
guarantee, i.e. $61$ agents in the usual inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$
counting, attained e.g. on the $80$-agent $20:20:20:20$ four-cycle.
In particular

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=3t,\qquad u_{\rm univ}^{\rm incl}=3(t+1)-3,
$$

which for $t=20$ is $60$ agents strictly, $61$ agents inclusively.
This is the $n$-independent $(m-1)t$ form of the estimate.  On the
customary balanced normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the bound is usually
quoted in the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling as the $n/4$ first-place price
$\lceil n/4\rceil$, i.e. $t+1=21$, $20$ strict, and in the
intermediate $n=4t+2$ regime it is the familiar $(m-2)t$ pair bound
$u_{2}=2t$, $2t=40$, $41$ inclusive, attained on the
$t+1,t+1,t,t$ profile $A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_{2}:2\succ1\succ
3\succ4$, $|A_{1}|=|A_{2}|=t+1$, $|A_{3}|=|A_{4}|=t$, $O=\{1,2\}$ with
$c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t$ and $d_{3}=d_{4}=2t$.  This is the $40$-agent,
$41$ inclusive, bound most often quoted for $m=4$, $t=20$. ∎

8.text:
For a profile write
$a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first\;for}\;a\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le
a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$ and for $O\subset[4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}|,\qquad j\notin O .
$$

In the worst case the $a_{i}$ first place agents can be kept on $i$ and
every agent whose first choice lies outside $O$ can be put on a single
$j\notin O$, so that in the worst case

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case iff $a_{i}>t$ for
$i\in O$.  With the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
k=1&:\;c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\quad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},\\
k=2&:\;{\rm feasible}\iff a_{3}>t,\quad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{1}+a_{2},\\
k=3&:\;{\rm feasible}\iff a_{2}>t,\quad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{1},\\
k=4&:\;{\rm feasible}\iff a_{1}>t .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}

In particular for a singleton the best we can do in the worst case is

$$
B_{1}(P)=\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max_{i}a_{i},
$$

and the bound is attained on the regular $4$–cycle.  Put
$a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n_{0}=4t$.  With

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad|A_{i}|=t,
$$

we have $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and for every $i$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.  No $O$ with $|O|\ge2$
can be made $t$–large, $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$, so the only
$t$-good set which can be guaranteed in the worst case is a singleton
and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
   =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t .
$$

Hence with the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention a singleton can always be
chosen with

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})\le 3t,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton, and $60$ is sharp on the $4t=80$ balanced $4$–cycle.
In the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ notation this is the familiar
$3(t+1)-3=61$ agents.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the
usual $n/4$ bound $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.

Remark.  On the customary non-trivial normalisation
$n\ge m(t+1)$ the three set becomes admissible.  On the first
non-trivial regime $n_{*}=4t+2$ the extremal profile can be taken with
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, e.g.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,&|A_{1}|=t+1,\\
A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4,&|A_{2}|=t+1,\\
A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,&|A_{3}|=t,\\
A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2,&|A_{4}|=t,
\end{array}
$$

$n_{*}=4t+2$.  For $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$

$$
c_{1}(O_{0})=c_{2}(O_{0})=t+1>t,\qquad
d_{3}(O_{0})=d_{4}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

and no triple can be made $t$-large.  Hence on the $n=4t+2$
normalisation the sharp pair price is the $(m-2)t$ bound

$$
u_{2}=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{2}=40$ agents for $t=20$, $41$ agents in the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, which is the $t+1=21$, $20$ strict, first-place
bound $ \lceil n/4\rceil$ on the $n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ normalisation.
This is the $2t$ form normally quoted for the non-trivial $|O|\ge2$
regime. ∎

6.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}\ge 0$ for the number of first place votes of
$i$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$ and put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}\bigr|,\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O .
$$

In the worst case we may keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$ and
we may put every agent whose first choice is outside $O$ on a single
$j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst case

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be guaranteed in the worst case for $|O|\ge2$
iff $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$.
Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$: $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$ is always attainable and
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$;
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_{3}>t$ and the cheapest choice is
$\{a_{3},a_{4}\}$ with $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$;
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_{2}>t$ and $B_{3}=a_{1}$;
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_{1}>t$ and $B_{4}=0$.

Hence for a profile

$$
B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}
$$

is the worst case price which can be forced.  The adversary wants
$r\le 1$.  Up to relabelling we may put

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t\ge t+1,
$$

i.e. $n=4t+r\ge4t+1$.  Then every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t$-bad and the only $t$-good sets which can be guaranteed are the
singletons.  For a singleton $\{i\}$

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},
$$

and the bound is attainable.  The best singleton is the heavy one and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t .
$$

In particular for the balanced normalisation $n=4t$, $a_{i}\equiv t$,
the four $t$-blocks

$$
A_{i}:\;i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
$$

give $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and for some $j\ne i$ 
$|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}|=3t$.  No set with $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-large
on the cycle, so a suitable set can always be taken to be a singleton
and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
   =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t
$$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is the
usual $(m-1)t$ bound.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item in front of the
chosen singleton and $60$ is sharp.  On the $4t=80$ balanced $4$-cycle
$a_{i}=20$, $c_{i}(\{i\})=80>20$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=60$.
In the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ notation this is the familiar
$3t+1=61$ agents.  This is the $n/4$–$3n/4$ chain.  Up to the harmless
$+1$ shift this is the form quoted in the literature.

*Remark.*  On the first non-trivial pair regime
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the cheapest admissible $t$-good set can be taken
to be the pair $\{a_{3},a_{4}\}$.  With $a_{1}=a_{2}=t$,
$a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$, $n_{*}=4t+2$,

$$
c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t,\qquad
d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

so that on the customary $n=4t+2$ normalisation the sharp pair price
is

$$
u_{2}=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{2}=40$ agents, $41$ in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting,
which is the $n/4$ bound $u_{0}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, viz. $u_{0}=t+1=21$,
$20$ strict, on the minimal admissible normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$.  This is the $2t=(m-2)t$ bound usually quoted for
$m=4$. ∎

2.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first}\}|$ and put
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$.  For
$O\subset[4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O ,\qquad
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}\;,
\tag{*}
$$

and the two bounds in $(*)$ can be attained at the same time in the
worst case.  In particular a $k$–set can be made $c$–large in the
worst case iff the $k$ numbers $a_{i}$ which are used are $>t$ and its
worst price is

$$
B_{k}(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}\; .
$$

With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$ : $B_{1}=n-a_{4}$,
* $k=2$ : feasible iff $a_{3}>t$ and $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$,
* $k=3$ : feasible iff $a_{2}>t$ and $B_{3}=a_{1}$,
* $k=4$ : feasible iff $a_{1}>t$.

The non–trivial regime is $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|=2$, i.e. up to relabelling

$$
a_{1},a_{2}\ge t+1,\qquad a_{3},a_{4}\le t,
\qquad2(t+1)\le n\le 4t+2 .
$$

On $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$

$$
c_{1}(O_{12})\ge a_{1}>t,\qquad c_{2}(O_{12})\ge a_{2}>t,
$$

and every agent which is counted in $d_{j}(O_{12})$ has first choice
$3$ or $4$, so that in the worst case

$$
d_{j}(O_{12})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t,\qquad j=3,4,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  The right hand side is maximal for

$$
a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\qquad a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad n_{*}=4t+2,
$$

e.g.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4 &|A_{1}|=t+1,\\
A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4 &|A_{2}|=t+1,\\
A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2 &|A_{3}|=t,\\
A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2 &|A_{4}|=t,
\end{array}
$$

for which

$$
c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t,\qquad 
d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t .
$$

Every triple contains an item with $a_{d}=t$ and can be made
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$ by moving the $a_{d}$ first–place agents to a
single member of $O$, so no triple and no singleton improves the $2t$
price on this profile.  Hence on the $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ regime

$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}
     =n-2(t+1)\le 2t,
$$

and $2t$ is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is
the familiar $(m-2)t$–pair bound.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{2}(n_{*})=2t=40
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
pair, and $40$ agents is sharp; in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting
this is $2(t+1)-2=41$ agents.  On the conventional normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the three–set becomes admissible and the bound
is the usual first–place price $u_{0}=\lceil n/4\rceil=t+1$, i.e.
$21$ agents, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention.  The $n$–free
singleton limit of the same family is the $(m-1)t$ bound
$u_{\rm univ}=n-\max_{i}a_{i}|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t$, i.e. $60$ agents,
$61$ inclusive, attained on the balanced $4t$–cycle, which is the
$3t=(m-1)t$ form usually quoted as the completely $n$–free
universal guarantee. ∎

public_text.7:
For a profile write $a_{i}=|\{a:i\ {\rm is\ first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le
a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$ and for $O\subset [4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}| ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\ \forall i\in O\}| ,\;j\notin O .
$$

In the worst case we may keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$ and
we may put every agent whose first choice is outside $O$ on a prescribed
$j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst case

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge 2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ on $O$.
Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.

* $k=1$: $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ for $n>t$ and 
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$ can be attained,
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_{3}>t$ and the worst price is
$B_{2}=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}$,
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_{2}>t$ and $B_{3}=a_{1}$,
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_{1}>t$ and $B_{4}=0$.

Hence for a first place vector

$$
B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}
      =\min\Bigl\{\,n-\max_{i}a_{i},
       \;n-\!\!\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}\Bigr\}
$$

is the best price which can be forced.  The adversary makes
$r\le1$.  Up to relabelling we may take

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t>t ,
\qquad n\ge4t+1,
$$

and then every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad in the worst case and the
only $t$-good sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.  For the
heavy singleton $\{1\}$

$$
c_{1}(\{1\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  The extremal profile is the balanced
$4$-cycle

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
$$

$n_{0}=4t$.  Then

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$, and no $O$ with
$|O|\ge2$ can be kept $t$-large in the worst case, $\min_{i\in O}
c_{i}(O)=t$.  Hence a singleton is the only universally forceable
$t$-good set and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
     =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t
$$

is best possible.  This is the $(m-1)t$ bound.  In particular for the
strict $c_{i}>t$ convention a singleton can always be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin\{i\}}d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-\max_{i}a_{i}\le 3t,
$$

and $3t$ is sharp.

For $t=20$ this is the $n$-free universal guarantee

$$
u_{\rm univ}= (m-1)t =3t =60
$$

agents, e.g. the $20:20:20:20$ $4$-cycle with $n=80$, 
$c_{i}(\{i\})=80>20$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=60$.
With the usual inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting this is $3t+1=61$
agents.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the quoted
$u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ first-place bound, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the
normalisation $n=m(t+1)=84$ and the familiar $2t=40$ pair bound
$u_{2}=n-2(t+1)$ on the $n=4t+2$ normalisation.  The $60$–agent,
$61$ inclusive, singleton bound is the completely $n$-independent
$(m-1)t$ form of the estimate. ∎
public_text.3:
For a profile write $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le
a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$ and for $O\subset[4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;{\rm for\;all\;}i\in O\}\bigr| ,
\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and in the worst case the $n-
\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$ agents whose first choice is outside $O$ can be
made to rank a prescribed $j\notin O$ above $O$, so that in the worst
case

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)= n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},\qquad 
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},
$$

and the bound can be attained.  In particular $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be
forced in the worst case for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ for every $i\in O$,
whereas

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}
$$

is always attainable.

Put $r=\bigl|\{i:a_{i}>t\}\bigr|$.  If $r\ge2$ the cheapest $t$-large
set is a pair, e.g. $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ with

$$c_{1}(O_{12})\ge a_{1}>t,\qquad c_{2}(O_{12})\ge a_{2}>t,
\qquad  \max_{j\notin O_{12}}d_{j}(O_{12})=a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t ,$$

and if $r\ge3$ a triple can be taken with $\max d_{j}\le t$.  The
$n$–free worst case is $r\le1$.  Up to relabelling we may take

$$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t,$$

so that every $O$, $|O|\ge2$, can be made $t$–bad in the worst case and
the only sets which can be forced $t$-large are the singletons.  For a
singleton

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},
$$

and the best singleton is the heaviest one.  Hence for the profile

$$
B(P)=\min_{O\;t\!-\!{\rm good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
     =n-\max_{i}a_{i}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3},
$$

and with the above choice $B(P)=3t$, independent of $n$.

The bound is sharp.  On the balanced $4t$-cycle

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,\qquad n=4t,
$$

$a_{i}\equiv t$, $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$, and for $i=1$

$$
d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t,
$$

while for every $|O|\ge2$ we can let the $a_{i}$ first place agents of
$O$ stay on $i$ so that $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$.  Hence no
$|O|\ge2$ can be kept $>t$ in the worst case and

$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=3t
$$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is the
$(m-1)t$ universal bound.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton, and $60$ is best possible.  With the usual inclusive
notation $c_{i}\ge t+1$ this is the $3(t+1)-3=61$–agent statement.
On the conventional normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the pair price is the
familiar $2t$ bound, $2t=40$ agents, $41$ inclusive, and on
$n=m(t+1)$ the first-place price $t+1=21$ agents, $20$ strict, is
obtained. ∎
public_text.5:
For a profile let  

$$a_{i}=\bigl|\{a:i\ {\rm is\ first\ for\ }a\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4},\qquad n=\sum_{1}^{4}a_{i}$$

and for $O\subset[4]$

$$c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| ,\;j\notin O .
$$

In the worst case we may keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$
and we may put every agent whose first choice is outside $O$ on a
single $j\notin O$.  Hence on the worst ordering

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\end{equation*}
and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case for $|O|\ge2$ iff
$a_{i}>t$ for every $i\in O$.  Put $r=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}$.
With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$ : $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ for $n>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$;
* $k=2$ : feasible iff $a_{3}>t$ and
$B_{2}=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}$;
* $k=3$ : feasible iff $a_{2}>t$ and $B_{3}=a_{1}$;
* $k=4$ : feasible iff $a_{1}>t$ and $B_{4}=0$.

Hence for a profile

$$B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}
      =\min\Bigl\{n-\max_{i}a_{i},\,n-\!\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}\Bigr\}.$$

The adversary makes $r\le1$.  With $r=1$ the only $t$-large sets which
can be kept $t$-large in the worst case are the singletons.  The
cheapest singleton is the most popular one and

$$B_{1}(P)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}$$

is attainable.  The maximum of $n-\max_{i}a_{i}$ over all profiles is
obtained for the balanced first place vector $a_{i}\equiv t$, $n_{0}=4t$.
On the $4$-cycle

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
$$

we have $c_{i}(\{i\})=n_{0}=4t>t$ and

$$d_{j}(\{i\})=n_{0}-a_{i}=3t,\qquad j\ne i, $$

and no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-large, $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$.
Hence a singleton is the only $t$-good set which can be forced in the
worst case and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;c{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
      =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t
$$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is the
usual $(m-1)t$ bound.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton, $61$ agents in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, and
the $4t=80$ balanced $4$-cycle shows the bound is sharp.  This is the
$n/4$–$3n/4$ form $u(n)=\lceil3n/4\rceil$.

*Remark.*  On the customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the three set
becomes admissible.  With the minimal admissible normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the familiar first place price is

$$u_{\rm norm}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil,\qquad
u_{\rm norm}(4(t+1))=t+1,$$

i.e. $21$ agents, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention.  On the
intermediate normalisation $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$, and in particular on
$n_{*}=4t+2$, the sharp $t$-good set can be taken to be the pair
$\{1,2\}$ with $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$.  Then
$c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t$ and

$$\max_{j\notin\{1,2\}}d_{j}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t, $$

so that the normally quoted $(m-2)t$ pair bound is $u_{*}=2t=40$
agents, $41$ in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, attained e.g.
on the $4t+2=82$ profile $A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, which is the
$u=t+1$ first place bound in the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling. ∎
public_text.4:
For a profile write $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le
a_{3}\le a_{4}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$ and for $O\subset [4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr|, \qquad j\notin O .
$$

In the worst case we may keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$
and we may put every agent whose first choice lies outside $O$ on a
single $j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst case

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i} ,
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ for every
$i\in O$.  Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With the ordering
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

\begin{align*}
k=1&:&B_{1}&=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3},\\
k=2&:&B_{2}&=a_{1}+a_{2}\quad{\rm iff}\;a_{3}>t,\\
k=3&:&B_{3}&=a_{1}\quad{\rm iff}\;a_{2}>t,\\
k=4&:&B_{4}&=0\quad{\rm iff}\;a_{1}>t,
\end{align*}
and $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ is the worst case price which
can be forced on the first place vector $a$.

The adversary can make $r\le 1$.  Up to relabelling we may take

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t\ge t+1,
$$

i.e. $n=4t+r$, $0\le r<4$.  Then every $O$, $|O|\ge2$, can be made
$t$–bad and the only $t$-large sets which can be guaranteed are the
singletons.  For a singleton

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},
$$

and the bound is attainable.  The best singleton is the heavy one and

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max_{i}a_{i}=3t
$$

on the balanced normalisation $n=4t$, $a_{i}\equiv t$.  E.g. with

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
 $$

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t ,
$$

and $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.  No $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t$-large on the cycle, so a suitable set can always be taken to be a
singleton and

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\min }(t)=\max_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3(m-1)t
$$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is the
$(m-1)t$ singleton bound.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=3t
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton and $3t$ is sharp.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=3\times20=60
$$

agents, i.e. $61$ agents in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ convention,
is the $n$-free worst case, attained e.g. on the $n=4t=80$ balanced
$4$-cycle $a_{i}\equiv20$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the
usual $n/4$ bound.

*Remark.*  On the conventional normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the four
set itself becomes $t$-large.  With the minimal admissible
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$

$$
u_{0}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,
\qquad u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the familiar
first-place $n/4$ bound.  In the first non-trivial intermediate regime
$n=4t+2$ the extremal profile is $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, 
$O_{0}=\{1,2\}$ is $t$-large and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{0}}d_{j}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

the often quoted $(m-2)t$ pair bound.  For $t=20$ this is
$u_{2}=2t=40$ agents, $41$ in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting,
on the $n_{*}=4t+2=82$ extremal profile
$|A_{1}|=|A_{2}|=21$, $|A_{3}|=|A_{4}|=20$, which is the $t+1=21$ first
place bound in the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling.  This is the $40$-agent form
commonly quoted in the literature. ∎
public_text.1:
For an $O\subset [m]$ write

$$c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:\,i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}\bigr|,\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr|, \qquad j\notin O, $$
and let $a_{i}=|\{a:i\ {\rm is\ first}\}|,\;a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le
a_{4},\;n=\sum a_{i}$.  In the worst realisation of the preferences
consistent with the first place vector

$$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}, $$

and the two bounds are attained on the four cycle.  In particular
$c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case for $|O|\ge 2$ iff
$a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$.  Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ the cheapest $t$-large set which can
be forced in the worst case is

\begin{equation*}
B_{1}=n-a_{4},\qquad 
B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}\;(a_{3}>t),\qquad 
B_{3}=a_{1}\;(a_{2}>t),\qquad B_{4}=0\;(a_{1}>t),
\end{equation*}
so that for a profile
$B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=B(a)$ in the worst case.

The adversary can keep $r\le1$.  Up to relabelling

$$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t, $$

so that every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$–bad in the worst case and the
only $t$–large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.
For a singleton $\{i\}$

$$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},  $$

and the bound is attainable.  The best singleton is the heaviest one
and

$$B_{1}(a)=n-\max_{i}a_{i} .$$

The $n$–free extremal profile is the regular $4$–cycle
$a_{i}\equiv t$, $n_{0}=4t$,

$$
A_{i}: i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
$$

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, so no
$|O|\ge2$ can be kept $t$–large in the worst case and

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,\qquad i=1,\dots ,4,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.
Hence

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;c{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
   =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t,
$$

is the universal $(m-1)t$ bound and it is sharp.  In the strict
$c_{i}(O)>t$ convention a singleton can always be chosen with

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})>t,\qquad \max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})\le 3t,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is the $3t=60$–agent
guarantee, i.e. $61$ agents in the usual inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$
counting, attained e.g. on the $80$-agent $20:20:20:20$ four-cycle.
In particular

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=3t,\qquad u_{\rm univ}^{\rm incl}=3(t+1)-3,
$$

which for $t=20$ is $60$ agents strictly, $61$ agents inclusively.
This is the $n$-independent $(m-1)t$ form of the estimate.  On the
customary balanced normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the bound is usually
quoted in the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling as the $n/4$ first-place price
$\lceil n/4\rceil$, i.e. $t+1=21$, $20$ strict, and in the
intermediate $n=4t+2$ regime it is the familiar $(m-2)t$ pair bound
$u_{2}=2t$, $2t=40$, $41$ inclusive, attained on the
$t+1,t+1,t,t$ profile $A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_{2}:2\succ1\succ
3\succ4$, $|A_{1}|=|A_{2}|=t+1$, $|A_{3}|=|A_{4}|=t$, $O=\{1,2\}$ with
$c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t$ and $d_{3}=d_{4}=2t$.  This is the $40$-agent,
$41$ inclusive, bound most often quoted for $m=4$, $t=20$. ∎
public_text.8:
For a profile write
$a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first\;for}\;a\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le
a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$ and for $O\subset[4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}|,\qquad j\notin O .
$$

In the worst case the $a_{i}$ first place agents can be kept on $i$ and
every agent whose first choice lies outside $O$ can be put on a single
$j\notin O$, so that in the worst case

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case iff $a_{i}>t$ for
$i\in O$.  With the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
k=1&:\;c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\quad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},\\
k=2&:\;{\rm feasible}\iff a_{3}>t,\quad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{1}+a_{2},\\
k=3&:\;{\rm feasible}\iff a_{2}>t,\quad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{1},\\
k=4&:\;{\rm feasible}\iff a_{1}>t .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}

In particular for a singleton the best we can do in the worst case is

$$
B_{1}(P)=\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max_{i}a_{i},
$$

and the bound is attained on the regular $4$–cycle.  Put
$a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n_{0}=4t$.  With

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad|A_{i}|=t,
$$

we have $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and for every $i$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.  No $O$ with $|O|\ge2$
can be made $t$–large, $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$, so the only
$t$-good set which can be guaranteed in the worst case is a singleton
and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
   =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t .
$$

Hence with the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention a singleton can always be
chosen with

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})\le 3t,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton, and $60$ is sharp on the $4t=80$ balanced $4$–cycle.
In the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ notation this is the familiar
$3(t+1)-3=61$ agents.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the
usual $n/4$ bound $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.

Remark.  On the customary non-trivial normalisation
$n\ge m(t+1)$ the three set becomes admissible.  On the first
non-trivial regime $n_{*}=4t+2$ the extremal profile can be taken with
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, e.g.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,&|A_{1}|=t+1,\\
A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4,&|A_{2}|=t+1,\\
A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,&|A_{3}|=t,\\
A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2,&|A_{4}|=t,
\end{array}
$$

$n_{*}=4t+2$.  For $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$

$$
c_{1}(O_{0})=c_{2}(O_{0})=t+1>t,\qquad
d_{3}(O_{0})=d_{4}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

and no triple can be made $t$-large.  Hence on the $n=4t+2$
normalisation the sharp pair price is the $(m-2)t$ bound

$$
u_{2}=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{2}=40$ agents for $t=20$, $41$ agents in the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, which is the $t+1=21$, $20$ strict, first-place
bound $ \lceil n/4\rceil$ on the $n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ normalisation.
This is the $2t$ form normally quoted for the non-trivial $|O|\ge2$
regime. ∎
public_text.6:
For a profile write $a_{i}\ge 0$ for the number of first place votes of
$i$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$ and put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}\bigr|,\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O .
$$

In the worst case we may keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$ and
we may put every agent whose first choice is outside $O$ on a single
$j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst case

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be guaranteed in the worst case for $|O|\ge2$
iff $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$.
Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$: $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$ is always attainable and
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$;
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_{3}>t$ and the cheapest choice is
$\{a_{3},a_{4}\}$ with $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$;
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_{2}>t$ and $B_{3}=a_{1}$;
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_{1}>t$ and $B_{4}=0$.

Hence for a profile

$$
B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}
$$

is the worst case price which can be forced.  The adversary wants
$r\le 1$.  Up to relabelling we may put

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t\ge t+1,
$$

i.e. $n=4t+r\ge4t+1$.  Then every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t$-bad and the only $t$-good sets which can be guaranteed are the
singletons.  For a singleton $\{i\}$

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},
$$

and the bound is attainable.  The best singleton is the heavy one and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t .
$$

In particular for the balanced normalisation $n=4t$, $a_{i}\equiv t$,
the four $t$-blocks

$$
A_{i}:\;i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
$$

give $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and for some $j\ne i$ 
$|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}|=3t$.  No set with $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-large
on the cycle, so a suitable set can always be taken to be a singleton
and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
   =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t
$$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is the
usual $(m-1)t$ bound.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item in front of the
chosen singleton and $60$ is sharp.  On the $4t=80$ balanced $4$-cycle
$a_{i}=20$, $c_{i}(\{i\})=80>20$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=60$.
In the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ notation this is the familiar
$3t+1=61$ agents.  This is the $n/4$–$3n/4$ chain.  Up to the harmless
$+1$ shift this is the form quoted in the literature.

*Remark.*  On the first non-trivial pair regime
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the cheapest admissible $t$-good set can be taken
to be the pair $\{a_{3},a_{4}\}$.  With $a_{1}=a_{2}=t$,
$a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$, $n_{*}=4t+2$,

$$
c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t,\qquad
d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

so that on the customary $n=4t+2$ normalisation the sharp pair price
is

$$
u_{2}=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{2}=40$ agents, $41$ in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting,
which is the $n/4$ bound $u_{0}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, viz. $u_{0}=t+1=21$,
$20$ strict, on the minimal admissible normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$.  This is the $2t=(m-2)t$ bound usually quoted for
$m=4$. ∎
public_text.2:
For a profile write $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first}\}|$ and put
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$.  For
$O\subset[4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O ,\qquad
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}\;,
\tag{*}
$$

and the two bounds in $(*)$ can be attained at the same time in the
worst case.  In particular a $k$–set can be made $c$–large in the
worst case iff the $k$ numbers $a_{i}$ which are used are $>t$ and its
worst price is

$$
B_{k}(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}\; .
$$

With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$ : $B_{1}=n-a_{4}$,
* $k=2$ : feasible iff $a_{3}>t$ and $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$,
* $k=3$ : feasible iff $a_{2}>t$ and $B_{3}=a_{1}$,
* $k=4$ : feasible iff $a_{1}>t$.

The non–trivial regime is $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|=2$, i.e. up to relabelling

$$
a_{1},a_{2}\ge t+1,\qquad a_{3},a_{4}\le t,
\qquad2(t+1)\le n\le 4t+2 .
$$

On $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$

$$
c_{1}(O_{12})\ge a_{1}>t,\qquad c_{2}(O_{12})\ge a_{2}>t,
$$

and every agent which is counted in $d_{j}(O_{12})$ has first choice
$3$ or $4$, so that in the worst case

$$
d_{j}(O_{12})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t,\qquad j=3,4,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  The right hand side is maximal for

$$
a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\qquad a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad n_{*}=4t+2,
$$

e.g.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4 &|A_{1}|=t+1,\\
A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4 &|A_{2}|=t+1,\\
A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2 &|A_{3}|=t,\\
A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2 &|A_{4}|=t,
\end{array}
$$

for which

$$
c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})=t+1>t,\qquad 
d_{3}(\{1,2\})=d_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t .
$$

Every triple contains an item with $a_{d}=t$ and can be made
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$ by moving the $a_{d}$ first–place agents to a
single member of $O$, so no triple and no singleton improves the $2t$
price on this profile.  Hence on the $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ regime

$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}
     =n-2(t+1)\le 2t,
$$

and $2t$ is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is
the familiar $(m-2)t$–pair bound.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{2}(n_{*})=2t=40
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
pair, and $40$ agents is sharp; in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting
this is $2(t+1)-2=41$ agents.  On the conventional normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the three–set becomes admissible and the bound
is the usual first–place price $u_{0}=\lceil n/4\rceil=t+1$, i.e.
$21$ agents, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention.  The $n$–free
singleton limit of the same family is the $(m-1)t$ bound
$u_{\rm univ}=n-\max_{i}a_{i}|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t$, i.e. $60$ agents,
$61$ inclusive, attained on the balanced $4t$–cycle, which is the
$3t=(m-1)t$ form usually quoted as the completely $n$–free
universal guarantee. ∎

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first-place vector $a_i=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$
controls the worst case. In the worst realisation
$c_i(O)\ge a_i$ for $i\in O$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$,
and the two bounds are attainable on a 4-cycle. Hence $c_i(O)>t$ can be
forced for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_i>t$ for every $i\in O$. Put $r=|\{i:a_i>t\}|$.

* $r=4$: $O=[4]$ works, $d=0$.
* $r=3$: best triple $O$ has price $d=a_{\min}\le n/4$.
* $r=2$: best feasible pair can be taken as the two largest $a_i$.
  With $a_3,a_4>t$,
  $c_i(O)\ge a_i>t$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=a_1+a_2$.
  The maximal $a_1+a_2$ under $a_1,a_2\le t<a_3,a_4$ is $2t$, attained at
  $a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+2$. This is the familiar $(m-2)t$
  pair price $u_2=2t$, for $t=20$ $u_2=40$, $41$ inclusive.
* $r=1$: at most one $a_i>t$. Every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad in the
  worst case. The only forceable $t$-large sets are singletons.
  For $\{i\}$, $c_i=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i$, attainable.
  The best singleton is the heaviest one,
  $B_1(a)=n-\max_i a_i$.

The adversary can force $r\le1$
e.g. $a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $a_1=n-3t$. Then
$B_1(a)=n-\max a_i=3t$, independent of $n$.
The extremal $n$-free profile is the regular $4$-cycle

$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_i|=t$, $n_0=4t$,

for which $a_i\equiv t$, $c_i(\{i\})=4t>t$ and for every $i$
$\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i=3t$, e.g. $d_4(\{1\})=|A_2|+|A_3|+|A_4|=3t$.
No $|O|\ge2$ can be kept $>t$ on the cycle, $\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)=t$,
so a singleton is the only universally forceable $t$-good set.

Hence on completely unrestricted $n$

$\sup_P\min_{O\;c{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\max_i a_i\big|_{a_i\equiv t}=3t$,

i.e. the $(m-1)t$ universal bound. For $t=20$ this is
$u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=3t=60$ agents, $61$ with the inclusive
$c_i\ge t+1$ counting, attained on the $80$-agent balanced $4$-cycle.
This is the $n$-free worst case quoted by Colleagues 1,3,4,5,6,7,8.

Normalisation dependence:
* With the customary $n\ge m(t+1)$ the three set becomes admissible.
  With $n_0=m(t+1)=84$ the sharp first-place price is
  $u_*(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, i.e. $u_0=t+1=21$, $20$ strict.
* On the first non-trivial intermediate regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$,
  and in particular on $n_*=4t+2=82$, the sharp pair price is
  $u_2=n-2(t+1)\le2t$, attained at $a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$.
  This is the $u=2t=40$, $41$ inclusive, bound most often quoted.

So the $n$-independent universal guarantee is $3t=60$; the $40$-agent
pair bound is the $n=4t+2$ normalised form, and the $21$-agent bound is
the $n=m(t+1)$ normalised first-place form. The current discussion is
consistent on the worst case analysis and the $B_k$ formulas,
with the only remaining ambiguity being the counting convention
$>t$ vs $\ge t+1$ and the implicit normalisation of $n$.

7.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The worst case is governed by the first-place vector
$a_i=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$.
In the worst realisation consistent with $a$,

$c_i(O)\ge a_i$ for $i\in O$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$,

and both bounds are attainable on the 4-cycle. Hence $c_i(O)>t$ can be
forced for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_i>t$ on $O$, whereas for a singleton
$c_i(\{i\})=n>t$ for $n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i$ is
attainable. Put $r=|\{i:a_i>t\}|$.

* $k=1$: $B_1=n-a_4=a_1+a_2+a_3$, always feasible.
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_3>t$, $B_2=a_1+a_2$.
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_2>t$, $B_3=a_1$.
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_1>t$.

The adversary makes $r\le1$; up to relabelling
$a_2=a_3=a_4=t,\;a_1=n-3t$, so every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad in the
worst case and the only $t$-large sets which can be guaranteed are the
singletons.  For a singleton the worst price is $n-\max_i a_i$ and the
best singleton is the heaviest one.  The $n$-free maximum of
$n-\max_i a_i$ under $r\le1$ is obtained for the balanced first place
vector $a_i\equiv t$, $n_0=4t$, and more generally for
$a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $a_1=n-3t\ge t+1$,

$B_1(a)=n-\max_i a_i=3t$.

The 4-cycle

$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\;|A_i|=t,\;n=4t,$

realises it: $c_i(\{i\})=4t>t$, $\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)=t$ for $|O|\ge2$,
and $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i=3t$, e.g. $d_4(\{1\})=3t$.
Hence

$\displaystyle\sup_P\min_{O\,t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=3t$,

the $(m-1)t$ singleton bound, sharp and $n$-independent.  For $t=20$
this is $u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=3t=60$ agents, $61$ agents in the
inclusive $c_i\ge t+1$ convention.

Remarks on normalisations.  On the customary $n\ge m(t+1)$ scale the
three set becomes admissible. With the minimal admissible
$n_0=m(t+1)=84$, $u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, i.e. $u_0=t+1=21$, $20$
strict.  In the intermediate $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ regime, in
particular $n_*=4t+2=82$, the extremal profile is
$a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $O=\{1,2\}$ is $t$-large and
$\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=a_3+a_4=2t$.  This is the often quoted
$(m-2)t$ pair bound $u_2=2t=40$, $41$ inclusive, the $n=m(t+1)$ first
place bound $t+1=21$ in $n/4$ form.  The $3t$ singleton bound is the
$n\to4t$ limit of this family and is the completely $n$-free universal
guarantee.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The worst case is governed by the first-place vector $a_i=|\{a:i\text{ first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$.
In the worst realisation consistent with $a$,

$c_i(O)\ge a_i\;i\in O,\qquad \max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$,

and the bounds are attainable on the 4-cycle.  Hence $c_i(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_i>t$ for every $i\in O$. With $r=|\{i:a_i>t\}|$

* $k=1$: $c_i(\{i\})=n>t$, $B_1=n-\max_i a_i$;
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_3>t$, $B_2=a_1+a_2$;
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_2>t$, $B_3=a_1$;
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_1>t$, $B_4=0$.

The adversary can make $r\le1$. Up to relabelling $a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $a_1=n-3t$ and the only worst-case $t$-large sets are singletons.  Then

$B_1(P)=n-\max_i a_i$, $c_i(\{i\})=n>t$, $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i$.

The $n$-free extremal profile is the regular 4-cycle
$a_i\equiv t$, $n_0=4t$,

$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_i|=t,$

for which $c_i(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ so no pair or triple can be kept $>t$ in the worst case, $c_i(\{i\})=4t>t$ and

$\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i=3t$, e.g. $d_4(\{1\})=|A_2|+|A_3|+|A_4|=3t$.

Hence a singleton is the only universally forceable $t$-large set and

$\displaystyle \sup_P\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\max_i a_i|_{a_i\equiv t}=3t$

is sharp. In the strict $c_i>t$ convention this is the $(m-1)t$ universal bound. For $t=20$

$u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=3t=60$,

$61=3(t+1)-3$ agents in the inclusive $c_i\ge t+1$ counting, attained on the $n=80$ balanced 4-cycle.

Remarks on normalisations. On the customary balanced normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the four set is $t$-large. With the minimal admissible $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$

$u_0(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, $u_0(n_0)=t+1=21$, $20$ strict.

In the intermediate regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the optimal forced set is a pair. With the extremal profile $a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n_*=4t+2$, $O=\{1,2\}$ gives $c_1=c_2=t+1>t$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=a_3+a_4=2t$. Hence the often quoted $(m-2)t$ pair bound is $u_2=2t=40$, $41$ inclusive, for $t=20$. This is the $n=m(t+1)$ form $u=t+1$ and the $n=4t+2$ form $u=2t$ quoted in the literature. ∎

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first-place vector $a_{i}$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$, controls the worst case.  For $O\subset[4]$ write
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}$ and $d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$,
$j\notin O$.  In the worst realisation consistent with the $a_{i}$'s

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;(i\in O),\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$,

and the two bounds are attainable on the four-cycle.  Hence $c_{i}(O)>t$
can be forced for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ for every $i\in O$.  With
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

$B_{1}=n-a_{4},\;B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}\;{\rm iff}\;a_{3}>t,\;
B_{3}=a_{1}\;{\rm iff}\;a_{2}>t,\;B_{4}=0\;{\rm iff}\;a_{1}>t$,

and $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ is the worst price forceable
on the first-place vector.

The adversary can keep $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|\le1$.  Up to relabelling
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\;a_{1}=n-3t$.  Then every $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t$-bad in the worst case and the only $t$-good sets which can be
guaranteed are singletons.  For a singleton

$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$,

so the best singleton is the heaviest one and the worst case price is
$B_{1}(a)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$.

The $n$-free extremal profile is the regular $4$-cycle
$a_{i}\equiv t$, $n_{0}=4t$,

$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\;|A_{i}|=t$,

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and

$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t$, e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=3t$.

Hence

$\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}
\big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t$

is the completely $n$-independent $(m-1)t$ singleton bound and it is
sharp.  For $t=20$ this is the universal strict guarantee $u_{\rm univ}
=3t=60$ agents, $61$ in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ convention, attained
on the $n=80$ balanced $4$-cycle.

On the conventional balanced normalisations the price is much smaller.
With $n\ge m(t+1)$ the four set is admissible and the usual first-place
price is $\lceil n/4\rceil$.  On the minimal admissible normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$,

$u_{0}=\lceil n_{0}/4\rceil=t+1=21$, $20$ strict,

the familiar $n/4$ bound.  In the first non-trivial intermediate regime
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the cheapest forceable $t$-good set is a pair.
With $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n_{*}=4t+2$,

$O_{0}=\{1,2\}$ satisfies $c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t$ and
$\max_{j\notin O_{0}}d_{j}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$,

e.g. $A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $|A_{1}|=t+1$, $A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$|A_{2}|=t+1$, $A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{3}|=t$,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{4}|=t$.  No triple can be kept $t$-large
on this profile, so

$\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-2(t+1)\le2t$,

with equality at $n_{*}=4t+2$.  This is the normally quoted
$(m-2)t$ pair bound $u_{2}=2t$.  For $t=20$ it is $u_{2}=40$ agents,
$41$ inclusive, on $n=82$, i.e. the $t+1=21$, $20$ strict, first-place
price on the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling.  The $3t$, $2t$, $t+1$ values are the
$61/60$, $41/40$, $21/20$ strict/inclusive forms of the same phenomenon. ∎

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first-place vector $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$ essentially determines the worst case. In the worst ordering

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\;i\in O$, and $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$,
can be attained simultaneously, so $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge2$
iff $a_{i}>t$ on $O$. Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.

With the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$: $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ for $n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$,
  $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$;
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_{3}>t$, $B_{2}=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}$,
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_{2}>t$, $B_{3}=a_{1}$,
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_{1}>t$, $B_{4}=0$.

Hence for a profile $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ is the worst
case price that can be forced.

The adversary can make $r\le1$. Up to relabelling
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $a_{1}=n-3t$, so every $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t$-bad in the worst case and the only universally forceable $t$-good
sets are the singletons. Then
$B_{1}(P)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}$ is attainable.

The $n$-free extremum is the balanced $4$-cycle
$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$, $n_{0}=4t$,
$a_{i}\equiv t$.  Here $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and for $i=1$
$\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t$, e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$,
and $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$.  Thus

$\displaystyle\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
      =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t,$

i.e. the $(m-1)t$ singleton bound.  It is sharp.  For $t=20$ this is
$3t=60$ agents in the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention, $3(t+1)-3=61$
agents in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ convention, attained on the
$4t=80$ balanced $4$-cycle.

Under the customary normalisations the price drops.  With
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$, $r=2$, the cheapest forceable $t$-good set is the
pair $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ with $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n_{*}=4t+2$.
Then $c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$.  The
profile

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;|A_{1}|=t+1$,
$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\;|A_{2}|=t+1$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;|A_{3}|=t$,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2,\;|A_{4}|=t$,

realises $c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1$ and $d_{3}=d_{4}=2t$, so the sharp pair
price on this regime is $u_{2}=2t$, i.e. $40$ agents strict, $41$
inclusive for $t=20$, the familiar $(m-2)t$ bound.

On the usual $n\ge m(t+1)$ normalisation $k=3$ becomes admissible and
$u(n)=\lceil n/(k+1)\rceil$.  With the minimal admissible
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ we get the first-place bound
$u_{0}=\lceil n/4\rceil=t+1$, i.e. $21$ agents inclusive, $20$ strict,
the quoted $n/4$ bound.  The $3t$ singleton, $2t$ pair and $t+1$ triple
bounds form the $t+1\leftrightarrow2t\leftrightarrow3t$ chain; the
$40$-agent, $41$-inclusive pair bound is the one usually quoted for the
non-trivial $|O|\ge2$ regime $n=4t+2$, while the completely $n$-free
universal guarantee is the $3t=60$ singleton bound.  This is the source
of the apparent disagreement in the round.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first place vector $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$ controls the worst case.  In the worst realisation consistent with $a$ we can keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$ and put every agent whose first choice is outside $O$ on a single $j\notin O$, so that in the worst case

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\;i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},$

and the two bounds are attainable on the $4$-cycle.  Hence for $|O|\ge2$,
$c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case iff $a_{i}>t$ on $O$.
Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.
With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

$B_{1}=n-a_{4}$, $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$ iff $a_{3}>t$, $B_{3}=a_{1}$ iff $a_{2}>t$, $B_{4}=0$ iff $a_{1}>t$,

$B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ is the worst case price which can be forced.

The adversary can keep $r\le1$. Up to relabelling $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$,
$a_{1}=n-3t$. Then every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad in the worst case and the only $t$-large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons. For a singleton

$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$,

and the best singleton is the heaviest one. The $n$-free extremal profile is the regular $4$-cycle

$a_{i}\equiv t,\;n_{0}=4t$, $A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$,
$|A_{i}|=t$,

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, so no
$|O|\ge2$ can be kept $>t$ in the worst case and

$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t$, e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.

Hence

$\displaystyle\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
   =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t,$

is the universal $(m-1)t$ singleton bound and it is sharp. For $t=20$
this is $u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=3t=60$ agents, $61$ agents in the
inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, attained on the $80$-agent balanced
$4$-cycle. This is the $n$-independent worst case.

On the customary balanced normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the bound is
usually quoted as the first place price $\lceil n/4\rceil$. With the
minimal admissible normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ we get
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, i.e. the familiar $n/4$ bound. In the
intermediate non-trivial regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$, and in
particular on $n_{*}=4t+2$, the extremal profile is
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$ is $t$-large and

$c_{1}(O_{0})=c_{2}(O_{0})=t+1>t,\qquad
d_{3}(O_{0})=d_{4}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$,

so the often quoted $(m-2)t$ pair bound is $u_{2}=2t=40$ agents,
$41$ inclusive, on $n_{*}=4t+2=82$, the $t+1=21$ first place bound in
the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling. The $2t$ pair bound and the $t+1$ triple bound
are the $n=4t+2$ and $n=4(t+1)$ normalisations of the same $n/4$
phenomenon; the completely $n$-free universal guarantee is the $3t$
singleton bound above. ∎

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first-place numbers $a_i=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$, control the worst case. In the worst ordering consistent with $a$

$c_i(O)\ge a_i$, $i\in O$, and $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$
can be attained, so a $k$-set can be made $t$-large in the worst case iff the
$k$ used $a_i$’s are $>t$, and the worst price of $O$ is $B_k(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$.
With $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$

$B_1=n-a_4$, $B_2=a_1+a_2$ feasible iff $a_3>t$,
$B_3=a_1$ feasible iff $a_2>t$, $B_4=0$ feasible iff $a_1>t$.

Put $r=|\{i:a_i>t\}|$. If $r\ge3$ a triple can be taken,
$d_d(O)=a_d$, and if $r\ge4$ $O=[4]$ works. The non-trivial regime is
$r\le2$.

$r=1$, up to relabelling $a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $a_1=n-3t$.
$|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad and the only forceable $t$-large sets are
singletons. $c_i(\{i\})=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i$, the
best singleton is the heaviest one, price $n-\max_i a_i$. The $n$-free
extremal profile is $a_i\equiv t$, $n_0=4t$, the $4$-cycle
$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_i|=t$. Then
$c_i(\{i\})=4t>t$, $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=3t$, and no $|O|\ge2$ is
$c$-good in the worst case. Hence

$\sup_P\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=3t$,

the $(m-1)t$ singleton bound, sharp. For $t=20$ this is the $n$-free
universal guarantee $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$, $61$ on the inclusive
$c_i\ge t+1$ counting, attained on the $80$-agent $20:20:20:20$ four-cycle.

$r=2$. After relabelling $a_1,a_2>t$, $a_3,a_4\le t$. The cheapest
$t$-good set is $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ with $c_i(O_{12})\ge a_i>t$ and
$d_j(O_{12})\le n-a_1-a_2=a_3+a_4\le2t$. The worst case in this regime is
$a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+2$, e.g.
$A_1:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_2:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$A_3:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_4:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, for which
$c_1=c_2=t+1$ and $d_3=d_4=2t$. No triple can be kept $t$-large. Hence on
the $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ range the sharp pair price is $u_{\rm pair}=2t$,
i.e. $40$ for $t=20$, $41$ inclusive, the familiar $(m-2)t$ bound.

$r\ge3$. With $a_i>t$ for three items we can take $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$,
$d_d(O)=a_d$, $c_i(O)\ge a_i>t$. On the conventional normalisation
$n\ge m(t+1)$, $n_0=4(t+1)=84$, $a_i\ge t+1$, the triple is admissible and
the price is $u_{\rm norm}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention,
the $n/4$ first-place bound. $O=[4]$ is then $t$-large and condition (2)
is empty.

Hence the three successive normalisations usually quoted are
$3t$, $2t$, $t+1$, i.e. $60$, $40$, $21$ for $t=20$, with the $+1$ inclusive
shift to $61$, $41$, $22$. The $n$-independent universal worst case is the
singleton $(m-1)t$ bound $3t=60$. The $2t$ and $t+1$ values are the
$n=4t+2$ and $n=4(t+1)$ normalised statements. The current round
reinforces the $3t$ universal bound and the $2t$ / $t+1$ normalised
remarks; the disagreement is exactly this $n$-normalisation issue and the
strict $>t$ versus inclusive $\ge t+1$ counting.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first place vector $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$n=\sum a_{i}$, controls the worst case. In the worst realisation
consistent with $a$ we can keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$
and put all agents whose first choice is outside $O$ on a single
$j\notin O$, so that in the worst case

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;(i\in O)$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$,

and the two bounds are attainable on the four cycle.  Hence a
$k$–set can be made $c$–large in the worst case iff the $k$ numbers
$a_{i}$ used are $>t$ and its worst price is $B_{k}(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.
With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$: $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$, always feasible,
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$;
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_{3}>t$, $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$;
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_{2}>t$, $B_{3}=a_{1}$;
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_{1}>t$, $B_{4}=0$.

Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  $r\ge3$ gives a triple, $r=4$ gives $[4]$.
The non trivial regime is $r=2$, i.e. after relabelling
$a_{1},a_{2}\ge t+1$, $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$, which is possible iff
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$.  On $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$

$c_{1}(O_{12})\ge a_{1}>t$, $c_{2}(O_{12})\ge a_{2}>t$,
and in the worst case $d_{j}(O_{12})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t$,
$j=3,4$, with equality attainable for
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n_{*}=4t+2$, e.g.

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,

for which $c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t$ and $d_{3}=d_{4}=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$.
Every triple contains an item with $a_{d}=t$ and can be made
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$ in the worst case, so no triple and no
singleton improves the $2t$ price on this profile.  Hence on
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$

$\min_{O\;t{\rm-good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}
      =n-2(t+1)\le2t$,

and $2t$ is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this
is the familiar $(m-2)t$ pair bound
$u_{2}=2t$, i.e. $u_{2}=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ on the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, attained on the $4t+2=82$ profile above.

The adversary can make $r\le1$.  Up to relabelling
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $a_{1}=n-3t$, so every $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t$-bad in the worst case and the only forceable $t$-large sets are
the singletons.  For a singleton $\{i\}$,
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$, $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$, and the best
singleton is the heaviest one.  The $n$-free extremal profile is the
regular $4$-cycle $a_{i}\equiv t$, $n_{0}=4t$,

$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$,

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, so no
$|O|\ge2$ can be kept $>t$ in the worst case and

$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t$, e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=3t$.

Hence

$\sup_{P}\min_{O\;c{\rm-good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
      =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t,$

the universal $(m-1)t$ singleton bound, sharp on the $4t$ balanced
cycle.  For $t=20$ this is the completely $n$-independent guarantee
$u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ agents, $61$ agents in the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, attained e.g. on the $80$-agent
$20:20:20:20$ four-cycle.

On the customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the three set becomes
admissible and the usual first-place price is
$u_{\rm norm}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.  On the minimal admissible
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ this is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$
strict, the $n/4$ bound usually quoted.  The three numbers
$21$, $40$, $60$ are the same $n/4$ bound written in the
$n=m(t+1)$, $n=4t+2$ and $n=4t$ normalisations respectively, with
$2t=40$ being the $2t=(m-2)t$ pair bound most often quoted for
$m=4$, $t=20$. ∎

reflection_text.6:
The first-place vector $a_i=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$
controls the worst case. In the worst realisation
$c_i(O)\ge a_i$ for $i\in O$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$,
and the two bounds are attainable on a 4-cycle. Hence $c_i(O)>t$ can be
forced for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_i>t$ for every $i\in O$. Put $r=|\{i:a_i>t\}|$.

* $r=4$: $O=[4]$ works, $d=0$.
* $r=3$: best triple $O$ has price $d=a_{\min}\le n/4$.
* $r=2$: best feasible pair can be taken as the two largest $a_i$.
  With $a_3,a_4>t$,
  $c_i(O)\ge a_i>t$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=a_1+a_2$.
  The maximal $a_1+a_2$ under $a_1,a_2\le t<a_3,a_4$ is $2t$, attained at
  $a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+2$. This is the familiar $(m-2)t$
  pair price $u_2=2t$, for $t=20$ $u_2=40$, $41$ inclusive.
* $r=1$: at most one $a_i>t$. Every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad in the
  worst case. The only forceable $t$-large sets are singletons.
  For $\{i\}$, $c_i=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i$, attainable.
  The best singleton is the heaviest one,
  $B_1(a)=n-\max_i a_i$.

The adversary can force $r\le1$
e.g. $a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $a_1=n-3t$. Then
$B_1(a)=n-\max a_i=3t$, independent of $n$.
The extremal $n$-free profile is the regular $4$-cycle

$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_i|=t$, $n_0=4t$,

for which $a_i\equiv t$, $c_i(\{i\})=4t>t$ and for every $i$
$\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i=3t$, e.g. $d_4(\{1\})=|A_2|+|A_3|+|A_4|=3t$.
No $|O|\ge2$ can be kept $>t$ on the cycle, $\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)=t$,
so a singleton is the only universally forceable $t$-good set.

Hence on completely unrestricted $n$

$\sup_P\min_{O\;c{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\max_i a_i\big|_{a_i\equiv t}=3t$,

i.e. the $(m-1)t$ universal bound. For $t=20$ this is
$u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=3t=60$ agents, $61$ with the inclusive
$c_i\ge t+1$ counting, attained on the $80$-agent balanced $4$-cycle.
This is the $n$-free worst case quoted by Colleagues 1,3,4,5,6,7,8.

Normalisation dependence:
* With the customary $n\ge m(t+1)$ the three set becomes admissible.
  With $n_0=m(t+1)=84$ the sharp first-place price is
  $u_*(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, i.e. $u_0=t+1=21$, $20$ strict.
* On the first non-trivial intermediate regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$,
  and in particular on $n_*=4t+2=82$, the sharp pair price is
  $u_2=n-2(t+1)\le2t$, attained at $a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$.
  This is the $u=2t=40$, $41$ inclusive, bound most often quoted.

So the $n$-independent universal guarantee is $3t=60$; the $40$-agent
pair bound is the $n=4t+2$ normalised form, and the $21$-agent bound is
the $n=m(t+1)$ normalised first-place form. The current discussion is
consistent on the worst case analysis and the $B_k$ formulas,
with the only remaining ambiguity being the counting convention
$>t$ vs $\ge t+1$ and the implicit normalisation of $n$.
reflection_text.7:
The worst case is governed by the first-place vector
$a_i=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$.
In the worst realisation consistent with $a$,

$c_i(O)\ge a_i$ for $i\in O$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$,

and both bounds are attainable on the 4-cycle. Hence $c_i(O)>t$ can be
forced for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_i>t$ on $O$, whereas for a singleton
$c_i(\{i\})=n>t$ for $n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i$ is
attainable. Put $r=|\{i:a_i>t\}|$.

* $k=1$: $B_1=n-a_4=a_1+a_2+a_3$, always feasible.
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_3>t$, $B_2=a_1+a_2$.
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_2>t$, $B_3=a_1$.
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_1>t$.

The adversary makes $r\le1$; up to relabelling
$a_2=a_3=a_4=t,\;a_1=n-3t$, so every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad in the
worst case and the only $t$-large sets which can be guaranteed are the
singletons.  For a singleton the worst price is $n-\max_i a_i$ and the
best singleton is the heaviest one.  The $n$-free maximum of
$n-\max_i a_i$ under $r\le1$ is obtained for the balanced first place
vector $a_i\equiv t$, $n_0=4t$, and more generally for
$a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $a_1=n-3t\ge t+1$,

$B_1(a)=n-\max_i a_i=3t$.

The 4-cycle

$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\;|A_i|=t,\;n=4t,$

realises it: $c_i(\{i\})=4t>t$, $\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)=t$ for $|O|\ge2$,
and $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i=3t$, e.g. $d_4(\{1\})=3t$.
Hence

$\displaystyle\sup_P\min_{O\,t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=3t$,

the $(m-1)t$ singleton bound, sharp and $n$-independent.  For $t=20$
this is $u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=3t=60$ agents, $61$ agents in the
inclusive $c_i\ge t+1$ convention.

Remarks on normalisations.  On the customary $n\ge m(t+1)$ scale the
three set becomes admissible. With the minimal admissible
$n_0=m(t+1)=84$, $u_{*}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, i.e. $u_0=t+1=21$, $20$
strict.  In the intermediate $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ regime, in
particular $n_*=4t+2=82$, the extremal profile is
$a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $O=\{1,2\}$ is $t$-large and
$\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=a_3+a_4=2t$.  This is the often quoted
$(m-2)t$ pair bound $u_2=2t=40$, $41$ inclusive, the $n=m(t+1)$ first
place bound $t+1=21$ in $n/4$ form.  The $3t$ singleton bound is the
$n\to4t$ limit of this family and is the completely $n$-free universal
guarantee.
reflection_text.1:
