The worst case is governed by the first-place vector $a_i=|\{a:i\text{ first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$.
In the worst realisation consistent with $a$,

$c_i(O)\ge a_i\;i\in O,\qquad \max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$,

and the bounds are attainable on the 4-cycle.  Hence $c_i(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_i>t$ for every $i\in O$. With $r=|\{i:a_i>t\}|$

* $k=1$: $c_i(\{i\})=n>t$, $B_1=n-\max_i a_i$;
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_3>t$, $B_2=a_1+a_2$;
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_2>t$, $B_3=a_1$;
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_1>t$, $B_4=0$.

The adversary can make $r\le1$. Up to relabelling $a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $a_1=n-3t$ and the only worst-case $t$-large sets are singletons.  Then

$B_1(P)=n-\max_i a_i$, $c_i(\{i\})=n>t$, $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i$.

The $n$-free extremal profile is the regular 4-cycle
$a_i\equiv t$, $n_0=4t$,

$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_i|=t,$

for which $c_i(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ so no pair or triple can be kept $>t$ in the worst case, $c_i(\{i\})=4t>t$ and

$\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i=3t$, e.g. $d_4(\{1\})=|A_2|+|A_3|+|A_4|=3t$.

Hence a singleton is the only universally forceable $t$-large set and

$\displaystyle \sup_P\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\max_i a_i|_{a_i\equiv t}=3t$

is sharp. In the strict $c_i>t$ convention this is the $(m-1)t$ universal bound. For $t=20$

$u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=3t=60$,

$61=3(t+1)-3$ agents in the inclusive $c_i\ge t+1$ counting, attained on the $n=80$ balanced 4-cycle.

Remarks on normalisations. On the customary balanced normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the four set is $t$-large. With the minimal admissible $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$

$u_0(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, $u_0(n_0)=t+1=21$, $20$ strict.

In the intermediate regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the optimal forced set is a pair. With the extremal profile $a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n_*=4t+2$, $O=\{1,2\}$ gives $c_1=c_2=t+1>t$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=a_3+a_4=2t$. Hence the often quoted $(m-2)t$ pair bound is $u_2=2t=40$, $41$ inclusive, for $t=20$. This is the $n=m(t+1)$ form $u=t+1$ and the $n=4t+2$ form $u=2t$ quoted in the literature. ∎
reflection_text.4:
The first-place vector $a_{i}$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$, controls the worst case.  For $O\subset[4]$ write
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}$ and $d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$,
$j\notin O$.  In the worst realisation consistent with the $a_{i}$'s

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;(i\in O),\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$,

and the two bounds are attainable on the four-cycle.  Hence $c_{i}(O)>t$
can be forced for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ for every $i\in O$.  With
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

$B_{1}=n-a_{4},\;B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}\;{\rm iff}\;a_{3}>t,\;
B_{3}=a_{1}\;{\rm iff}\;a_{2}>t,\;B_{4}=0\;{\rm iff}\;a_{1}>t$,

and $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ is the worst price forceable
on the first-place vector.

The adversary can keep $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|\le1$.  Up to relabelling
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\;a_{1}=n-3t$.  Then every $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t$-bad in the worst case and the only $t$-good sets which can be
guaranteed are singletons.  For a singleton

$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$,

so the best singleton is the heaviest one and the worst case price is
$B_{1}(a)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$.

The $n$-free extremal profile is the regular $4$-cycle
$a_{i}\equiv t$, $n_{0}=4t$,

$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\;|A_{i}|=t$,

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and

$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t$, e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=3t$.

Hence

$\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}
\big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t$

is the completely $n$-independent $(m-1)t$ singleton bound and it is
sharp.  For $t=20$ this is the universal strict guarantee $u_{\rm univ}
=3t=60$ agents, $61$ in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ convention, attained
on the $n=80$ balanced $4$-cycle.

On the conventional balanced normalisations the price is much smaller.
With $n\ge m(t+1)$ the four set is admissible and the usual first-place
price is $\lceil n/4\rceil$.  On the minimal admissible normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$,

$u_{0}=\lceil n_{0}/4\rceil=t+1=21$, $20$ strict,

the familiar $n/4$ bound.  In the first non-trivial intermediate regime
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the cheapest forceable $t$-good set is a pair.
With $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n_{*}=4t+2$,

$O_{0}=\{1,2\}$ satisfies $c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t$ and
$\max_{j\notin O_{0}}d_{j}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$,

e.g. $A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $|A_{1}|=t+1$, $A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$|A_{2}|=t+1$, $A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{3}|=t$,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{4}|=t$.  No triple can be kept $t$-large
on this profile, so

$\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-2(t+1)\le2t$,

with equality at $n_{*}=4t+2$.  This is the normally quoted
$(m-2)t$ pair bound $u_{2}=2t$.  For $t=20$ it is $u_{2}=40$ agents,
$41$ inclusive, on $n=82$, i.e. the $t+1=21$, $20$ strict, first-place
price on the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling.  The $3t$, $2t$, $t+1$ values are the
$61/60$, $41/40$, $21/20$ strict/inclusive forms of the same phenomenon. ∎
reflection_text.5:
The first-place vector $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$ essentially determines the worst case. In the worst ordering

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\;i\in O$, and $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$,
can be attained simultaneously, so $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge2$
iff $a_{i}>t$ on $O$. Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.

With the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$: $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ for $n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$,
  $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$;
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_{3}>t$, $B_{2}=n-a_{3}-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}$,
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_{2}>t$, $B_{3}=a_{1}$,
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_{1}>t$, $B_{4}=0$.

Hence for a profile $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ is the worst
case price that can be forced.

The adversary can make $r\le1$. Up to relabelling
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $a_{1}=n-3t$, so every $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t$-bad in the worst case and the only universally forceable $t$-good
sets are the singletons. Then
$B_{1}(P)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}$ is attainable.

The $n$-free extremum is the balanced $4$-cycle
$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$, $n_{0}=4t$,
$a_{i}\equiv t$.  Here $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and for $i=1$
$\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t$, e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$,
and $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$.  Thus

$\displaystyle\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
      =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t,$

i.e. the $(m-1)t$ singleton bound.  It is sharp.  For $t=20$ this is
$3t=60$ agents in the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention, $3(t+1)-3=61$
agents in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ convention, attained on the
$4t=80$ balanced $4$-cycle.

Under the customary normalisations the price drops.  With
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$, $r=2$, the cheapest forceable $t$-good set is the
pair $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ with $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n_{*}=4t+2$.
Then $c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$.  The
profile

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;|A_{1}|=t+1$,
$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\;|A_{2}|=t+1$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;|A_{3}|=t$,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2,\;|A_{4}|=t$,

realises $c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1$ and $d_{3}=d_{4}=2t$, so the sharp pair
price on this regime is $u_{2}=2t$, i.e. $40$ agents strict, $41$
inclusive for $t=20$, the familiar $(m-2)t$ bound.

On the usual $n\ge m(t+1)$ normalisation $k=3$ becomes admissible and
$u(n)=\lceil n/(k+1)\rceil$.  With the minimal admissible
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ we get the first-place bound
$u_{0}=\lceil n/4\rceil=t+1$, i.e. $21$ agents inclusive, $20$ strict,
the quoted $n/4$ bound.  The $3t$ singleton, $2t$ pair and $t+1$ triple
bounds form the $t+1\leftrightarrow2t\leftrightarrow3t$ chain; the
$40$-agent, $41$-inclusive pair bound is the one usually quoted for the
non-trivial $|O|\ge2$ regime $n=4t+2$, while the completely $n$-free
universal guarantee is the $3t=60$ singleton bound.  This is the source
of the apparent disagreement in the round.
reflection_text.8:
The first place vector $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$ controls the worst case.  In the worst realisation consistent with $a$ we can keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$ and put every agent whose first choice is outside $O$ on a single $j\notin O$, so that in the worst case

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\;i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},$

and the two bounds are attainable on the $4$-cycle.  Hence for $|O|\ge2$,
$c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case iff $a_{i}>t$ on $O$.
Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.
With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

$B_{1}=n-a_{4}$, $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$ iff $a_{3}>t$, $B_{3}=a_{1}$ iff $a_{2}>t$, $B_{4}=0$ iff $a_{1}>t$,

$B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ is the worst case price which can be forced.

The adversary can keep $r\le1$. Up to relabelling $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$,
$a_{1}=n-3t$. Then every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad in the worst case and the only $t$-large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons. For a singleton

$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$,

and the best singleton is the heaviest one. The $n$-free extremal profile is the regular $4$-cycle

$a_{i}\equiv t,\;n_{0}=4t$, $A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$,
$|A_{i}|=t$,

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, so no
$|O|\ge2$ can be kept $>t$ in the worst case and

$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t$, e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.

Hence

$\displaystyle\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
   =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t,$

is the universal $(m-1)t$ singleton bound and it is sharp. For $t=20$
this is $u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=3t=60$ agents, $61$ agents in the
inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, attained on the $80$-agent balanced
$4$-cycle. This is the $n$-independent worst case.

On the customary balanced normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the bound is
usually quoted as the first place price $\lceil n/4\rceil$. With the
minimal admissible normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ we get
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, i.e. the familiar $n/4$ bound. In the
intermediate non-trivial regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$, and in
particular on $n_{*}=4t+2$, the extremal profile is
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$ is $t$-large and

$c_{1}(O_{0})=c_{2}(O_{0})=t+1>t,\qquad
d_{3}(O_{0})=d_{4}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$,

so the often quoted $(m-2)t$ pair bound is $u_{2}=2t=40$ agents,
$41$ inclusive, on $n_{*}=4t+2=82$, the $t+1=21$ first place bound in
the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling. The $2t$ pair bound and the $t+1$ triple bound
are the $n=4t+2$ and $n=4(t+1)$ normalisations of the same $n/4$
phenomenon; the completely $n$-free universal guarantee is the $3t$
singleton bound above. ∎
reflection_text.3:
The first-place numbers $a_i=|\{a:i\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $n=\sum a_i$, control the worst case. In the worst ordering consistent with $a$

$c_i(O)\ge a_i$, $i\in O$, and $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$
can be attained, so a $k$-set can be made $t$-large in the worst case iff the
$k$ used $a_i$’s are $>t$, and the worst price of $O$ is $B_k(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_i$.
With $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$

$B_1=n-a_4$, $B_2=a_1+a_2$ feasible iff $a_3>t$,
$B_3=a_1$ feasible iff $a_2>t$, $B_4=0$ feasible iff $a_1>t$.

Put $r=|\{i:a_i>t\}|$. If $r\ge3$ a triple can be taken,
$d_d(O)=a_d$, and if $r\ge4$ $O=[4]$ works. The non-trivial regime is
$r\le2$.

$r=1$, up to relabelling $a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $a_1=n-3t$.
$|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad and the only forceable $t$-large sets are
singletons. $c_i(\{i\})=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i$, the
best singleton is the heaviest one, price $n-\max_i a_i$. The $n$-free
extremal profile is $a_i\equiv t$, $n_0=4t$, the $4$-cycle
$A_i:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_i|=t$. Then
$c_i(\{i\})=4t>t$, $\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=3t$, and no $|O|\ge2$ is
$c$-good in the worst case. Hence

$\sup_P\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=3t$,

the $(m-1)t$ singleton bound, sharp. For $t=20$ this is the $n$-free
universal guarantee $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$, $61$ on the inclusive
$c_i\ge t+1$ counting, attained on the $80$-agent $20:20:20:20$ four-cycle.

$r=2$. After relabelling $a_1,a_2>t$, $a_3,a_4\le t$. The cheapest
$t$-good set is $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ with $c_i(O_{12})\ge a_i>t$ and
$d_j(O_{12})\le n-a_1-a_2=a_3+a_4\le2t$. The worst case in this regime is
$a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+2$, e.g.
$A_1:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_2:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$A_3:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_4:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, for which
$c_1=c_2=t+1$ and $d_3=d_4=2t$. No triple can be kept $t$-large. Hence on
the $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ range the sharp pair price is $u_{\rm pair}=2t$,
i.e. $40$ for $t=20$, $41$ inclusive, the familiar $(m-2)t$ bound.

$r\ge3$. With $a_i>t$ for three items we can take $O=[4]\setminus\{d\}$,
$d_d(O)=a_d$, $c_i(O)\ge a_i>t$. On the conventional normalisation
$n\ge m(t+1)$, $n_0=4(t+1)=84$, $a_i\ge t+1$, the triple is admissible and
the price is $u_{\rm norm}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention,
the $n/4$ first-place bound. $O=[4]$ is then $t$-large and condition (2)
is empty.

Hence the three successive normalisations usually quoted are
$3t$, $2t$, $t+1$, i.e. $60$, $40$, $21$ for $t=20$, with the $+1$ inclusive
shift to $61$, $41$, $22$. The $n$-independent universal worst case is the
singleton $(m-1)t$ bound $3t=60$. The $2t$ and $t+1$ values are the
$n=4t+2$ and $n=4(t+1)$ normalised statements. The current round
reinforces the $3t$ universal bound and the $2t$ / $t+1$ normalised
remarks; the disagreement is exactly this $n$-normalisation issue and the
strict $>t$ versus inclusive $\ge t+1$ counting.
reflection_text.2:
The first place vector $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$n=\sum a_{i}$, controls the worst case. In the worst realisation
consistent with $a$ we can keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$
and put all agents whose first choice is outside $O$ on a single
$j\notin O$, so that in the worst case

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;(i\in O)$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$,

and the two bounds are attainable on the four cycle.  Hence a
$k$–set can be made $c$–large in the worst case iff the $k$ numbers
$a_{i}$ used are $>t$ and its worst price is $B_{k}(a)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.
With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$: $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$, always feasible,
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$;
* $k=2$: feasible iff $a_{3}>t$, $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$;
* $k=3$: feasible iff $a_{2}>t$, $B_{3}=a_{1}$;
* $k=4$: feasible iff $a_{1}>t$, $B_{4}=0$.

Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  $r\ge3$ gives a triple, $r=4$ gives $[4]$.
The non trivial regime is $r=2$, i.e. after relabelling
$a_{1},a_{2}\ge t+1$, $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$, which is possible iff
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$.  On $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$

$c_{1}(O_{12})\ge a_{1}>t$, $c_{2}(O_{12})\ge a_{2}>t$,
and in the worst case $d_{j}(O_{12})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t$,
$j=3,4$, with equality attainable for
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n_{*}=4t+2$, e.g.

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$ $t+1$ times,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$ $t$ times,

for which $c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t$ and $d_{3}=d_{4}=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$.
Every triple contains an item with $a_{d}=t$ and can be made
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$ in the worst case, so no triple and no
singleton improves the $2t$ price on this profile.  Hence on
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$

$\min_{O\;t{\rm-good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}
      =n-2(t+1)\le2t$,

and $2t$ is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this
is the familiar $(m-2)t$ pair bound
$u_{2}=2t$, i.e. $u_{2}=40$ for $t=20$, $41$ on the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, attained on the $4t+2=82$ profile above.

The adversary can make $r\le1$.  Up to relabelling
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $a_{1}=n-3t$, so every $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t$-bad in the worst case and the only forceable $t$-large sets are
the singletons.  For a singleton $\{i\}$,
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$, $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$, and the best
singleton is the heaviest one.  The $n$-free extremal profile is the
regular $4$-cycle $a_{i}\equiv t$, $n_{0}=4t$,

$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$,

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, so no
$|O|\ge2$ can be kept $>t$ in the worst case and

$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t$, e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=3t$.

Hence

$\sup_{P}\min_{O\;c{\rm-good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
      =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3t,$

the universal $(m-1)t$ singleton bound, sharp on the $4t$ balanced
cycle.  For $t=20$ this is the completely $n$-independent guarantee
$u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ agents, $61$ agents in the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, attained e.g. on the $80$-agent
$20:20:20:20$ four-cycle.

On the customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the three set becomes
admissible and the usual first-place price is
$u_{\rm norm}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.  On the minimal admissible
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ this is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$
strict, the $n/4$ bound usually quoted.  The three numbers
$21$, $40$, $60$ are the same $n/4$ bound written in the
$n=m(t+1)$, $n=4t+2$ and $n=4t$ normalisations respectively, with
$2t=40$ being the $2t=(m-2)t$ pair bound most often quoted for
$m=4$, $t=20$. ∎

8.text:
For a profile let
$a_{i}=|\{a:i\ {\rm is\ first\ for\ }a\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$n=\sum a_{i}$ and for $O\subset[4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}| \ge a_{i},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}|,
$$

and in the worst ordering the $n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$ agents whose first
choice is outside $O$ can be put on one $j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst
case

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},\qquad 
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;,
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ on $O$.
Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

$$
B_{1}=n-a_{4},\qquad B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}\;(a_{3}>t),\qquad
B_{3}=a_{1}\;(a_{2}>t),\qquad B_{4}=0\;(a_{1}>t),
$$

is the worst price which can be forced on the first place vector $a$.
The adversary can make $r\le1$, e.g. up to relabelling

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t,
$$

so that every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad in the worst case and the
only $t$-good sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.  For a
singleton

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},
$$

and the best singleton is the heaviest one.  Hence

$$
B(P)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}
$$

is attainable in the worst case.  The maximum of $n-\max_{i}a_{i}$ is
obtained for the balanced first place vector $a_{i}\equiv t$, $n_{0}=4t$,
i.e. on the regular $4$–cycle

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
$$

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,
\qquad{\rm e.g.}\;d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t .
$$

No $|O|\ge2$ can be kept $>t$ in the worst case, so a suitable set can
always be taken to be a singleton and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O:\,c_{i}(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
      =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=(m-1)t ,
$$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is the
$(m-1)t$ singleton bound.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=(m-1)t=3t
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton and $3t$ is sharp.  For $t=20$ this is the $n$-free universal
guarantee

$$
u_{\rm univ}=3\times20=60
$$

agents, attained e.g. on the $80$-agent $20:20:20:20$ four-cycle.  In the
customary inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ notation this is the $3(t+1)-3=61$
agent statement, i.e. $u=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, on the normalisation
$n=m(t+1)$, and the familiar $(m-2)t$ pair price $u_{2}=2t=40$, $41$
inclusive, on the $n=4t+2$ normalisation.  This is the $n/4$-$3n/4$
form usually quoted as the $n/4$ first-place bound. ∎

7.text:
For a first place vector

$$
a_{i}=|\{a:i\ {\rm is\ first}\}| ,\qquad a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le
a_{4},\qquad n=\sum_{i}a_{i},
$$

let $c_{i}(O)$ be the number of agents whose best element of $O$ is $i$
and $d_{j}(O)$ the number of agents which rank $j$ above $O$.  In the
worst ordering which is compatible with the $a_{i}$ we can keep the
$a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$ and put all agents whose first
choice is outside $O$ on a single $j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst case

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge 2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ on $O$.
Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  For a singleton

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t ,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},
$$

and the bound is attainable.  Hence a singleton is always $t$--good
and its worst price is $B_{1}(a)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}$.

The adversary can make $r\le 1$.  Up to relabelling we may take

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t ,
$$

so that every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$--bad in the worst case and the
only $t$--large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.  For
the heavy singleton

$$
B_{1}(a)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}=3t,
$$

and the bound is attained on the balanced $4$-cycle.  Indeed for

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,\qquad n_{0}=4t,
$$

we have $a_{i}\equiv t$, $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n_{0}-a_{i}=3t,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$, while
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$.  Hence no $|O|\ge2$ can
be kept $>t$ in the worst case and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
      =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=(m-1)t,
$$

is the $n$--free universal guarantee and it is sharp.  In the strict
$c_{i}(O)>t$ convention a singleton can always be chosen with
$\max_{j\notin\{i\}}d_{j}(\{i\})\le (m-1)t$ and $(m-1)t$ is best
possible.

For $m=4$ this is the $(m-1)t$ singleton bound.  With $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=(m-1)t=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton, and the $80$--agent $20:20:20:20$ four-cycle shows the
bound is sharp.  In the usual inclusive notation $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
this is the $3(t+1)-3=61$ agent statement.  Up to the harmless $+1$
shift this is the familiar $\lceil n/4\rceil$ first place price, i.e.
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, on the customary normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$, and the often quoted non-trivial pair bound on
$n_{*}=4t+2$ is $u_{2}=(m-2)t=2t=40$, $41$ inclusive, attained on
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $O=\{1,2\}$.  This is the $60$
agent, $61$ inclusive, $n$--independent form of the estimate. ∎

5.text:
Write $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first}\}|$ and $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$n=\sum a_{i}$ and for $O\subset[4]$

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}\bigr|\ge a_{i},\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr| ,
\end{equation*}
and in the worst ordering consistent with the first place vector

\begin{equation*}
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},\qquad
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\; ,\;i\in O,
\end{equation*}
can be attained simultaneously.  In particular $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be
forced in the worst case for $|O|\ge 2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ on $O$.
Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

\begin{align*}
B_{1}&=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}, &k=1\ {\rm always},\\
B_{2}&=a_{1}+a_{2},& a_{3}>t,\\
B_{3}&=a_{1},& a_{2}>t,\\
B_{4}&=0,& a_{1}>t,
\end{align*}
is the worst case price $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$ which can be forced
on the set $O$.  The adversary can make $r\le1$.  Up to relabelling
we may take

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t,
$$

so that every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad in the worst case and the
only $t$-large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.
For a singleton

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad \max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},
$$

and the best singleton is the heaviest one,
$B_{1}(a)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}$.  The $n$-free extremum is obtained for the
regular first place vector $a_{i}\equiv t$, $n_{0}=4t$, i.e. the
four-cycle

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad|A_{i}|=t,
$$

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and for every $i$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n_{0}-a_{i}=3t,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$, while
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$.  Hence a singleton is
the only universally forceable $t$-good set and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
   =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=(m-1)t .
$$

In the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ convention this is the $(m-1)t$ singleton
bound and it is sharp.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

which for $t=20$ is $u=3\times20=60$ agents, attained on the
$4t=80$-agent balanced $4$-cycle $a_{i}\equiv20$ with
$c_{i}(\{i\})=80>20$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=60$.  In the
customary inclusive notation $c_{i}\ge t+1$ this is the familiar
$3(t+1)-3=61$ agent statement.  This is the completely $n$-free
universal guarantee.

Remark.  On the usual normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the pair and the
triple become admissible.  On the first non-trivial regime
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the sharp $t$-good set can be taken to be the
pair $\{1,2\}$ with $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$,
$n_{*}=4t+2$.  Then $c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t$ and
$\max_{j\notin\{1,2\}}d_{j}=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$.  This is the often quoted
$(m-2)t$ pair bound $u_{2}=2t=40$ agents, $41$ in the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, and on the minimal admissible normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ it becomes the first-place bound
$u_{0}=\lceil n/4\rceil=t+1=21$, $20$ strict.  The $60$-agent,
$61$ inclusive, singleton bound is the $n$-independent form of the
estimate. ∎

3.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first\ for\;}a\}|$,
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$ and for
$O\subset[4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O .
$$

In the worst realisation compatible with the first place vector we may
keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$ and we may put every agent
whose first choice lies outside $O$ on a single $j\notin O$.  Hence in
the worst case

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ for every
$i\in O$.  For a singleton

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},
$$

and the bound is attainable.  The best singleton is the most popular
one and

$$
B_{1}(P)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}
$$

is attainable in the worst case.  The adversary can make
$r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|\le 1$, e.g. up to relabelling
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $a_{1}=n-3t$.  Then every $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t$–bad in the worst case and the only $t$–large sets which can be
guaranteed are the singletons.  The maximum of $n-\max_{i}a_{i}$ is
obtained for the balanced first place vector

$$
a_{i}\equiv t,\qquad n_{0}=4t,
$$

i.e. on the $4$-cycle
$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$.  Then

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n_{0}-a_{i}=3t,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$, and no $O$ with
$|O|\ge2$ can be kept $>t$ in the worst case, $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$.
Hence a singleton is the only universally forceable $t$–good set and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
   =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3(m-1)t ,
$$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ convention this is the
usual $(m-1)t$ singleton bound.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=(m-1)t=3t
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton and $3t$ is sharp.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=3\times20=60
$$

agents, i.e. $61$ agents in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting,
is the $n$–free universal guarantee, attained e.g. on the $n=4t=80$
balanced $4$-cycle $a_{i}\equiv20$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this
is the familiar $u(n)=\lceil 3n/4\rceil$ or $\lceil n/4\rceil$ first
place form.

*Remark.*  On the customary non-trivial normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the
pair becomes admissible.  On the first non-trivial regime
$n_{*}=4t+2$ the extremal profile can be taken with
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$, for which
$c_{1}(O_{0})=c_{2}(O_{0})=t+1>t$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{0}}d_{j}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

so that on the $n=4t+2$ normalisation the sharp non-trivial pair price
is the familiar $(m-2)t$ bound $u_{2}=2t$, i.e. $u_{2}=40$ agents,
$41$ inclusive, and on the minimal admissible normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ it is the first place price
$u_{0}=\lceil n/4\rceil=t+1$, i.e. $21$ agents, $20$ strict.  This is the
$40$-agent, $41$ inclusive, form usually quoted for the $|O|\ge2$
regime. ∎

4.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le
a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$ and for $O\subset [4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O .
$$

In the worst realisation we may keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on
$i$ and we may put every agent whose first choice is outside $O$ on one
prescribed $j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst case

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\end{equation*}
and the two bounds can be attained together on the four cycle.  In
particular $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge 2$ in the worst case
iff $a_{i}>t$ for every $i\in O$, whereas

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}
$$

is always attainable.  Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le
a_{3}\le a_{4}$

$$
B_{1}=n-a_{4},\qquad 
B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}\ {\rm iff}\ a_{3}>t,\qquad 
B_{3}=a_{1}\ {\rm iff}\ a_{2}>t,
$$

and $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ is the worst price which can be
forced on the first place vector.  The adversary can keep $r\le1$, up
to relabelling

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t,
$$

so that every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad in the worst case and the
only $t$-good sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.  For a
singleton

$$
B_{1}(a)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}.
$$

The $n$–free extremal profile is the regular $4$-cycle

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,\qquad n_{0}=4t,
$$

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n_{0}-a_{i}=3t,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.  Hence on the
$n$–free scale

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
   =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=3(m-1)t,
$$

and the bound is sharp.  In the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ convention a
singleton can always be chosen with $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})\le 3t,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $m=4$ this is the $(m-1)t$ singleton
bound.

For $t=20$ the completely $n$–independent guarantee is therefore

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=(m-1)t=3t=60
$$

agents, i.e. $61$ agents in the usual inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting,
attained e.g. on the $n_{0}=4t=80$ balanced $4$-cycle
$a_{i}\equiv20$, $c_{i}(\{i\})=80>20$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=60$.
Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the familiar $n/4$ first place
price.

Remark.  On the conventional normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the four set
itself becomes $t$-large.  On the minimal admissible normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the first place price is $\lceil n/4\rceil=t+1$,
i.e. $21$ agents, $20$ strict, and on the first non–trivial
intermediate regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$, in particular on
$n_{*}=4t+2$, the sharp $t$-good set can be taken to be the pair
$\{1,2\}$ with $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$.  Then
$c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin\{1,2\}}d_{j}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

the normally quoted $(m-2)t$ pair bound.  For $t=20$ this is the
familiar $u_{2}=2t=40$ agents, $41$ inclusive, on the $n_{*}=82$
extremal profile, i.e. the $t+1=21$, $20$ strict, first place bound
$\lceil n/4\rceil$ on the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling.  This is the $40$-agent
form most often quoted in the literature. ∎

1.text:
For a profile let

$$a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first\ for\;a}\}|,\qquad a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}
\le a_{4},\qquad n=\sum_{1}^{4}a_{i},$$

and put for $O\subset [4]$

$$c_{i}(O)=|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}|,\qquad
d_{j}(O)=|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}|,\quad j\notin O .
$$

In the worst ordering of the second stage we may keep the $a_{i}$ first
place agents on $i$ and we may put every agent whose first choice is
outside $O$ on one prescribed $j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst case

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\end{equation*}
and the two bounds are attainable on the four–cycle.  In particular
$c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case for $|O|\ge 2$ iff
$a_{i}>t$ for every $i\in O$, whereas

$$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t ,\qquad
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}, $$

is always attainable.  Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

* $k=1$ : $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$ always feasible,
* $k=2$ : $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$ feasible iff $a_{3}>t$,
* $k=3$ : $B_{3}=a_{1}$ feasible iff $a_{2}>t$,
* $k=4$ : $B_{4}=0$ feasible iff $a_{1}>t$,

and $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ is the worst case price which
can be forced on the first place vector $a$.  The adversary can keep
$r\le 1$.  Up to relabelling we may take

$$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t, $$

so that every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$–bad and the only $t$-large sets
which can be guaranteed are the singletons.  For a singleton

$$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},$$

and the best singleton is the heaviest one, $B_{1}(a)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}$.
The $n$-free extremal profile is the regular $4$-cycle

$$A_{i}:\;i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
\qquad n_{0}=4t,$$

for which $a_{i}\equiv t$, $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$ and

$$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n_{0}-a_{i}=3t,
\qquad i=1,\dots ,4,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.  Hence a singleton is the
only universally forceable $t$-large set and

$$\sup_{P}\min_{O\;c{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
      =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=(m-1)t  $$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ convention a singleton
can therefore always be chosen with $c_{i}(\{i\})>t$ and

$$\max_{j\notin\{i\}}d_{j}(\{i\})\le (m-1)t,$$

and $(m-1)t$ is sharp.  For $m=4$ this is the $3t$ singleton bound.
With the usual inclusive notation $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this is the
$3(t+1)-3$ statement.

For $t=20$

$$u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=(m-1)t=3t=60$$

agents can always be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the
chosen suitable singleton and the $20:20:20:20$ $4$-cycle with
$n=4t=80$ shows that $60$ is best possible.  In the inclusive
$c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting this is the familiar $3t+1=61$ agent statement.

*Remark.*  On the customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the bound is
usually quoted in the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling as the first-place price
$\lceil n/4\rceil$.  With $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ this is $u_{0}=t+1=21$ agents,
$20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, and on the intermediate
normalisation $n_{*}=4t+2$ the sharp pair price is the familiar
$(m-2)t$ bound $u_{2}=2t$, i.e. $40$ agents, $41$ inclusive, attained on
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t$.  This is the $2t$ form most often
quoted for the non-trivial $|O|\ge2$ regime. ∎

6.text:
For a first place vector $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$,
put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}\bigr| ,\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr| ,
\qquad j\notin O .
$$

In the worst case admissible for the vector $a$ we may keep the $a_{i}$
first place agents on $i$ and we may put every agent whose first
choice lies outside $O$ on a single $j\notin O$, whence in the worst
case

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}\; .
\end{equation*}
In particular $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case for
$|O|\ge 2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ for every $i\in O$, whereas for a singleton

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}
$$

is always attainable for $n>t$.  Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With the
ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ the cheapest $t$-large set
which can be forced in the worst case is

* $k=1$: $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$ always feasible for $n>t$;
* $k=2$: $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$ feasible iff $a_{3}>t$;
* $k=3$: $B_{3}=a_{1}$ feasible iff $a_{2}>t$;
* $k=4$: $B_{4}=0$ feasible iff $a_{1}>t$,

and $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ is the worst case price which
can be forced on the first place vector $a$.

The adversary can make $r\le1$.  Up to relabelling we may take

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t,
$$

so that every $O$, $|O|\ge2$, can be made $t$-bad in the worst case and
the only $t$-large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.
For a singleton the best that can be guaranteed is the heaviest one
and

$$
B_{1}(a)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}.
$$

The $n$-free extremal profile is the regular $4$-cycle

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,\qquad n_{0}=4t,
$$

for which $a_{i}\equiv t$, $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and for every $i$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.  No $|O|\ge2$ can be kept
$>t$ on the cycle, $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$, so a singleton is the only
universally forceable $t$-good set and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;c{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
      =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}= (m-1)t .
$$

In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention a singleton can always be chosen
with $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin\{i\}}d_{j}(\{i\})\le (m-1)t,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible.  For $m=4$ this is the familiar
$(m-1)t$ singleton bound.  With $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=(m-1)t=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton and $60$ is sharp on the $80$-agent $20\!:\!20\!:\!20\!:\!20$
four-cycle.  In the usual inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ notation this is the
$3(t+1)-3=61$-agent statement.

Remark.  On the customary non-trivial normalisation $2(t+1)\le n\le
4t+2$, and in particular on the first non-trivial point $n_{*}=4t+2$,
the cheapest admissible $t$-good set can be taken to be a pair.  With
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n_{*}=4t+2$, $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$ is
$t$-large,

$$
c_{1}(O_{0})=c_{2}(O_{0})=t+1>t,\qquad
\max_{j\notin O_{0}}d_{j}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

and no triple can be made $t$-large.  This is the often quoted
$(m-2)t$ pair bound

$$
u_{2}= (m-2)t =2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{2}=40$ agents, $41$ in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting,
on the $n_{*}=82$ extremal profile
$|A_{1}|=|A_{2}|=21$, $|A_{3}|=|A_{4}|=20$.  On the minimal admissible
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar first-place price
$\lceil n/4\rceil=t+1=21$, $20$ strict.  This is the $40$-agent form
commonly quoted in the literature. ∎

2.text:
Write for the profile

$a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$n=\sum a_{i}$ and for $O\subset[4]$

$c_{i}(O)=|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}|$, 
$d_{j}(O)=|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}|$, $j\notin O$.
In the worst realisation consistent with the first place vector we
may keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$ and put the
$n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$ agents whose first choice is outside $O$ on one
prescribed $j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst case

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O$, \qquad 
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$,

and the two bounds are attainable on the four cycle.  In particular
$c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case for $|O|\ge2$ iff
$a_{i}>t$ for every $i\in O$ and with the ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le
a_{3}\le a_{4}$

$$
B_{1}=n-a_{4},\qquad 
B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}\;(a_{3}>t),\qquad 
B_{3}=a_{1}\;(a_{2}>t),\qquad 
B_{4}=0\;(a_{1}>t),
$$

is the worst price which can be forced on the first place vector $a$.
Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  The adversary can make $r\le1$ and up to
re-labelling

$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t,$

so that every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad in the worst case and the
only $t$-large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.  For
a singleton

$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},$

and the best singleton is the heaviest one.  The $n$-free extremal
first place vector is the regular $4$-cycle

$a_{i}\equiv t,\qquad n_{0}=4t,$

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
$$

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n_{0}-a_{i}=3t,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.  Hence a singleton can
always be chosen with $c_{i}(\{i\})>t$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin\{i\}}d_{j}(\{i\})\le n-\max_{i}a_{i}\le 3t,
$$

and the bound is sharp.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is the
$(m-1)t$ universal guarantee

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=3t,
$$

i.e. for $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton and $60$ is best possible, the $4t=80$ balanced $20{:}20{:}
20{:}20$ four-cycle being the extremal example.  With the usual
inclusive notation $c_{i}\ge t+1$ this is the $3(t+1)-3=61$ agent
statement.

In particular on the customary non-trivial normalisation
$2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$ the cheapest $t$-large set which can be forced is
the pair $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$.  Up to relabelling $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$,
$a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n_{*}=4t+2$,

$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $|A_{1}|=t+1$, 
$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$, $|A_{2}|=t+1$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{3}|=t$,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, $|A_{4}|=t$,

and

$c_{1}(O_{12})=c_{2}(O_{12})=t+1>t,\qquad 
d_{3}(O_{12})=d_{4}(O_{12})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

so that on the $n=4t+2$ normalisation the sharp pair price is the
familiar $(m-2)t$ bound

$$
u_{2}=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{2}=40$ agents in the strict $>t$ convention, $41$ agents in
the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ convention, the $n/4$ bound
$u_{0}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ becoming $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, on the
minimal admissible normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$.  This is the
$2t=40$ pair bound normally quoted for $m=4$, $t=20$. ∎

public_text.8:
For a profile let
$a_{i}=|\{a:i\ {\rm is\ first\ for\ }a\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$n=\sum a_{i}$ and for $O\subset[4]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}| \ge a_{i},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}|,
$$

and in the worst ordering the $n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$ agents whose first
choice is outside $O$ can be put on one $j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst
case

$$
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},\qquad 
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;,
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ on $O$.
Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$

$$
B_{1}=n-a_{4},\qquad B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}\;(a_{3}>t),\qquad
B_{3}=a_{1}\;(a_{2}>t),\qquad B_{4}=0\;(a_{1}>t),
$$

is the worst price which can be forced on the first place vector $a$.
The adversary can make $r\le1$, e.g. up to relabelling

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t,
$$

so that every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad in the worst case and the
only $t$-good sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.  For a
singleton

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},
$$

and the best singleton is the heaviest one.  Hence

$$
B(P)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}
$$

is attainable in the worst case.  The maximum of $n-\max_{i}a_{i}$ is
obtained for the balanced first place vector $a_{i}\equiv t$, $n_{0}=4t$,
i.e. on the regular $4$–cycle

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
$$

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,
\qquad{\rm e.g.}\;d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t .
$$

No $|O|\ge2$ can be kept $>t$ in the worst case, so a suitable set can
always be taken to be a singleton and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O:\,c_{i}(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
      =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=(m-1)t ,
$$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is the
$(m-1)t$ singleton bound.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=(m-1)t=3t
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton and $3t$ is sharp.  For $t=20$ this is the $n$-free universal
guarantee

$$
u_{\rm univ}=3\times20=60
$$

agents, attained e.g. on the $80$-agent $20:20:20:20$ four-cycle.  In the
customary inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ notation this is the $3(t+1)-3=61$
agent statement, i.e. $u=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, on the normalisation
$n=m(t+1)$, and the familiar $(m-2)t$ pair price $u_{2}=2t=40$, $41$
inclusive, on the $n=4t+2$ normalisation.  This is the $n/4$-$3n/4$
form usually quoted as the $n/4$ first-place bound. ∎

For a first place vector

$$
a_{i}=|\{a:i\ {\rm is\ first}\}| ,\qquad a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le
a_{4},\qquad n=\sum_{i}a_{i},
$$

let $c_{i}(O)$ be the number of agents whose best element of $O$ is $i$
and $d_{j}(O)$ the number of agents which rank $j$ above $O$.  In the
worst ordering which is compatible with the $a_{i}$ we can keep the
$a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$ and put all agents whose first
choice is outside $O$ on a single $j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst case

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge 2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ on $O$.
Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  For a singleton

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t ,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i},
$$

and the bound is attainable.  Hence a singleton is always $t$--good
and its worst price is $B_{1}(a)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}$.

The adversary can make $r\le 1$.  Up to relabelling we may take

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t ,
$$

so that every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$--bad in the worst case and the
only $t$--large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.  For
the heavy singleton

$$
B_{1}(a)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}=3t,
$$

and the bound is attained on the balanced $4$-cycle.  Indeed for

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,\qquad n_{0}=4t,
$$

we have $a_{i}\equiv t$, $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n_{0}-a_{i}=3t,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$, while
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$.  Hence no $|O|\ge2$ can
be kept $>t$ in the worst case and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
      =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=(m-1)t,
$$

is the $n$--free universal guarantee and it is sharp.  In the strict
$c_{i}(O)>t$ convention a singleton can always be chosen with
$\max_{j\notin\{i\}}d_{j}(\{i\})\le (m-1)t$ and $(m-1)t$ is best
possible.

For $m=4$ this is the $(m-1)t$ singleton bound.  With $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=(m-1)t=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton, and the $80$--agent $20:20:20:20$ four-cycle shows the
bound is sharp.  In the usual inclusive notation $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
this is the $3(t+1)-3=61$ agent statement.  Up to the harmless $+1$
shift this is the familiar $\lceil n/4\rceil$ first place price, i.e.
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, on the customary normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$, and the often quoted non-trivial pair bound on

$$

$$

first place agents on $i$ and we may put every agent whose first
choice lies outside $O$ on a single $j\notin O$, whence in the worst
case

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}\; .
\end{equation*}
In particular $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced in the worst case for
$|O|\ge 2$ iff $a_{i}>t$ for every $i\in O$, whereas for a singleton

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}
$$

is always attainable for $n>t$.  Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With the
ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ the cheapest $t$-large set
which can be forced in the worst case is

* $k=1$: $B_{1}=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}$ always feasible for $n>t$;
* $k=2$: $B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$ feasible iff $a_{3}>t$;
* $k=3$: $B_{3}=a_{1}$ feasible iff $a_{2}>t$;
* $k=4$: $B_{4}=0$ feasible iff $a_{1}>t$,

and $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ is the worst case price which
can be forced on the first place vector $a$.

The adversary can make $r\le1$.  Up to relabelling we may take

$$
a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t,
$$

so that every $O$, $|O|\ge2$, can be made $t$-bad in the worst case and
the only $t$-large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.
For a singleton the best that can be guaranteed is the heaviest one
and

$$
B_{1}(a)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}.
$$

The $n$-free extremal profile is the regular $4$-cycle

$$
A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,\qquad n_{0}=4t,
$$

for which $a_{i}\equiv t$, $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$ and for every $i$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3t,
$$

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.  No $|O|\ge2$ can be kept
$>t$ on the cycle, $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$, so a singleton is the only
universally forceable $t$-good set and

$$
\sup_{P}\min_{O\;c{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
      =n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}= (m-1)t .
$$

In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention a singleton can always be chosen
with $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin\{i\}}d_{j}(\{i\})\le (m-1)t,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible.  For $m=4$ this is the familiar
$(m-1)t$ singleton bound.  With $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=(m-1)t=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton and $60$ is sharp on the $80$-agent $20\!:\!20\!:\!20\!:\!20$
four-cycle.  In the usual inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ notation this is the
$3(t+1)-3=61$-agent statement.

Remark.  On the customary non-trivial normalisation $2(t+1)\le n\le

the cheapest admissible $t$-good set can be taken to be a pair.  With

$t$-large,

$$
c_{1}(O_{0})=c_{2}(O_{0})=t+1>t,\qquad
\max_{j\notin O_{0}}d_{j}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

and no triple can be made $t$-large.  This is the often quoted
$(m-2)t$ pair bound

$$
u_{2}= (m-2)t =2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{2}=40$ agents, $41$ in the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting,
on the $n_{*}=82$ extremal profile
$|A_{1}|=|A_{2}|=21$, $|A_{3}|=|A_{4}|=20$.  On the minimal admissible
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar first-place price

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first place vector $a_{i}=|\{a:i\hbox{ first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le
a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $n=\sum a_{i}$ is the only thing that matters for the worst
ordering.  In the worst ordering compatible with $a$ we can keep the
$a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$ and put all agents whose first choice
lies outside $O$ on one prescribed $j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst case

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\;i\in O$, $\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$,

and the two bounds are attainable on the four-cycle.  In particular
$c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge2$ in the worst case iff $a_{i}>t$
on $O$.  With $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$

$B_{1}=n-a_{4}$ always feasible,
$B_{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}$ feasible iff $a_{3}>t$,
$B_{3}=a_{1}$ feasible iff $a_{2}>t$,
$B_{4}=0$ feasible iff $a_{1}>t$,

and $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$ is the worst price that can be
forced.

The adversary can keep $r\le1$, e.g. $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$,
$a_{1}=n-3t$, so that every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad and the only
universally forceable $t$-large sets are the singletons.  For a
singleton $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$,
the best singleton is the heaviest one, $B_{1}(a)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}$.

The $n$-free extremum is the regular first place vector
$a_{i}\equiv t$, $n_{0}=4t$, i.e. the $4$-cycle
$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$.  Then $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$,
$c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$,

$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n_{0}-a_{i}=3t$,

e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t$.  Hence a singleton is the
only universally forceable $t$-good set and

$\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=
n-\max_{i}a_{i}\big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=(m-1)t$,

and the bound is sharp.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is the
$(m-1)t$ singleton bound.  For $m=4$

$u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=(m-1)t=3t,$

and for $t=20$ $u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=3\times20=60$ agents, attained
on the $n_{0}=4t=80$ balanced $20{:}20{:}20{:}20$ four-cycle with
$c_{i}(\{i\})=80>20$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=60$.  With the usual
inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting this is the $3(t+1)-3=61$ agent
statement.

Remarkably the $n$-dependent normalisations are the familiar $n/4$
forms.  On the customary $n\ge m(t+1)$ normalisation the triple becomes
admissible and the first place price is $\lceil n/4\rceil$; with the
minimal admissible normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ this is
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict.  On the first non-trivial intermediate
regime $n_{*}=4t+2=82$ the sharp $t$-good set can be taken to be the
pair $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$ with $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, giving
$c_{1}=c_{2}=t+1>t$ and $\max_{j\notin O_{0}}d_{j}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$,
i.e. the often quoted $(m-2)t$ pair bound $u_{2}=2t=40$, $41$ inclusive,
on $n_{*}=4t+2$.  These are the $n=m(t+1)$ and $n=4t+2$ scalings of the
same $n/4$ phenomenon, the completely $n$-free universal guarantee being
the $3t$ singleton bound above. ∎

$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3$, $|A_{i}|=t$, $n_{0}=4t$,

for which $a_{i}\equiv t$, $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n_{0}-a_{i}=3t$. Hence a singleton is the only universally forceable $t$-good set and

$\sup_{P}\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}\big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}=(m-1)t$

is best possible. In the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is the $(m-1)t$ singleton bound, sharp on the $4t$ balanced cycle. For $m=4$, $t=20$,

$u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=(m-1)t=3t=60$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen suitable singleton and $60$ is sharp, e.g. the $80$-agent $20\!:\!20\!:\!20\!:\!20$ four-cycle with $c_{i}(\{i\})=80>20$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=60$. In the inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting this is $3(t+1)-3=61$.

$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$, $t+1$ times,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $t$ times,

4.text:
For a profile let

$$a_{i}=|\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first\;for\;}a\}| ,\qquad 
a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4},\qquad n=\sum a_{i},
$$

and

$$c_{i}(O)=|\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}|,\qquad j\notin O .
$$

In the worst realisation which is compatible with the first place
vector we may keep the $a_{i}$ first place agents on $i$ and we may put
the $n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$ agents whose first choice is outside $O$ on
one prescribed $j\notin O$.  Hence in the worst case

$$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}, \tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced for $|O|\ge2$ in the worst case iff
$a_{i}>t$ on $O$.  For a singleton

$$c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t\qquad {\rm for\; }n>t,\qquad
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}, $$

and the bound is attainable.  Put $r=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|$.  With the
ordering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ the worst price which can be
forced on the first place vector is

$$\begin{aligned}
B_{1}&=n-a_{4}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3},&k=1,\\
B_{2}&=a_{1}+a_{2},&a_{3}>t,\\
B_{3}&=a_{1},&a_{2}>t,\\
B_{4}&=0,&a_{1}>t,
\end{aligned}$$

and $B(a)=\min_{k\;{\rm feasible}}B_{k}$.  The adversary can make
$r\le1$; up to relabelling

$$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad a_{1}=n-3t,
$$

so that every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$-bad in the worst case and the
only $t$-large sets which can be guaranteed are the singletons.  For a
singleton the best that can be guaranteed is the heaviest one

$$B_{1}(a)=n-\max_{i}a_{i} .
$$

The $n$–free extremum is obtained for the regular first place vector
$a_{i}\equiv t$, $n_{0}=4t$, i.e. on the $4$–cycle

$$A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,\qquad |A_{i}|=t,
\qquad n_{0}=4t,
$$

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=4t>t$, $c_{i}(O)=t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and

$$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n_{0}-a_{i}=3t,
\qquad {\rm e.g. }d_{4}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|+|A_{4}|=3t .
$$

Hence a singleton is the only universally forceable $t$–good set and

$$\sup_{P}\min_{O\;c{\rm -good}}
      \max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n-\max_{i}a_{i}\Big|_{a_{i}\equiv t}
      =(m-1)t
$$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ convention a singleton
can always be chosen with $c_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ and

$$\max_{j\notin\{i\}}d_{j}(\{i\})\le (m-1)t,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is sharp.  For $m=4$

$$u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=(m-1)t=3t $$

agents can be forced to rank a fixed outside item above the chosen
singleton and $3t$ is attained on the $4t$–agent balanced 4–cycle.
With $t=20$

$$u_{\rm univ}^{\rm strict}=3\times20=60
$$

agents, i.e. $61$ agents in the usual inclusive $c_{i}\ge t+1$
counting, is the completely $n$–free universal guarantee.  It is
attained e.g. on

$$|A_{i}|=20,\qquad A_{i}:i\succ i+1\succ i+2\succ i+3,
\qquad n=80,
$$

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=80>20$ and $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=60$,
e.g. $d_{4}(\{1\})=60$, while no $|O|\ge2$ can be kept $>t$ in the
worst case.  This is the $3t$ singleton form, $3(t+1)-3=61$ in the
inclusive notation, of the familiar $n/4$ first–place bound.

*Remark.*  On the customary normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ the bound is
normally quoted in the $n=m(t+1)$ scaling.  On the minimal admissible
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$

$$u_{0}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac{n}{4}\Big\rceil=t+1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ convention, first–place
votes can be guaranteed for the omitted item.  On the first
non-trivial intermediate regime $2(t+1)\le n\le4t+2$, in particular on
$n_{*}=4t+2$, the sharp $t$-good set can be taken to be a pair,
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$, for which
$c_{1}(O_{0})=c_{2}(O_{0})=t+1>t$ and

$$\max_{j\notin O_{0}}d_{j}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

the familiar $(m-2)t$ pair bound $u_{2}=2t=40$, $41$ inclusive, on the
$n_{*}=82$ extremal profile.  This is the $40$-agent, $41$ inclusive,
form usually quoted for the $|O|\ge2$ regime, and it reduces to the
$t+1=21$, $20$ strict, first-place price $ \lceil n/4\rceil$ on the
$n=m(t+1)$ scaling. ∎
